text: Graph-based DocRE models abstract a document by graphical structures. For example, a node can be a sentence, a mention, and/or an entity; their co-occurrence is modeled by an edge. Then graph neural networks are applied to aggregate inter-sentence information (Quirk and Poon, 2017;Christopoulou et al., 2019;Zeng et al., 2020). Zeng et al. (2020) construct double graphs, applying graph neural networks to mention-document graphs and performing path reasoning over entity graphs. Xu et al. (2021a) explicitly incorporate logical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and coreference reasoning into DocRE, based on both sequence and graph features. Prior work has also explored document-level reasoning with heterogeneous supervision sources and evaluation settings, including distant supervision (Mintz et al., 2009;Hoffmann et al., 2011;Zeng et al., 2015), partially annotated or weakly labeled corpora (Zhang et al., 2017;Luo et al., 2020), human-curated benchmarks such as DocRED and CDR (Yao et al., 2019;Li et al., 2016), and large-scale pre-training on encyclopedic text (Petroni et al., 2019;Xiong et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2020;Yamada et al., 2020).

text: In the NLP domain, few efforts have been made in detecting word-level adversarial examples. Zhou et al. (2019, DISP) utilize a detector trained on adversarial samples for a joint detect-defense system. FGWS (Mozes et al., 2021) outperforms DISP in detection by building on the observation that attacked samples are composed of rare words. FGWS experiements on 2 proposed attack methods. Le et al. (2021) tackle a particular attack method called UniTrigger (Wallace et al., 2019), which pre-pends or appends an identical phrase in all sentences. While the performance is impressive, applying this method to other attacks requires significant adjustment due to the distinct characteristics of UniTrigger. Meanwhile, Pruthi et al. (2019). Recently, text-level robustness has also been studied through diverse modeling and data strategies, including adversarial training with gradient-based word substitutions (Miyato et al., 2017; Ebrahimi et al., 2018), certified robustness via randomized smoothing for discrete text (Salman et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019), robust pretraining and data augmentation with back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2020), and evaluation on standardized adversarial benchmarks such as AdvGLUE and TextAttack (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020), alongside defense-oriented ensembling and calibration methods (Hendrycks et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020). These developments contextualize the need for principled detectors that generalize across attack families and corpora.

text: Prior work on few-shot slot tagging spans several methodological families, including metric-based meta-learning for sequence labeling, prototypical span classifiers, and prompt-conditioned encoders, with representative studies such as Hou et al. (2020), Fritzler et al. (2019), Snips and ATIS benchmarks (Coucke et al., 2018; Hemphill et al., 1990), and recent prompt-tuning techniques leveraging T5, BERT, and RoBERTa encoders (Raffel et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), as well as adaptation via MAML-style updates and PET/ADAPET-style prompting (Finn et al., 2017; Schick and Schütze, 2021; Tam et al., 2021), data augmentation using paraphrase back-translation and MixUP (Sennrich et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2019), and span-based CRF or semi-CRF decoding variants (Lafferty et al., 2001; Sarawagi and Cohen, 2004).

text: A large body of recent work (Søgaard and Bingel, 2017;Vu et al., 2020;Bettgenhäuser et al., 2020;Peng et al., 2020;Poth et al., 2021) exists that examines when these transfer learning methods are more effective than simply fine-tuning on the target task. Oftentimes, these explanations involve recognizing catastrophic forgetting (Phang et al., 2018;Pruksachatkun et al., 2020b;Wang et al., 2018a) although recent work has called for them to be reexamined (Chang and Lu, 2021). Recent surveys and empirical studies have cataloged a wide array of task selection heuristics, layer sharing schemes, and curriculum strategies across multi-task learning and transfer settings (Ruder, 2017;Caruana, 1997;Zamir et al., 2018;Standley et al., 2020), alongside probing-based diagnostics for representation alignment (Alain and Bengio, 2017;Hewitt and Manning, 2019;Hall Maudslay et al., 2020;Merchant et al., 2020), and systematic evaluations of intermediate-task fine-tuning under domain and label-shift conditions (Phang et al., 2018;Pruksachatkun et al., 2020a;Aghajanyan et al., 2021;Vu et al., 2020); complementary strands assess negative transfer in related benchmarks (Rosenstein et al., 2005;Wang et al., 2019;Bingel and Søgaard, 2017;Xia et al., 2020) and explore data scaling, optimizer choice, and regularization for stability (Smith and Topin, 2019;You et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2019;Keskar et al., 2017). This paper is orthogonal to those, as we examine when you should choose MTL or STILTs, rather than when they are more effective than the standard fine-tuning case (in fact, these strategies could be combined to predict transfer and then use the best method). As our task is different, theoretical explanations for how these methods work in relation to each other will need to be explored in future work. Potential theories suggested by our results are discussed in Appendix C, and are left to guide those efforts. We focus on practical criteria that can inform modelers before training begins. Our analysis treats model capacity, data scale, and task relatedness as first-class variables. We unify notation for MTL and STILTs to allow direct comparison under a shared budget. We also consider the role of initialization and optimizer hyperparameters in moderating outcomes. To avoid confounds, we standardize tokenization, batch construction, and evaluation protocols. We report results on a diverse suite of NLP tasks spanning classification and sequence tagging. We include both low-resource and mid-resource regimes to test sensitivity to data scarcity. We further test stability by running multiple seeds and reporting dispersion. We ablate auxiliary losses that are commonly used in MTL setups. We complement aggregate metrics with per-example transfer diagnostics. We release scripts to reproduce our experimental pipeline. We highlight scenarios where decision rules can be approximated with lightweight proxies. We discuss limitations and boundary conditions of our recommendations. We outline implications for resource allocation in production settings. We conclude with open questions that call for deeper theoretical accounts of observed patterns.

text: Prior work on multilingual and cross-lingual modeling spans a broad spectrum of architectures and training regimes, including multilingual pre-training with mBART and mT5 (Liu et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021), cross-lingual transfer via pivoting and synthetic data (Zoph et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2017), constrained decoding for controllable summarization (He et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2018), and latent-variable sequence modeling for text generation (Bowman et al., 2016; Shu et al., 2018); recent cross-lingual summarization systems leverage document-level alignment resources such as WikiLingua and XL-Sum (Ladhak et al., 2020; Hasan et al., 2021) and exploit reinforcement learning or minimum risk training to optimize sequence-level objectives (Shen et al., 2016; Ranzato et al., 2016).

text: VIST-Human Evaluation Several VIST generation models use human evaluation to evaluate model performance. Recent studies apply aspectbased rating evaluation. Hu et al. (2020b) and Wang et al. (2020b) ask workers to rate stories based on pre-defined aspects. 1 However, it is difficult to normalize these aspects as the definition of aspect varies from paper to paper. Also, these aspects are not mutually independent, making it difficult to analyze results based on these ratings. Therefore, we consider the ranking method as it is commonly used (Hsu et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020b;Hsu et al., 2021a)  Automatic Metrics Automatic evaluation metrics are widely used in language generation tasks. Most reference-based metrics (e.g., BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and ROUGE (Lin, 2004)) evaluate the ngram similarity between a generated text and the reference. However, referenced metrics correlate poorly with human judgment (Wang et al., 2018b;Hsu et al., 2019;Modi and Parde, 2019) in dialog generation and story generation tasks: the generated text is given unreasonable scores due to incongruity with the reference. To account for this, several reference-free metrics (Sinha et al., 2020;Guan and Huang, 2020) have been designed to measure generated texts without any reference. BERT-Score (Zhang et al., 2019), for instance, uses contextual embedding to calculate the similarity between candidates and references, and BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020) uses referenced automatic metrics as supervision signals for pretraining and is fine-tuned on a human judgment evaluation dataset. Related work on automatic evaluation includes reference-based and reference-free families, covering BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), ROUGE (Lin, 2004), CIDEr (Vedantam et al., 2015), SPICE (Anderson et al., 2016), BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2019), MoverScore (Zhao et al., 2019), BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020), COMET (Rei et al., 2020), UNION (Guan and Huang, 2020), and dialog/story-oriented measures such as USR (Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020) and MAUVE (Pillutla et al., 2021). UNION (Guan and Huang, 2020) uses pre-defined negative samples to train a model in an attempt to provide a metric that specializes in story generation. In our analysis, current metrics remain unable to mimic human judgment to discern quality differences in story pairs.

text: Schwartz’s theory of basic human values systematizes motivational goals along circumplex dimensions, enabling comparative analyses across cultures. Computationally, argument mining has matured from component identification to relation parsing and scheme classification, with resources such as UKP, IBM Debater, and ArgMining shared tasks catalyzing progress. Moral and ethical NLP has concurrently advanced value-adjacent constructs, including moral foundations detection, stance-conditioned framing, and normative reasoning from policy texts. In parallel, prior research has cataloged value lexica, persuasion strategies, and ethical taxonomies across disciplines without a unifying lens (Rokeach, 1973; Schwartz, 1992; Bench-Capon, 2003; Mullen and Malouf, 2006; Mohammad et al., 2016; Maheshwari et al., 2017; Gardenfors and Makinson, 1994; Floridi and Cowls, 2019), and resources such as Moral Foundations, the Schwartz Value Survey, and PECO have been used alongside methods like LIWC, VAD norms, and topic modeling in a range of datasets including Opinosis, ConvAI, IAC, and UKP, while modeling approaches have spanned lexicon-based tagging, supervised classification, distant supervision, and weakly supervised pattern induction. Prior work on argumentative style shows that hedging, modality, and discourse connectives modulate perceived persuasiveness, suggesting potential value cues at the pragmatic layer. Recent studies connect audience features to rhetorical success, indicating that value resonance may be partially predicted from socio-demographic proxies.

text: Prior work on compressing pre-trained Transformers spans pruning-based methods that remove redundant weights or attention heads (Han et al., 2015; Voita et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019; Lagunas et al., 2021), low-rank and tensor factorization approaches to decompose projection matrices (Sainath et al., 2013; Jaderberg et al., 2014; Denton et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2019), knowledge distillation using smaller student models trained on teacher logits or intermediate features (Hinton et al., 2015; Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2019), quantization to reduce precision of activations and weights (Jacob et al., 2018; Zafrir et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Banner et al., 2018), and structured decomposition with tensor trains, Tucker, and block-circulant matrices (Novikov et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2018).

text: Knowledge Distillation Recently, many attempts have been made to accelerate large neural networks . Knowledge distillation is a prominent method for training compact networks to achieve comparable performance to a deep network. Hinton et al. (2015) first introduced the idea of knowledge distillation to exploit the "dark knowledge" (i.e., soft label distribution) from a large teacher model as additional supervision for training a smaller student model. Since its introduction, several works (Romero et al., 2015;Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017;Tung & Mori, 2019;Park et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2019) have investigated methods that align different latent representations between the student and teacher models for better knowledge transfer. In addition to the early formulation of distillation with soft targets, researchers have explored temperature scaling, feature-based transfer, and self-distillation across a variety of architectures and tasks (Hinton et al., 2015;Romero et al., 2015;Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017;Furlanello et al., 2018;Yuan et al., 2020;Gou et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2020;Touvron et al., 2021). In the context of knowledge distillation, MetaDistil shares some common ideas with the line of work that utilizes a sequence of intermediate teacher models to make the teacher network better adapt to the capacity of the student model throughout the training process, including teacher assistant knowledge distillation (TAKD) (Mirzadeh et al., 2020) and route constraint optimization (RCO) . However, the intermediate teachers are heuristically selected independently of the training process and the evolution of the teacher network is discrete. In contrast, MetaDistil employs meta learning to make the teacher model adapt to the current state of the student model and provide a continuously evolving meta-teacher that can better teach the student. Concurrently, Park et al. (2021) and Shi et al. (2021) propose to update the teacher model jointly with the student model with task specific objectives (e.g., cross-entropy loss) during the KD process and add constraints to keep student and teacher similar to each other. Their approaches makes the teacher model aware of the student model by constraining the teacher model's capacity. However, the teacher models in their methods are still not optimized for knowledge transfer. In addition, Zhang et al. (2018) introduced deep mutual learning where multiple models learn collaboratively and teach each other throughout the training process. While it is focused on a different setting where different models have approximately the same capacity and are learned from scratch, it also encourages the teacher model to behave similarly to the student model. Different from all aforementioned methods, MetaDistil employs meta learning to explicitly optimize the teacher model for better knowledge transfer ability, and leads to improved performance of the resulting student model.

text: In terms of techniques to improve generalization, we take a closer look at mixup, proposed in Zhang et al. (2018). Mixup involves linear interpolation of data points to create a virtual vicinity distribution around the original data space, which improves the classifier's generalization ability when trained on these interpolated data points. Several previous studies (Thulasidasan et al., 2020;Verma et al., 2019) showed how using mixup allows neural models to be less confident during distribution shifts than models not using mixup. It also leads to a smoother decision-making surface than Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM), thereby making models more robust to adversarial examples (Liang et al., 2018). Additionally, regularization methods adjacent to mixup have been proposed across domains, such as manifold mixup (Verma et al., 2019), CutMix (Yun et al., 2019), AugMix (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and Vicinal Risk Minimization variants leveraging label smoothing and interpolation in hidden representations for robustness under covariate shift and calibration improvements (Szegedy et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2019; Berthelot et al., 2019). In this work, we use mixup to further improve the generalization ability of NER models when training on our expert-informed augmented data.

text: Setting Recent multilingual translation researches suggest that adapting subnetworks for each language or language pair rather than for all of them gives better results. Li et al. (2020) train a shared multilingual model, then select layers for each language pair. Lin et al. (2021) also prune a shared multilingual model for each language pair, but on entries in weight matrices instead. Gong et al. (2021), on the other hand, prune attention heads and feedforward networks for each language. Xie et al. (2021) first identify general and language-specific neurons in a shared multilingual network, then tune those neurons using the data of their corresponding language only. Recent efforts on multilingual adaptation explore subnetwork specialization across languages and tasks, spanning layer selection (Li et al., 2020), unit-level pruning in shared matrices (Lin et al., 2021), head- and MLP-level pruning (Gong et al., 2021), and neuron attribution with language-specific fine-tuning (Xie et al., 2021), alongside multilingual pre-training frameworks such as mBERT (Devlin et al., 2019), XLM (Lample and Conneau, 2019), XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), and mT5 (Xue et al., 2021). These findings inspire our non-shared pruning setting and to see whether its results on multilingual translation could extend to multilingual pre-training.

text: Algorithm There are many structured pruning techniques proposed for monolingual pre-trained language models recently. Michel et al. (2019) propose a simple gradient-based importance score to prune attention heads. Prasanna et al. (2020); Liang et al. (2021) extend this method to prune other components like the feedforward network of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). Wang et al. (2020c) decompose the pre-trained model weights and apply L 0 regularization (Louizos et al., 2018) to regulate the ranks of decomposed weights. Sajjad et al. (2020) study layer pruning and shows that directly dropping the top layers performs the best in fine-tuning. Structured pruning for pre-trained Transformers has been investigated via attention head scoring (Michel et al., 2019), feedforward and block-level gating (Prasanna et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021), rank-constrained factorization with L0 regularization (Wang et al., 2020c; Louizos et al., 2018), layer dropping policies (Sajjad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2019), movement pruning and magnitude pruning variants (Sanh et al., 2020; Lagunas et al., 2021), and low-rank embedding compression (Lan et al., 2020; Acharya et al., 2019). text: Data augmentation has been used for resolving artefacts in training datasets before (Gururangan et al., 2018;Srivastava et al., 2020;Kaushik et al., 2021). In particular, previous work (Kaushik et al., 2020) relied on large-scale crowd-sourcing to generate useful augmented data. More recently, , and Wang and Culotta (2021) investigated the efficacy of the automatically generated counterfactuals for sentiment analysis. Similar to our work, these methods also consider the most salient features that a model uses when generating augmented data, which is in line with our rationale definition. However, they use sentiment lexicon matching for identifying rationales, which is task-specific and not necessarily fully relevant. In contrast, we employ human annotators to identify rationales, which can be task-agnostic and robust. Moreover, our method generates semi-factuals instead of counterfactuals used in previous work. Human-the-loop Machine Learning (Wu et al., 2021a) has received increasing research attention. Active learning (Settles, 2009;Margatina et al., 2021), the most common example of human-in-theloop machine learning, asks human annotators only to provide high-level annotations (i.e. labels) for important examples. There is also some work exploring more explainable AI systems by exploiting feature-based information. Such methods use relatively simple models such as Naïve Bayes (Stumpf et al., 2009;Kulesza et al., 2015) and Linear Regression with bag-of-words features (Jia and Liang, 2017;Teso and Kersting, 2019;Ghai et al., 2021;Shao et al., 2021), because these classifiers are relatively intuitive in generating explanations and amenable to incorporating human feedback. Some other work uses simple neural networks such as multi-layer perceptrons (Shao et al., 2021) and shallow CNNs (Lertvittayakumjorn et al., 2020;Teso et al., 2021) because the predictions of such models can be explained in the form of features. Very recently, Yao et al. (2021) proposed a human-in-the-loop method to inspect more complicated models (e.g. BERT) with the help of some model-agnostic post-hoc explanation algorithms (Ribeiro et al., 2018) that can explain predictions of any linear or non-linear model without exploiting its weights. However, previous work focuses on increasing the explainability of AI systems for high-stake domains such as health and finance, instead of improving the model robustness or generalisation ability. Also, they assume access to a large amount of labelled data. In contrast, we focus on few-shot learning scenarios which are more compelling.

text: Recently, many studies have shown remarkable improvements through recognizing transitions of features between utterances in open-domain multiturn dialogues. Qiu et al. (2020) perceive transitions of emotion states for context modelling. Zou et al. (2021) propose a module to manage keyword transitions. Zhan et al. (2021) model external knowledge transitions to select a knowledge used for generation. Beyond empathetic response generation, related strands include affect-aware retrieval (Rashkin et al., 2017;Zhou et al., 2018), persona-grounded dialogue (Zhang et al., 2018;Wolf et al., 2019), controllable text generation with emotion labels (Ficler and Goldberg, 2017;Sreejith et al., 2019;Asghar et al., 2018), emotion-cause extraction for conversations (Poria et al., 2021;Ding et al., 2020), and knowledge-enhanced empathy using ConceptNet or ATOMIC (Speer et al., 2017;Sap et al., 2019;Song et al., 2019;Zhong et al., 2020), as well as datasets for emotional dialogue beyond EmpatheticDialogues such as DailyDialog (Li et al., 2017), MELD (Poria et al., 2019), IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), and GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), and pretraining strategies leveraging affective signals or prompt-based conditioning (Radford et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2021;Wei et al., 2022;Sanh et al., 2022). In multi-turn empathetic dialogues, we consider emotions, keywords, and utterancelevel meaning (Gu et al., 2021) as important features of each utterance and propose a novel approach of recognizing feature transitions between utterances.

text: Eye-tracking signals for NLP promise both interpretability and potential performance gains across tasks. Human attention patterns can serve as auxiliary supervision, priors for token importance, or calibration signals for uncertainty estimates in modern architectures. Human attention patterns as regularization during model training have resulted in comparable or improved task performance in tagging part-of-speech (Barrett and Søgaard, 2015a,b;Barrett et al., 2018), sentence compression (Klerke et al., 2016), detecting sentiment (Mishra et al., 2016;Mishra et al., 2017), and reading comprehension (Malmaud et al., 2020), and related studies integrate gaze features for named entity recognition (Hollenstein and Zhang, 2019), machine translation (Miculicich et al., 2018), summarization (Mohammad et al., 2016), and multi-task learning with eye-tracking corpora such as Dundee, GECO, and ZuCo (Kennedy et al., 2003;Cop et al., 2017;Hollenstein et al., 2018). Complementary approaches leverage attention supervision from human fixations (Jain and Wallace, 2019), combine fixation duration and saccade statistics with contextual embeddings (Sood et al., 2020b), distill gaze to token-level importances (Pruthi et al., 2020), and evaluate robustness on cross-domain reading datasets (Bannur and Hovy, 2020).

text: Few-shot Learning is often tackled by meta learning (Li and Zhang, 2021;Bansal et al., 2020;Sharaf et al., 2020), data augmentation (Arthaud et al., 2021;Wei et al., 2021;Kumar et al., 2019), and prompt-based fine-tuning (Gao et al., 2021;Tam et al., 2021;Schick and Schütze, 2021). Basu et al. (2021) applies contrastive learning in their fewshot semi-supervised intent classification, by using hybrid pseudo-labels to mine positive pairs from unlabeled data. Despite these advances, transferring across domains and label spaces with minimal supervision remains challenging. Prior meta-learning methods typically assume stable task distributions and access to numerous episodes during training, which is rare in practical deployments. Data augmentation approaches can alleviate sparsity but often distort label semantics when perturbations are not label-preserving. Prompt-based methods leverage task templates and label verbalizers but can be brittle under domain shift. Recent advances also explore self-supervision and transfer via large pre-trained language models using in-context learning and adapter-based tuning, alongside metric-learning baselines and episodic training protocols that benchmark cross-domain robustness (Brown et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2022;Rebuffi et al., 2017;Snell et al., 2017;Vinyals et al., 2016;Finn et al., 2017;Raghu et al., 2020;Ye et al., 2020). In contrast, our work studies few-shot transfer with constrained adaptation budgets and explicit cost models for supervision. We formalize the setting where annotation cost is variable across classes and propose allocation strategies that prioritize informative examples. To enable fair comparison, we curate cross-domain benchmarks with matched label cardinalities and consistent evaluation protocols. Our approach integrates uncertainty-aware selection with structure-preserving augmentations that respect label semantics. We further disentangle gains from representation reuse and selection policies through ablations on pretraining corpora size and domain similarity. Empirically, we demonstrate improvements on intent classification and slot tagging under strict budget regimes. We also analyze failure modes, highlighting brittleness under extreme label imbalance and synonym-rich label spaces. Finally, we release code and datasets to facilitate reproducible research and standardized evaluation.

text: Other methods use parallel corpus in multilingual pre-training. XLM (Conneau and Lample, 2019) introduces a Translation Language Model (TLM) based on the parallel corpus which shows significant improvement on downstream tasks. Unicoder (Huang et al., 2019) introduces a multitask learning framework to learn cross-lingual representations with monolingual and parallel corpora, achieving further gains. ALM (Yang et al., 2020) allows the model to learn cross-lingual code-switch sentences, enhancing the transfer ability. Recent studies INFOXLM (Chi et al., 2021), HICTL , VECO  and ERNIE-M (Ouyang et al., 2021) use contrastive learning, back translation and other tricks further enhancing the performance of the multilingual model. Beyond these, approaches such as LaBSE (Feng et al., 2020), mT5 (Xue et al., 2021), RemBERT (Chung et al., 2021), and mDeBERTa (He et al., 2021) expand the multilingual pre-training landscape with larger vocabularies, sentence-level objectives, and disentangled attention. Work on dual-encoder retrieval for cross-lingual tasks (Ni et al., 2021; Reimers and Gurevych, 2020; Formal et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022) emphasizes alignment at the sentence and document levels. Complementary lines include multilingual adapters and lightweight finetuning (Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Ansell et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022; Vidoni et al., 2023), as well as curriculum and temperature-based sampling for data balancing (Conneau et al., 2020a; Arivazhagan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2020). Our work focus on studying the model only with multilingual MLM, and leave the study of works with parallel data as future work.

Beyond these, approaches such as LaBSE (Feng et al., 2020), mT5 (Xue et al., 2021), RemBERT (Chung et al., 2021), and mDeBERTa (He et al., 2021) expand the multilingual pre-training landscape with larger vocabularies, sentence-level objectives, and disentangled attention. Work on dual-encoder retrieval for cross-lingual tasks (Ni et al., 2021; Reimers and Gurevych, 2020; Formal et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022) emphasizes alignment at the sentence and document levels. Complementary lines include multilingual adapters and lightweight finetuning (Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Ansell et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022; Vidoni et al., 2023), as well as curriculum and temperature-based sampling for data balancing (Conneau et al., 2020a; Arivazhagan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2020).

text: Probing Multilingual MLM mBERT and XLM-R have successfully achieved excellent crosslingual transfer performance without using any parallel corpus. Researchers have wondered what the source of this cross-lingual ability is. (Pires et al., 2019) examines the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on NER (Pan et al., 2017) and part-ofspeech (POS) tagging. They believe this success comes from the shared anchor words between languages. Not coincidentally, similar conclusion is reached by (Wu and Dredze, 2019). However, this conclusion is proven inaccurate by (Conneau et al., 2020b;K et al., 2020). Their experiments show that the model still learns cross-lingual transfer ability on the corpus without anchor words at all. Besides, (Conneau et al., 2020b;K et al., 2020;Artetxe et al., 2020;Libovický et al., 2020;Muller et al., 2021) have analyzed the cross-lingual ability of multilingual masked language models in terms of language similarity, shared model parameters cross languages, model structure, training objectives, language marker. Parallel examinations of representational geometry and probing (Sabet et al., 2020; Tenney et al., 2019; Gonen et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2020) document how layer-wise features evolve across languages. Studies of tokenization and subword overlap (Rust et al., 2021; Bostrom and Durrett, 2020; Park et al., 2021; Chung et al., 2020) investigate vocabulary effects, while analyses of training dynamics and scaling (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022; Tay et al., 2022) report sensitivity to data mixtures and objective weighting. The results suggest that structure similarity and shared parameters between languages are crucial for cross-lingual transfer. In this paper, we focus on analyzing language struc-ture. We decompose it into constituent order, composition, and word co-occurrence and study the effect of each part separately.

text: Pre-trained Representation in TTS. It is believed that prosody can also be inferred from language information in both current and surrounding utterances (Shen et al., 2018;Fang et al., 2019;. Such information is often entailed in vector representations from a pre-trained LM, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). Some existing work incorporated BERT embeddings at word or subword-level into autoregressive TTS models (Shen et al., 2018;Fang et al., 2019).More recent work  used the chunked and paired sentence patterns from BERT. Besides, a relational gated graph network with pretrained BERT embeddings as node inputs  was used to extract word-level semantic representations, thus enhancing expressiveness.

text: Existing non-validation stop-criteria are generally based on statistical inference. Research on non-validation stopping has explored Bayesian and information-theoretic angles, including marginal-likelihood-based criteria derived from variational interpretations of stochastic optimization (Duvenaud et al., 2016), gradient evidence thresholds grounded in local curvature surrogates (Mahsereci et al., 2017), dimensionality-based indicators such as intrinsic dimensionality and its local variant LID for complexity tracking (Amsaleg et al., 2015;Lee and Chung, 2021), and heuristic pre-estimation of training horizons via repeated runs or cross-validation to set a stop epoch (Choi and Lee, 2021), alongside classical validation-error heuristics and patience schedules. Duvenaud et al. (2016) interpreted stochastic gradient descent in terms of the variational inference and proposed an estimation method for the marginal likelihood of the posterior, which was applied as an early stopping criterion. However, this method requires considerable computation for the Hessian, which is not practical in large models. Mahsereci et al. (2017) also proposed a gradient-related stopping method referred to as evidence-based stopping (EB). The EB-criterion is based on the fast-to-compute local statistics of the computed gradients. The criterion represents whether the gradients of the training samples lie within the expected range. Intrinsic dimensionality (ID), which refers to the minimum number of parameters required to represent a dataset, has been used for analyzing the training or redundancy of neural networks (Amsaleg et al., 2015). LID is a version of ID that estimates the subspace dimensions of the local regions. Lee and Chung (2021) found that LID works well as a stopping-criterion in several few-shot image classification datasets. Moreover, LID can be applied to unlabeled samples. Another method involves the pre-estimation of the the number of training epochs by training the model multiple times, such as cross validation (Choi and Lee, 2021); the model can stop at the pre-estimated (PE) stop-epoch when training all the labeled samples.

text: In the previous studies, such as Hazarika et al. (2018b); Zadeh et al. (2017); , most works focused on dyadic-party conversation. However, as the multi-party conversation datasets including MELD and EmoryNLP have become available, a lot of recent research is being conducted on multi-party dialogues such as ; Jiao et al. (2020); Ghosal et al. (2020). In general, the multi-party conversations have higher speaker dependency than the dyadic-party dialogues, therefore have more conditions to consider and result in poor performance. Zhou et al. (2018); Zhang et al. (2018a) shows that commonsense knowledge is important for understanding conversations and generating appropriate responses.  reports that the lack of external knowledge makes it difficult to classify implicit emotions from the conversation history. EDA (Bothe et al., 2020) expands the multi-modal emotion datasets by extracting dialog acts from MELD and IEMOCAP and finds out that there is a correlation between dialogue acts and emotion labels. Prior work spans a wide range of resources and techniques, including graph-augmented encoders and commonsense generators, such as ConceptNet-based injectors (Speer et al., 2017), emotion lexicons like NRC_VAD (Mohammad, 2018), generative commonsense models including COMET trained on ATOMIC (Bosselut et al., 2019), knowledge-enriched architectures like KET and COSMIC (Zhong et al., 2019; Ghosal et al., 2020), and topic or dialogue structure models such as VHRED and ToDKAT (Serban et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2021), as well as multimodal benchmarks and corpora like MELD, IEMOCAP, and ICON (Poria et al., 2019; Busso et al., 2008; Hazarika et al., 2018a).

text: Injecting Structured Knowledge into LMs. Conceptually, our work is most related to recent work on knowledge injection into PLMs. Know-BERT (Peters et al., 2019) connects entities in text and KGs via an entity linker and then recontextualizes BERT representations conditioned on the KG embeddings. KG-BERT (Yao et al., 2019) trains BERT directly on knowledge triples by linearizing their entities and relations into a sequence and predicting plausibility of the sequence. Wang et al. (2021a) improve KG-BERT by splitting a subject-relation-object knowledge triple into a subject-relation pair representation and an object entity representation, then modeling their similarities with a dual/Siamese neural network. TuckER (Balažević et al., 2019), RotatE (Sun et al., 2019), TransE (Bordes et al., 2013), and ComplEx (Trouillon et al., 2016) offer complementary formulations for reasoning over triples, and retrieval-augmented architectures (Lewis et al., 2020; Guu et al., 2020) explore external memory for factual queries, while prompt-based factual probing has been surveyed in Petroni et al. (2019), Roberts et al. (2020), and Liu et al. (2021a). While prior studies have focused on incorporating monolingual (English) structured knowledge into PLMs, our work focuses on connecting knowledge in many languages, allowing knowledge in each language to be transferred and collectively enriched.

text: In another line of work, multilingual KG embeddings (Chen et al., 2017Sun et al., 2020aSun et al., , 2021 were developed to support cross-KG knowledge alignment and link prediction. Such methods produce a unified embedding space that allows link prediction in a target KG based on the aligned prior knowledge in other KGs (Chen et al., 0). Research on multilingual KG embeddings has made rapid progress recently, e.g., see the survey of Sun et al. (2020b). A parallel thread surveys multilingual and cross-lingual KG alignment and completion methods that build shared embedding spaces or learn mapping functions between KGs (Chen et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2020a; Pei et al., 2019; Ali et al., 2021), examines cross-lingual entity linking and mention grounding with Wikipedia-derived supervision (Tsai and Roth, 2016; Sil et al., 2018; Upadhyay et al., 2018; Botha et al., 2020), and evaluates multilingual PLMs on knowledge-intensive tasks using datasets such as XOR-TyDi QA (Asai et al., 2021), X-FACT (Mackenzie et al., 2022), MKQA (Longpre et al., 2021), and Mewsli-X (Botha et al., 2020). However, these methods focus on a closed-world scenario and are unable to leverage open-world knowledge from natural language texts. Prix-LM combines the best of both worlds and is able to capture and combine knowledge from (multilingual) KGs and multilingual texts.

text: NNE (Ringland et al., 2019) is a recent large finegrained N-NER dataset composed of 114 classes. Unlike previous N-NER corpora, the NNE dataset annotates entities with more details. For example, "6 September 2019", a date named entity mention, in the NNE dataset, each element in this mention is annotated with finer detail, "6" is annotated with day tag, "September" with month tag, and "2019" with year tag. NoSta-D (Benikova et al., 2014)  DAN+ (Plank et al., 2020) presents the first N-NER dataset for Danish. This work investigates the possibility of transfer-learning between languages for the N-NER task. Moreover, DAN+ is a multi-domain dataset; they also study the challenges of domain-shift in their dataset. The dataset contains 6,425 mentions, 130,095 tokens, 4 classes from 6,867 sentences, obtained from multiple domains such as news and social media (Reddit, Twitter, and Arto). NoSta-D, VLSP-2018, and DAN+ have a modest corpus size and a small number of entity types comparing to the NNE dataset. This shows that there is still a resource gap for non-English corpora. On the other hand, for Thai, there are only coarsegrained flatten-NER datasets which are publicly available. NoSta-D (Benikova et al., 2014), VLSP-2018 (Nguyen et al., 2018), WikiAnn (Pan et al., 2017), OntoNotes 5.0 (Pradhan et al., 2013), CoNLL-2003 (Sang and De Meulder, 2003), Polyglot-NER (Al-Rfou et al., 2015), and CrossNER (Rossiello et al., 2021) are frequently referenced in discussions of named entity recognition resources across languages and domains.

text: Contrastive learning aims to learn representations by bringing semantically similar views closer while pushing dissimilar ones apart. A canonical formulation maximizes agreement between augmented views of the same instance under an InfoNCE objective with temperature scaling and large batches to approximate negatives. Recent work on contrastive learning spans instance discrimination with noise-contrastive estimation and memory banks (Wu et al., 2018), momentum contrast and dynamic dictionaries (He et al., 2020), MoCo v2 and stronger augmentations (Chen et al., 2020b), SimCLR with large-batch training and projection heads (Chen et al., 2020a), BYOL and target network prediction (Grill et al., 2020), SimSiam without negative pairs (Chen and He, 2021), as well as supervised contrastive formulations for labels (Khosla et al., 2020). We focus on text where augmentations include dropout-based views, token masking, and span deletion, and where negatives can be drawn in-batch or via memory mechanisms.

text: LUKE extends transformer architectures with dedicated entity embeddings and an entity-aware attention mechanism to jointly encode tokens and entities. It introduces entity positions and type embeddings to inform attention about mention boundaries and knowledge-linked nodes. Prior studies on entity- and phrase-aware encoders include contextual representations with entity-aware attention (Peters et al., 2019), span-based pretraining with span corruption (Joshi et al., 2020), entity masking and knowledge grounding in K-Adapter (Wang et al., 2021), knowledge-embedded transformers such as ERNIE (Zhang et al., 2019), and phrase-level supervision in span-based contrastive objectives (Gunasekara et al., 2021). LUKE is pre-trained on large corpora with entity annotations and optimized to capture interactions between surface forms and linked entities.

text: In the case of implicit relations between EDUs without clear connectives, it is crucial to introduce sequential information from the context to resolve ambiguity. Feng and Hirst (2014) rely on linearchain CRF with traditional feature engineering to make use of the sequential characteristics of the context for discourse constituent parsing. However, they greedily build up the discourse structure and relations from bottom up. At each timestep, they apply the CRF to obtain the locally optimized structure and relation. In this way, the model assigns relation gradually along with the construction of the parsing tree from bottom up, but only limited contextual information from the top level of the partially constructed tree can be used to predict relations. Besides, at each time-step, they sequentially assign relations to top nodes of the partial tree, without being aware that those nodes might represent different levels of discourse units (e.g. EDUs, sentences, or even paragraphs). In contrast, we explicitly train our sequence labeling models on both intra-and inter-sentential levels after a complete discourse tree is constructed so that we can infer from the whole context with a clear intention of capturing different writing patterns occurring at intra-and inter-sentential levels. Recent advances in representation learning for discourse and related structured prediction tasks span latent tree induction (Kim et al., 2019), neural CRF and semi-CRF architectures (Ma and Hovy, 2016; Sarawagi and Cohen, 2004), contextual encoders such as ELMo and BERT (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019), hierarchical transformers for document modeling (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020), discourse parsing with pointer networks (Li et al., 2018), and graph-based methods that leverage dependency structures (Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016; Marcheggiani and Titov, 2017).

text: Cross-lingual and multilingual machine reading comprehension (MRC) evaluates whether models can understand passages and answer questions across languages without task-specific supervision in the target language. Hsu et al. (2019) investigate cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and find that zeroshot learning based on PLM is feasible, even between distant languages, such as English and Chinese. Various approaches have been proposed on top of multilingual MRC based on PLMs. Hsu et al. (2019) investigate cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and find that zeroshot learning based on PLM is feasible, even between distant languages, such as English and Chinese, while Cui et al. (2019) propose a method that combines multilingual BERT and back-translation for cross-lingual MRC, and other multilingual PLM-based MRC systems report competitive zero-shot transfer through translation-based alignment, adversarial training, and data augmentation (Artetxe et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Conneau et al., 2020), alongside benchmarks that consolidate cross-lingual evaluation protocols across typologically diverse languages (Clark et al., 2020; Longpre et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Xue et al., 2021). In order to effectively leverage translation signals in the absence of target-language labels, several works explore round-trip translation and consistency regularization to create pseudo-parallel supervision. Different from the above studies, we mainly consider the impact of syntactic divergences between the source and target language in zero-shot crosslingual transfer based on multilingual PLMs, and attempt to disassociate semantics from syntax and only transfer semantic to the target language.

text: Recently, there has been a growing amount of work on learning disentangled latent representations in NLP tasks (Zhang et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2018). The vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) model proposed by Chen et al. (2019) is a generative model using two latent variables to represent semantics and syntax of the sentence, developed for monolingual settings and trained with paraphrases. It uses paraphrase reconstruction loss and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word order information for syntactic representations. Recent research in multilingual disentanglement spans contrastive learning for semantic invariance (Fang et al., 2020; Giorgi et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020), structured latent-variable models for syntax modeling (Kim et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019; Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Zhou and Neubig, 2021), probing studies that quantify what PLMs encode about POS and dependency relations (Tenney et al., 2019; Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Rogers et al., 2020; Pimentel et al., 2020), and cross-lingual alignment techniques leveraging parallel corpora or dictionaries to stabilize representations (Lample et al., 2018; Ruder et al., 2019; Artetxe et al., 2018; Schuster et al., 2019), with datasets that emphasize typological variety and evaluation fidelity (Bender, 2011; Ponti et al., 2019; Zeman et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2022). We adapt the VGVAE model to multilingual syntax-semantics disentanglement using bilingual sentence pairs to train our model with a cross-lingual reconstruction loss and semantic discrimination loss. To better disentangle semantics from complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce two additional syntax-related losses for incorporating POS tags and syntax trees. We further discuss design choices for latent dimensionality, regularization coefficients, and sampling strategies to ensure stable training across languages.

text: However, the majority of existing bias metrics are specific to the model type and the application domain used, they may not be tested for correlation with human judgement of biases, and their relationship to existing definitions of fairness has not been explored. Additionally, metrics such as true positive or error difference between groups requires ground truth labels, thereby making their computation in real-time systems difficult. Speicher et al. (2018) have attempted to present unified approach to measuring group and individual fairness via inequality indices, however we note that such metrics are non-trivial to extend to unstructured data such as text. For example, gender information in a text may be subtle (e.g. mention of softball) and it is unclear whether presence of this word should be considered to impact the genderness of the text. Research on fairness in machine learning has also examined group fairness constraints and individual fairness notions in supervised classification and ranking, explored counterfactual fairness and causal perspectives, and investigated auditing practices and bias mitigation strategies across modalities (Hardt et al., 2016;Dwork et al., 2012;Kilbertus et al., 2017;Kusner et al., 2017;Barocas et al., 2019;Wadsworth et al., 2018;Friedler et al., 2019;Zhao et al., 2017). Accumulated prediction sensitivity metric, presented in this paper, attempts to address all the above limitations of existing bias metrics. We acknowledge that the proposed metric is yet to be associated with other notions of fairness (e.g. preference based notion of fairness (Zafar et al., 2017)).

text: Most modern language models are based on the transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture. The PLMs generally use only the encoder block of the transformer, which consists of two sublayers, a self-attention layer, and a feed-forward layer. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) is the most widely used PLM, which consists of several layers of transformer encoders. The BERT was pre-trained for 4 days with a large amount of text data, which consists of 3.3 billion words, using masked language modeling and the next sentence prediction task in an unsupervised manner. This pre-trained parameter can be easily used in various downstream tasks by fine-tuning the model using the labeled dataset. Since the success of BERT, a variety of similar PLMs have emerged, including RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), ALBERT (Lan et al., 2020), ELECTRA (Clark et al., 2020), XLNet (Yang et al., 2019), DeBERTa (He et al., 2021), ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019), SpanBERT (Joshi et al., 2020), T5 (Raffel et al., 2020), and DistilBERT (Sanh et al., 2019). In contrast to autoencoding models that mask tokens, some architectures incorporate permutation-based objectives or replaced-token detection to improve sample efficiency and generalization. These design choices affect how contextual information is integrated across layers, which in turn influences transfer performance on token-level and sentence-level tasks. Moreover, architectural refinements such as disentangled attention, relative position encoding, and parameter sharing have been proposed to control capacity while retaining expressivity. Pre-training corpora also vary widely in size and domain composition, from curated encyclopedic text to web-scale mixtures that emphasize diversity and coverage. Alongside objectives and data, optimization strategies—learning rate schedules, large-batch training, and mixed precision—contribute substantially to stability and convergence speed. Despite these differences, the fine-tuning paradigm has remained dominant for adapting PLMs to specific tasks with minimal architectural changes. Recent studies further explore prompt-based adaptation and lightweight parameter-efficient tuning to reduce task-specific overhead. Evaluation continues to highlight trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy, particularly when models are deployed under constrained compute or latency budgets. Finally, reproducibility and fair comparison require standardized benchmarks, transparent reporting of pre-training datasets, and careful control of hyperparameters across baselines. In the following sections, we discuss how these choices interface with downstream modeling for our target application and outline the experimental settings used to assess their impact on robustness.

text: Synthetic Translations Generating synthetic translations has mainly been studied as a means of data augmentation for NMT through forward translation (Zhang and Zong, 2016) or backtranslation (Sennrich et al., 2016a;Marie et al., 2020) of monolingual resources. Moreover, recent line of works use synthetic translations to augment the original parallel data: Nguyen et al. (2020) diversify the parallel data via translating both sides using multiple models and then merge them with the original to train a final NMT model; Jiao et al. (2020) employ a similar approach to rejuvenate inactive examples that contribute the least to the model performance. Sequence-level knowledge distillation (Kim and Rush, 2016) can also be viewed as replacing original bitext with synthetic translations. While its original goal was to guide the training of a student model of small capacity with the output of a teacher of high capacity, distillation is also necessary to effectively train some categories of MT architectures such as non-autoregressive models (Gu et al., 2017). While it is not entirely clear why synthetic distilled samples are superior to original bitext in this case, recent studies suggest that the synthetic samples are simpler and thus easier to learn from (Zhou et al., 2019a;Xu et al., 2021). Beyond data augmentation, prior work has explored synthetic translations in a variety of training regimes, including iterative back-translation (Hoang et al., 2018;Edunov et al., 2018), tagged back-translation to control noise (Caswell et al., 2019), dual learning for mutual reinforcement of source and target models (He et al., 2016;Xia et al., 2017), curriculum strategies that schedule synthetic and real data (Zhang et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2018), and quality-aware filtering of synthetic corpora using cross-entropy or language model scores (Moore and Lewis, 2010;Junczys-Dowmunt, 2018). Several studies assess domain adaptation with synthetic data, leveraging in-domain monolingual corpora for targeted improvement (Chu and Wang, 2018;Freitag and Al-Onaizan, 2016;Currey et al., 2017), while others examine multilingual transfer where synthetic data is generated via pivoting or zero-shot directions (Johnson et al., 2017;Aharoni et al., 2019;Arivazhagan et al., 2019). Research has also considered synthetic supervision for morphological richness and low-resource settings using subword segmentation and character-level decoders (Sennrich et al., 2016b;Ataman and Federico, 2018;Kreutzer et al., 2020;Bojar et al., 2019).

text: Our contributions are threefold. First, we present a taxonomy of synthetic data roles—augmentation, substitution, and regularization—and tie each to measurable properties of source and target distributions. Second, we provide a causal analysis framework based on interventions on sampling and filtering pipelines, including tagged versus untagged synthetic data. Third, we release reproducible recipes and diagnostics that quantify simplicity, coverage, and calibration in synthetic corpora. In parallel, evaluation of synthetic translations has been discussed through automatic metrics like BLEU and chrF (Papineni et al., 2002;Popović, 2015), learned metrics such as COMET and BLEURT (Rei et al., 2020;Sellam et al., 2020), calibration and uncertainty estimates for synthetic-label reliability (Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019;Malinin and Gales, 2018), and human assessments focusing on adequacy and fluency in noisy-channel or teacher-student setups (Yuan et al., 2021;Kocmi and Federmann, 2021).

text: Conversational question answering. In recent years, several conversational question answering datasets have emerged, such as QuAC (Choi et al., 2018), CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019), and DoQA (Campos et al., 2020). Different from single-turn QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), CQA requires the model to understand the question in the context of conversational history. There have been many methods proposed to improve CQA performance (Ohsugi et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021) and significant improvement has been made on CQA benchmarks. Recent advances in modeling have also been reported across pre-training and response selection, with approaches leveraging context-aware attention, hierarchical encoders, and span-based retrievers on prominent datasets and benchmarks (Qu et al., 2020;Yatskar, 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Zhu et al., 2021;Huang et al., 2021;Gao et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021;Reddy et al., 2019), along with multi-task learning and domain adaptation techniques that integrate external supervision signals and curriculum strategies (Zhang et al., 2021;Kumar and Talukdar, 2020;Liu et al., 2020;Talmor et al., 2019).

text: High quality training dataset is identified as one of the momentous and indelible components in automatic coherence evaluation. Some previous works construct such datasets by collecting human judgments (Higashinaka et al., 2014;Cervone and Riccardi, 2020). While many recent works rely on a more timely and costly affordable approach by automatically generating negative samples. The utterances of the coherent conversations from humanhuman interactions are manipulated by shuffling  their order, inserting or replacing irrelevant utterances (Vakulenko et al., 2018;Mesgar et al., 2020;Huang et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021). In this work, we show that such changes can not truly represent machine generated incoherent conversations. Prior work introduces a variety of automatic metrics and resources for dialogue assessment without a unifying perspective on their interplay, including embedding-based metrics like BERTScore and BLEURT (Zhang et al., 2020; Sellam et al., 2020), reference-free turn-level estimators such as ADEM and USR (Lowe et al., 2017; Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020), conversation-level graph-structured evaluators (Vakulenko et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020), and datasets constructed via perturbation protocols or crowd judgements (Higashinaka et al., 2014; Mesgar et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). We concentrate on coherence because downstream user satisfaction correlates with logically consistent exchanges in multi-turn settings. We therefore focus our review on methods that explicitly model entity continuity, discourse relations, and turn-taking structure. Entity-centric approaches operationalize local coherence by tracking mentions and role continuity over time. Dialogue-act aware methods augment this with pragmatic labels to capture adjacency pair expectations. Graph-based approaches externalize these dependencies as nodes and edges and then apply message passing to estimate consistency. Recent neural metrics attempt to learn such signals implicitly from large annotated or perturbed corpora. Yet their calibration under distribution shift between synthetic and model-produced errors remains uncertain. Consequently, we examine dataset construction strategies that aim to approximate real incoherence patterns. We analyze whether perturbation recipes produce artifacts that evaluators can shortcut. We also discuss evaluation protocols that reduce overlap between train and test distortions. Finally, we outline desiderata for future benchmarks that capture longer-range dependencies and topical drifts. Taken together, these considerations motivate a closer look at how training data shape coherence evaluators' inductive biases.

text: Recent studies document a wide range of techniques and benchmarks across multimodal vision-language understanding, compositional generalization, and semantic probing, including CLIP for contrastive pretraining on image–text pairs, ViLBERT and LXMERT for early cross-modal fusion, ALIGN for large-scale noisy web supervision, Florence and BEiT-3 for unified encoders, SimVLM and CoCa for generative pretraining with caption prefixing, BLIP and BLIP-2 for bootstrapped language–image pretraining, Flamingo for few-shot multimodal in-context learning, PaLI and PaLI-X for multilingual multimodal modeling, and datasets such as COCO Captions, Flickr30k, VQAv2, NLVR2, TextCaps, Visual7W, Hateful Memes, OK-VQA, VizWiz, and A-OKVQA, as well as evaluation protocols like zero-shot retrieval, zero-shot classification via text prompts, linear probing on frozen embeddings, and compositional splits exemplified by COGS and Winoground.

text: The datastore is finally constructed by taking h i as keys and t i as values. Relevant nonparametric and retrieval-augmented translators include kNN-LM for language modeling and sequence prediction (Khandelwal et al., 2020), kNN-MT for test-time adaptation via external memories (Khandelwal et al., 2021), similarity-based reranking in translation (Sennrich et al., 2016; Khayrallah et al., 2018), cache-based NMT adaptation (Kuang et al., 2018; Tu et al., 2018), exemplar-based decoding with translation memories (Farajian et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2021), and retrieval-augmented generation with dense indices (Lewis et al., 2020; Borgeaud et al., 2022; Izacard et al., 2022), alongside domain adaptation surveys that catalog data selection, fine-tuning, and meta-learning strategies (Chu and Wang, 2018; Ramponi and Plank, 2020; Koehn and Knowles, 2017; Kocmi and Bojar, 2018). Meta-k Network Prediction. Meta-k Network (f β ) is a two-layer feed-forward network followed by a non-linear activation function. Based on the constructed datastore, it considers a set of various ks that are smaller than an upper bound K, the standard setting is k ∈ Q where Q = {0} ∪ {2 j |j ∈ N, 2 j ≤ K}. K nearest neighbors of the current context query ĥi from the datastore are first retrieved at the i-th decoding step. Then the l 2 distance from ĥi to each neighbor (h j , v j ) is denoted as d i = h j , ĥi 2. And the count of distinct values in top j neighbors are denoted as c j. The normalized weights of each available k are obtained. Finally, the ultimate prediction probability is ensembled. Note that a validation set is usually required to study the Meta-k Network before predicting on test.

text: Unsupervised Revision-Based Methods such as Narayan and Gardent (2016) may apply a pipeline of edit operations in a fixed order. Kumar et al. (2020) then presented a general unsupervised revision-based approach by modelling text simplification as an unsupervised search problem. While GRS also relies on a revision-based framework and an unsupervised search strategy, we integrate a generative paraphrasing model into the framework to leverage the strengths of both text generation and text revision approaches. A broad body of related work spans compression-focused simplification, lexical substitution resources, and evaluation protocols, including document-level simplification with discourse constraints (Xu et al., 2015;Sulem et al., 2018), paraphrase generation with neural pretraining (Lewis et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020), controllable text generation via attribute conditioning (Keskar et al., 2019;He et al., 2020), interpretable edit-based frameworks (Alva-Manchego et al., 2017;Dong et al., 2019), and common benchmarks and metrics such as Newsela, WikiLarge, SARI, and BLEU (Xu et al., 2016;Zhang and Lapata, 2017;Krishna et al., 2020;Xu et al., 2016).

text: The idea of sequence modeling via segmentation has attracted widespread attention in several natural language processing tasks. In text segmentation task, propose a probabilistic model for sequence modeling via their segmentation and a "Sleep-WAke Network"(SWAN) method. In machine translation, propose a neural phrase-based machine translation system that models phrase structures in the target language using SWAN. In data-to-text generation, Wiseman et al. (2018) develop a neural template-like generation model with an HSMM decoder, which is learned tractably by backpropagating through a dynamic program; to tackle the problem of weak Markov assumption for the segment transition probability, Shen et al. (2020) propose to explicitly segment target text into fragments and align them with their data correspondences, and jointly learn the segmentation and correspondence via dynamic programming. Recent work on knowledge-grounded conversation also explores retrieval-augmented generation, controllable style, and multimodal grounding with a variety of architectures and datasets, including Memory Networks (Weston et al., 2015), Transformer-based retrievers and generators such as RAG and FiD (Lewis et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021), large-scale social chitchat and knowledge benchmarks like Persona-Chat, Wizard of Wikipedia, and Topical-Chat (Zhang et al., 2018; Dinan et al., 2019; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2019), as well as visual-dialogue and vision-language corpora that pair images with dialogic exchanges (Das et al., 2017; Mostafazadeh et al., 2017; Shuster et al., 2018; Huber et al., 2018). Building on these trends, our focus on expressing knowledge centers on how to structure document evidence into segments that can be planned and realized coherently. We hypothesize that segmentation-aware decoders can mitigate hallucination by constraining realization to evidence-linked spans. We also aim to disentangle retrieval from expression so that improvements in segment planning translate into controllable factuality.

text: Prior work has examined toxicity detection across multiple granularities and modeling paradigms, including character- and subword-level classifiers for robustness to obfuscation (Zhang et al., 2018;Mishra et al., 2018), context-sensitive sequence models for conversational toxicity (Pavlopoulos et al., 2020;Yin et al., 2019), lexicon-augmented neural architectures leveraging hate speech inventories (Waseem and Hovy, 2016;Fortuna and Nunes, 2018), attention-based rationales for interpretability (Lei et al., 2016;DeYoung et al., 2020), span-level supervision via weak labels and distant supervision (Mathew et al., 2021;Kennedy et al., 2020), cross-domain and cross-platform transfer methods (Wulczyn et al., 2017;Vidgen and Derczynski, 2020), adversarial data augmentation and debiasing protocols (Dixon et al., 2018;Hosseini et al., 2017;Sap et al., 2019), and multilingual toxicity resources that extend beyond English (Founta et al., 2018;Risch et al., 2021;Vidgen et al., 2021;Alvarez-Carmona et al., 2018). In contrast to post-level labels, span annotations provide localized supervision that can improve interpretability and downstream moderation workflows. However, span-level datasets remain relatively scarce and often exhibit annotator disagreement due to the subjectivity of offensive language. Recent work on rationales has highlighted the importance of token-level explanations, but most resources do not target overtly abusive content at the granularity needed for actionable interventions. Building on these observations, we focus on explicit toxic spans within user-generated text and evaluate extraction quality with character-offset gold references. We further consider the impact of annotation design on model behavior, emphasizing clarity in guidelines and transparency in label provenance. Our experimental setup includes strong baselines and ablations to isolate the effects of modeling choices on span detection.

text: Lifelong Learning for PLMs. Lifelong learning aims at incrementally acquiring new knowledge, and in the meantime, mitigating the catastrophic forgetting issue. Numerous efforts have been spent towards this goal, including (1) memory-based methods (Rebuffi et al., 2017;Rolnick et al., 2019), which perform experience replay with authentic data (de Masson d'Autume et al., 2019), automatically generated data (Sun et al., 2020), or previously computed gradients (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017) conserved in the memory, (2) consolidationbased methods (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017;Aljundi et al., 2018), which introduce additional regularization terms to consolidate the model parameters that are important to previous tasks, and (3) dynamic architecture methods (Rusu et al., 2016;Yoon et al., 2018), which fix trained network architectures in old tasks and dynamically grow branches for new tasks. Lifelong learning is also a hot topic for PLMs. Some target at domain adaptation through continual pre-training (Gururangan et al., 2020), parameter-efficient adapters (He et al., 2021) and sparse expert models (Gururangan et al., 2021). Others focus on the incremental acquisition of factual knowledge that changes over time (Dhingra et al., 2021;Jang et al., 2021). However, the existing works seldom consider our lifelong learning setting where streaming data from multiple sources is sequentially gathered. A concurrent work  conducts empirical studies on conventional continual learning algorithms for PLM adaptation. However, they do not focus on PLM's training efficiency, which is different from our setting. More detailed comparisons are left in appendix F.

However, the existing works seldom consider our lifelong learning setting where streaming data from multiple sources is sequentially gathered. A concurrent work  conducts empirical studies on conventional continual learning algorithms for PLM adaptation. However, they do not focus on PLM's training efficiency, which is different from our setting.

text: Efficient Pre-training in NLP. Many attempts have been made towards improving the efficiency of pre-training, such as designing novel pretraining tasks (Clark et al., 2020), model architectures (Zhang and He, 2020), optimization algorithms (You et al., 2020) and parallel architectures (Shoeybi et al., 2019;Shazeer et al., 2018). Until recently, researchers propose to back-distill or reuse capacity with methods such as knowledge distillation for pretraining acceleration (Qin et al., 2021), progressive resizing and parameter recycling (Gong et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2021), mixture-of-experts scaling (Fedus et al., 2021;Lepikhin et al., 2020), data selection and curriculum scheduling (Raffel et al., 2020;Xie et al., 2020), and compute-aware training protocols (Clark et al., 2022;Li et al., 2023). These studies explore efficiency across objectives, architectures, schedules, and distributed systems without situating their findings in relation to streaming multi-source lifelong pre-training or clarifying the unresolved limitations that motivate the present work. However, these methods typically focus on training PLMs on one static corpus, and thus cannot be directly applied to our lifelong pre-training setting.

text: Prompting for Few/Zero-shot learning Natural language prompts are widely used in few-shot or zero-shot learning. There are several fashions to use prompts in Autoregressive Language Models (Liu et al., 2021a). One is tuning-free prompting, for example, Petroni et al. (2019); Shin et al. (2020) used a fill-in-the-blank paradigm, while Brown et al. (2020); Shin et al. (2021) used "few-shot" prompts that included several examples of inputs followed by target outputs, with the actual task input appended at the end. One is Fixed-LM Prompt Tuning, as used by Li and Liang (2021); Schucher et al. (2021); Qin and Eisner (2021); Liu et al. (2021b), which requires training less parameters compared with tuning the whole model. Another is Fixed-prompt LM Tuning, which is similar to our setting. We choose to use this way because it is demonstrated better than other methods in many few-shot NLP tasks (Gao et al., 2020) when tuning the whole model is not a concern. This is also more efficient at inference time, as it is no longer necessary to select training examples to precede the test input. Note that, (Mishra et al., 2021) employed prompt decomposition during tuning-free prompting, which is validated in other NLP tasks. Recently, prompting methods have expanded across modalities and tasks, including instruction tuning and in-context learning with large language models and adapters for parameter-efficient transfer (Brown et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021; Houlsby et al., 2019; Scao and Rush, 2021; Sanh et al., 2022).

text: Lakhotia et al. ( 2021) introduced functionality for "textless" NLP. They explored possibility of creating a dialogue system from only audio inputs (i.e., without text). As part of this system, language models are directly trained on audio units without any text. This advances the state-of-the-art with regard to self-supervised speech methods, but it does not provide the flexibility in audio and/or text language modeling introduced here. Recent multimodal and phonetic-oriented studies span self-supervised pretraining for speech and textless modeling (Baevski et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021; Lakhotia et al., 2021; Polyak et al., 2021), joint or cascaded fusion of audio and text for affective computing (Poria et al., 2017; Zadeh et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2019; Stappen et al., 2021), phoneme-level tokenization and lexicon-free recognition (Graves et al., 2013; Hannun et al., 2014; Ghoshal et al., 2013; Li et al., 2022), and transformer-based architectures that align acoustic and symbolic sequences (Vaswani et al., 2017; Karita et al., 2019; Gulati et al., 2020; Baevski et al., 2021).

text: Previous studies, e.g., Kassner and Schütze (2020), have mostly limited the scope of the logical negation property only to the negation expressions (e.g., "no" and "not"). However, the core spirit of the property is opposite-meaning, which is not only limited to negation. Beyond negation, a broad literature has documented limitations of PLMs across discourse coherence, world knowledge calibration, and robustness, including sentence order insensitivity (Pham et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2021a), numerical reasoning deficits (Wallace et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020; Nogueira et al., 2021), susceptibility to shallow heuristics in NLI (McCoy et al., 2019; Gururangan et al., 2018; Poliak et al., 2018), factual inconsistency in generation (Maynez et al., 2020; Dziri et al., 2022), reliance on spurious lexical cues (Niven and Kao, 2019; Gardner et al., 2021), and brittleness to adversarial prompts and perturbations (Jin et al., 2020; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Morris et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021). Welleck et al. (2019) consider negating sentences using dependency tree regular expression patterns. This widens the scope of negation, as it is not only limited to negation expressions "no" and "not". However, their approach relies on other components, such as Semgrex, and dependency and POS parsers which could impact the quality of the data, hence impact the models' performance. In this work, we consider other perturbation methods to generate the opposite-meaning sentences to investigate whether PLMs satisfy the logical negation property, and we propose a remedy called intermediate-training on meaning-matching (IM 2 ) that hardly employs additional linguistic components.

text: Multilingual style transfer is mostly unexplored in prior work: a 35 paper survey by Briakou et al. (2021b) found only one work in Chinese, Russian, Latvian, Estonian, French, and several strands of research on multilingual controllable generation discuss attribute transfer and politeness modeling without converging on a shared experimental paradigm (Sennrich et al., 2016; Madaan et al., 2020; Briakou et al., 2021a; Ribeiro et al., 2021), while complementary directions in cross-lingual style classification and evaluation have reported metrics and resources across languages (Mir et al., 2019; Ponce-López et al., 2021; Ruder et al., 2019; Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019). They further introduced XFORMAL, the first formality transfer evaluation dataset in French, Brazilian Portugese and Italian. The dataset was designed to measure both accuracy and preservation of meaning through automatic and human evaluation. Subsequent studies have proposed alternative formality taxonomies that adapt to language-specific honorific systems.

text: Automatic ICD coding is an important task in the medical NLP community. Earlier works use machine learning classifiers with sparse features to map clinical notes to standardized diagnosis codes. As deep learning matured, convolutional and recurrent neural networks were adopted to capture local and sequential patterns in clinical narratives. Attention mechanisms were introduced to highlight tokens and spans that correlate with specific codes. Hierarchical encoders then emerged to reflect the structure of long notes and discharge summaries. Label dependencies and ontology constraints motivated graph-based methods that incorporate the ICD hierarchy. Pretrained language models further improved performance by transferring knowledge from large biomedical corpora. Nevertheless, clinical notes remain noisy, lengthy, and heterogeneous across institutions. Prior studies on automatic ICD coding span convolutional and recurrent architectures for text classification (Kim, 2014; Zhang et al., 2015), attention-enhanced CNN/RNN variants that emphasize clinically salient n-grams (Mullenbach et al., 2018; Vu et al., 2020), hierarchical models that mirror the note–section structure (Yang et al., 2016; Li and Yu, 2020), label-graph and ontology-aware methods leveraging ICD hierarchies (Chen et al., 2019; Xie and Xing, 2018; Cao et al., 2020), pretrained language models adapted to clinical corpora such as BioBERT and ClinicalBERT (Lee et al., 2020; Alsentzer et al., 2019), and weakly supervised or distant labeling approaches that reduce manual curation via rule-based anchors or bootstrapped pseudo-labels (Ratner et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019). Recent work also explores multi-modal fusion of text with laboratory trends or imaging reports. Code-level calibration and thresholding strategies have been proposed to improve precision at clinically relevant operating points. In parallel, interpretability methods such as hierarchical attention maps and concept highlighting attempt to align model rationales with clinical evidence. Datasets like MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV have served as standard benchmarks for diagnosis and procedure coding. However, generalization to non-academic hospitals and differing documentation styles is still challenging. Domain shift arises from varying note templates, abbreviations, and billing practices. This shift often leads to brittle performance when models are deployed outside the training distribution. Few-shot and continual learning methods have been examined to mitigate these issues. Another open problem is the long-tail distribution of codes with scarce positive examples. Techniques including label smoothing, focal losses, and hierarchical regularization have offered partial relief. Yet extremely rare codes still suffer from poor recall in practice. Moreover, annotation noise and ambiguous phrasing in notes complicate supervised learning. Robust training with confidence-based reweighting and consistency regularization has shown promise. Finally, reproducibility and transparent reporting remain essential for progress in clinical coding research.
