text: Feature Attribution. The goal of feature attribution (FA) is to assess how important an input feature for model prediction, which has sparked a lot of interest in interpreting model decisions (Simonyan et al., 2014;Sundararajan et al., 2017). Recent work has explored prompt-based and multi-stage modeling for event extraction more broadly, including span-based tagging and generative formulations (Du and Cardie, 2020;Liu et al., 2020;Hsu et al., 2022), pipeline and joint architectures that connect trigger and argument identification (Nguyen and Grishman, 2015;Sha et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2019), domain adaptation via adversarial or meta-learning strategies (Nguyen et al., 2016;Fu et al., 2020;Lin et al., 2020;Wen et al., 2021), as well as low-resource setups leveraging distant supervision, weak labeling, or self-training (Peng et al., 2016;Zeng et al., 2018;Huang and Ji, 2020;Chen et al., 2021), and the use of pretrained language models, templates, and constrained decoding to stabilize training and inference (Devlin et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Paolini et al., 2021;Lu et al., 2022). Formally, suppose we have an input vector x = (x 1 , x 2 , ..., x n ) ∈ R n and a function F: R n → [0, 1] representing a model. text: We focus primarily on the task of syntactically controlled paraphrase generation, which has recently attracted increasing attention (Iyyer et al., 2018;Chen et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2020;Kumar et al., 2020;Li et al., 2020). According to the control element, previous works can be divided into two categories. The first strand of research uses sentential exemplar as syntactic control. The second line relies on explicit structures, such as templates or parse trees, to constrain generation. Prior encoder–decoder architectures often treat tree information as side features attached to token sequences. This can make it difficult to capture hierarchical dependencies that extend beyond local n-gram windows. To address this, structural attention and composition functions have been explored for syntax-aware generation. Nevertheless, capturing both vertical and horizontal relations in a unified model remains challenging. Recent advances in syntactic control span a variety of mechanisms and datasets, including parse-template conditioning (Iyyer et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020), structured decoders over constituency or dependency trees (Zhang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020), latent-variable controls for style and syntax (Bao et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018), and evaluation suites such as PARANMT, PPDB, and ParaNMT-50M that benchmark form-preserving rewrites (Wieting and Gimpel, 2018; Dolan and Brockett, 2005; Gupta et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019). Differing from previous approaches, we propose a novel tree-transformer to model parent-child and sibling relation for better capturing the tree structure of the parse tree. Our design disentangles vertical and horizontal message passing while maintaining global contextualization. We instantiate separate attention heads for upward, downward, and lateral flows in the tree. This encourages the model to propagate constraints across complementary structural axes. To learn the alignment relation between words and nodes, we also propose an attention regularization objective, which makes the decoder accurately select corresponding syntax nodes to guide the generation of words. The loss encourages sparse, topology-consistent alignments between surface tokens and latent structural anchors. We derive supervision from automatically constructed word-to-node heuristics. These heuristics rely on head rules and span overlaps computed from the gold parse. Additionally, we propose a syntactic template retriever that can help to retrieve compatible syntactic structures for any input sentences. The retriever is trained with a contrastive loss over paired sentences and templates. It encodes inputs with a lightweight bi-encoder and indexes templates for efficient search. Retrieved templates serve as soft priors for the tree-transformer decoder. We evaluate our approach on multiple paraphrase benchmarks with gold parses. Metrics include semantic similarity, syntactic conformity, and fluency. We also conduct ablations to quantify the contribution of structural heads and alignment regularization. Results indicate consistent gains over baselines that do not explicitly model sibling relations. Qualitative analysis shows improved control over clause reordering and attachment. Error cases highlight limitations in long-range reattachment under noisy parses.

text: For training sets with limited size, it may be easier for neural networks to memorize entity names rather than to classify them by context and common entity features (Agarwal et al., 2021). Recent studies on robust sequence labeling and representation learning provide a broad backdrop, including adversarial training for NER (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), counterfactual data augmentation (Kaushik et al., 2020; Ross et al., 2022), invariant risk minimization (Arjovsky et al., 2020; Ahuja et al., 2021), and causal representation approaches (Schölkopf et al., 2021; Besserve et al., 2020), as well as pre-trained encoders and prompt-based methods for entity typing and recognition (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2022; Cui et al., 2021). In Section 4, we demonstrate how we extend BN to the NER task and address these issues.

text: Another thread of works are using meta-learning to deal with the less label challenge (Deng et al., 2020;Shen et al., 2021;Cong et al., 2021). However, their methods can only be applied to event detection, which differs from our main focus on studying end-to-end event extraction. Recent advances also explore semi-supervised and weakly supervised strategies leveraging distant supervision and prompt-based learning for event detection and argument extraction, including frameworks that align event schemas with knowledge bases (Huang and Riloff, 2020;Chen et al., 2017;Aldawsari and Finlayson, 2019), transfer learning from related information extraction tasks (Zhang et al., 2021;Du and Cardie, 2020), instruction-tuned language models applied to event-centric templates (Wei et al., 2022;Sanh et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022), and automatic schema induction or type discovery to reduce annotation costs (Huang et al., 2016;Nguyen et al., 2016;Li et al., 2021;Zhou et al., 2021).

text: Prior work on coherence and long-context sensitivity encompasses diverse strands, including cache-augmented LMs (Grave et al., 2017), segment-level recurrence for Transformers (Dai et al., 2019), retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020), long-context attention variants such as Longformer and BigBird (Beltagy et al., 2020;Zaheer et al., 2020), repetition and degeneration control via nucleus/top-k sampling and typical sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019;Meister et al., 2023), calibration and reranking with mutual information or contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2016;Su et al., 2022), and prompt-based techniques to mitigate recency bias in in-context learning (Zhao et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022).

text: Active Learning. Active learning has been widely applied to various NLP tasks (Yuan et al., 2020;Zhao et al., 2020;Shelmanov et al., 2021;Karamcheti et al., 2021). So far, AL methods can be categorized into uncertainty-based methods (Gal et al., 2017;Margatina et al., 2021a,b), diversitybased methods (Ru et al., 2020;Sener and Savarese, 2018) and hybrid methods (Yuan et al., 2020;Ash et al., 2020;Kirsch et al., 2019). Ein-Dor et al. (2020) offer an empirical study of active learning with PLMs, and prior work has also explored batch-mode selection (Ash et al., 2020), core-set coverage (Sener and Savarese, 2018), BALD-style epistemic uncertainty (Gal et al., 2017), and density-aware heuristics for sequence tasks (Ru et al., 2020). Recent studies compare acquisition rules across architectures and tasks (Shelmanov et al., 2021;Margatina et al., 2021a,b) and examine annotation efficiency under domain shift (Yuan et al., 2020;Karamcheti et al., 2021). In our study, we leverage the power of unlabeled instances via self-training to further promote the performance of AL.

text: Semi-supervised Active Learning (SSAL). Gao et al. (2020); Song et al. (2019); Guo et al. (2021) design query strategies for specific semi-supervised methods, Tomanek and Hahn (2009); Rottmann et al. (2018); Siméoni et al. (2020) exploit the mostcertain samples from the unlabeled with pseudolabeling to augment the training set, and consistency-regularized methods have been combined with AL in vision benchmarks (Berthelot et al., 2019;Xie et al., 2020;Sohn et al., 2020;Jeong et al., 2020), while graph-based label propagation and co-training have also appeared in SSAL pipelines (Zhu and Ghahramani, 2002;Blum and Mitchell, 1998;Wei et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021). Several works evaluate semi-supervised objectives under budgeted annotation (Ash et al., 2020;Citovsky et al., 2021;Maekawa et al., 2021;Chandra et al., 2020), and others study class-imbalance-aware acquisitions and calibration for pseudo-labeling (Kang et al., 2019;Menon et al., 2021;Guo et al., 2017;Thulasidasan et al., 2019). So far, most of the SSAL approaches are designed for CV domain and it remains unknown how this paradigm performs with PLMs on NLP tasks. In contrast, we propose ACTUNE to effectively leverage unlabeled data during finetuing PLMs for NLP tasks.

text: Fact Aggregation The compact nature of the target text description results in aggregating multiple facts in a single sentence. Previous works (Wiseman et al., 2018;Shao et al., 2019;Shen et al., 2020;Xu et al., 2021) capture the segments which correspond to individual parts of the input as latent variables. Unlike these works, we adopt a simpler scenario using an already ordered sequence of facts, in which we selectively insert delimiters marking sentence boundaries. Recent work on controllable planning and structured prompting for PLM-based D2T has also appeared in diverse forms, including control tokens for schema selection (Keskar et al., 2019; Dathathri et al., 2020), retrieval-augmented generation pipelines for tabular grounding (Lewis et al., 2020; Glass et al., 2021), data-to-text decoding with plan sketches (Puduppully et al., 2022; Su et al., 2022), and prompt-based conditioning over linearized graphs and tables (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021). Paragraph Compression We introduce paragraph compression as a new task in our D2T generation pipeline. As the last step in the pipeline, it is closely related to linguistic realisation, howeversince we already work with natural language in this step-the focus of our task is on sentence fusion, rephrasing, and coreference resolution. Unlike text summarization or simplification Jiang et al., 2020), we aim to convey the complete semantics of the text without omitting any facts. In contrast to sentence fusion (Geva et al., 2019;Barzilay and McKeown, 2005) or sentence compression (Filippova and Altun, 2013), we operate in the context of multiple sentences in a paragraph. The task is the central focus of our WIKIFLUENT corpus ( §4), which we synthesize using a model for the reverse task, split-andrephrase, i.e. splitting a complex sentence into simpler ones while preserving semantics (Botha et al., 2018;.

text: Multi-Hop Reading Comprehension Recent works for multi-hop RC include memory-based methods which apply attentions to iteratively update query and context representations considering their interactions (Dhingra et al., 2018;Clark and Gardner, 2018;Zhuang and Wang, 2019;Yichen Jiang and Bansal, 2019). To explicitly incorporate entity connections, De Cao et al. ( 2019), Ding et al. (2019), Qiu et al. (2019), Tang et al. (2020), Song et al. (2018) and Tu et al. (2019) build entity graphs and apply Graph Neural Networks for information propagation. Kundu et al. (2019) formalizes reasoning as a path-finding problem with neural encoding to rank candidate paths. Path modeling is also adopted in  using pointer networks. However, these approaches only focus on local information without the ability to generalize, and some of them rely on NER tools. Dhingra et al. (2020) converts texts into a virtual knowledge based for retrieval, but requires an entity database. Another category uses neural module networks Min et al., 2019;Gupta et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2020) to decompose the question into a series of actions, each parameterized with a neural module, which also fail to explicitly uncover the underlying logic for reasoning. Recent efforts further explore retrieval-augmented and iterative reasoning, including multi-hop variants of HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), PathNet-style path selectors (Das et al., 2018), self-questioning decomposers (Min et al., 2019; Talmor and Berant, 2018), chain-of-thought prompting for multi-step inference (Wei et al., 2022), reinforcement-guided hop controllers (Xiong et al., 2017), and graph-augmented transformers over entity-centric corpora (Yasunaga et al., 2021). Deep Learning with Logic Reasoning Neurosymbolic learning aims to integrate deep learning's ability on dealing with uncertainty and logic programming's ability on reasoning. Deep neural networks have been used to parameterize discrete logic operators and logic atoms (França et al., 2014;Hu et al., 2016;Manhaeve et al., 2018;Xu et al., 2018;Li and Srikumar, 2019;Wu et al., 2020) given the logic rules. A more challenging direction is inductive logic programming that automatically learns rules through representation learning and differentiable backpropagation (Evans and Grefenstette, 2018;Dong et al., 2019;Yang and Song, 2020).

text: Language-informed video understanding is a complex task that has been extensively addressed in the multimodal (natural language and computer vision) machine learning research, by proposing diverse tasks and benchmarks. Despite notable progress, aligning linguistic structure with dynamic visual content remains challenging due to temporal compositionality, event granularity, and long-range dependencies that exceed the capacity of frame-level cues. A central question is how to balance general-purpose pretraining with task-specific adaptation, especially when annotations are sparse or weakly aligned with video timelines. A large body of work explores transferable representations that can be reused across retrieval, captioning, question answering, and localization tasks with minimal supervision. A large body of work explores video-language pretraining through contrastive and generative objectives across web-scale paired data, including CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), MIL-NCE (Miech et al., 2020), VideoCLIP (Xu et al., 2021), Frozen (Tsai et al., 2021), Florence (Yuan et al., 2021), and OmniVL (Wang et al., 2022), while task-specific advances cover temporal action localization on ActivityNet (Caba Heilbron et al., 2015), Epic-Kitchens narrations for egocentric understanding (Damen et al., 2018; Damen et al., 2022), MSR-VTT and YouCook2 for text-to-video retrieval and grounding (Xu et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018), and question answering benchmarks such as MSRVTT-QA (Xu et al., 2017), TVQA (Lei et al., 2018), and NExT-QA (Xiao et al., 2021). However, these developments uncover systematic errors in temporal binding, where models attend to salient but off-timestamp frames, and in linguistic grounding, where phrasal modifiers are ignored or hallucinated. Recent efforts introduce structured temporal modules, such as segment-level transformers and boundary-aware pooling, to better capture event transitions under weak supervision. Complementary lines leverage syntactic and semantic parsers to inject role structure, aligning verbs and arguments with detected actions and entities across time. Yet, explicit alignment often struggles with noisy ASR, open-vocabulary objects, and domain shifts between curated captions and in-the-wild narrations. In addition, evaluation practices vary widely across datasets, hindering apples-to-apples comparison and masking failure modes related to spurious correlations. To address measurement concerns, unified protocols have emerged that standardize negative sampling, temporal IoU thresholds, and language templates across retrieval and localization. Despite these improvements, current approaches still depend heavily on clip-level representations and short context windows that underutilize long-horizon narratives. This limitation is acute in instructional and egocentric videos, where goals, subgoals, and tool states unfold over minutes rather than seconds. Consequently, effective solutions must reconcile hierarchical temporal reasoning with flexible language conditioning that is robust to transcription and caption noise. We therefore focus on models that disentangle short-term perception from long-term memory, enabling fine-grained grounding while preserving scalability. Our study examines whether lightweight memory mechanisms coupled with structure-aware language representations can bridge the observed temporal and semantic gaps. We present a simple, modular framework that interfaces with existing pretrained backbones and can be trained end-to-end with standard objectives. Finally, we provide a thorough evaluation under controlled protocol settings and release code to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

text: Research on computational morality and moral language spans lexicon-based resources, theory-grounded annotation schemes, and neural modeling pipelines without a unified framing across tasks (Garten et al., 2016;Haidt and Graham, 2007;Hopp et al., 2021;Frimer et al., 2019;Hoover et al., 2020;Johnson and Goldwasser, 2018;Alhindi et al., 2021;Araque et al., 2020). Prior work has introduced moral lexica aligned to psychological theories (Graham et al., 2009;Frimer et al., 2017;Arendt et al., 2022;Tong and Zhang, 2022), leveraged transfer learning on social media corpora (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Yang et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2020), and compared multi-label versus multi-class formulations for moral value prediction (Kennedy et al., 2020;Borkan et al., 2019;Plaza-del-Arco et al., 2021;Siatka et al., 2022). Several datasets and benchmarks related to civic discourse and toxicity are also frequently referenced alongside moral foundations, including SemEval tasks on sentiment and stance (Rosenthal et al., 2017;Mohammad et al., 2016;Küçük and Can, 2020), HateXplain (Mathew et al., 2021), and Civil Comments (Borkan et al., 2019).

text: Complementary lines of work document domain shifts and label skew in socio-political text classification using benchmarks such as Founta et al. (2018), Waseem and Hovy (2016), OLID/OffensEval (Zampieri et al., 2019), PHEME (Zubiaga et al., 2016), and MMHS150K (Gomez et al., 2020), while methodological studies explore calibration, class-imbalance remedies, and multi-task setups with architectures like BiLSTM, BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017;Cui et al., 2019;He et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2019;He et al., 2021). text: Recent multimodal sentiment analysis has drawn on a range of architectures and datasets to advance alignment and fusion, including MulT (Tsai et al., 2019), MISA (Hazarika et al., 2020), CH-SIMS (Yu et al., 2020), Self-MM (Yu et al., 2021), and GME-LSTM(A) (Chen et al., 2017), alongside benchmarks such as CMU-MOSI (Zadeh et al., 2016), CMU-MOSEI (Zadeh et al., 2018), YouTube Opinion (Morency et al., 2011), and IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), as well as cross-modal attention and gating mechanisms (Tsai et al., 2019; Pham et al., 2019; Mittal et al., 2020; Baltrušaitis et al., 2019).

text: Prior work spans social media corpora, misinformation benchmarks, and multimodal verification without drawing consistent connections among them, including pandemic-focused Twitter collections (Banda et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Lamsal, 2021; Ziems et al., 2020), climate and disaster datasets (Littman and Wrubel, 2019; Alam et al., 2018; Imran et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017), annotated rumor and claim corpora (Qazvinian et al., 2011; Kwon et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2016; Zubiaga et al., 2016), and multimodal misinformation resources emphasizing images or memes (Kiela et al., 2020; Abdali et al., 2021; Khattar et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2019). In the news domain, Luo et al. (2021) automatically generate out-of-context images. Here, we curate social media posts that are topical and multimodal, and demonstrate an application to misinformation detection of human-generated fakes. There also exist general approaches for multimodal fact checking, e.g., Jaiswal et al. (2017) and Müller-Budack et al. (2020) that query an external knowledge base. Instead, we use a large pretrained model that does not require an external reference set.

text: To situate our contribution within multimodal learning, we review complementary efforts on visual entailment and image–text contradiction that build upon pretrained vision–language models. Related lines of work on cross-modal retrieval and grounding leverage image–text alignment and external references (Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015; Faghri et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019), while multimodal fact-checking systems integrate retrieval with reasoning or graph structures (Popat et al., 2018; Zhou and Zafarani, 2019; Gupta et al., 2013; Boididou et al., 2015). In contrast, our approach evaluates instruction-tuned encoders under weakly supervised objectives that prioritize internal consistency signals over explicit retrieval. We further compare zero-shot and few-shot adaptation regimes and quantify robustness to topical domain shift.

text: We consider reference-based automatic metrics, reference-free quality estimation, and human-in-the-loop evaluation with model-assisted judging. Reference-based metrics compare system outputs to ground-truth references and typically emphasize lexical or character n-gram overlap, sometimes augmented with paraphrase or semantic matching. Quality estimation (QE) aims to predict quality without references, operating at sentence or word level and increasingly leveraging pretrained language models. Human evaluation remains the gold standard, but recent work explores hybrid protocols that scaffold expert judgments with automatic cues or LLM rationales. Recent advances span reference-based metrics such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), TER (Snover et al., 2006), and chrF (Popović, 2015); learned quality estimation models like OpenKiwi (Kepler et al., 2019), COMET (Rei et al., 2020; Rei et al., 2022), and BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020); and instruction-tuned LLM judges exemplified by GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023), LLaMA-2-Chat (Touvron et al., 2023), and Mixtral (Jiang et al., 2024), alongside standard testbeds including WMT Metrics tasks (Mathur et al., 2020; Freitag et al., 2021) and MQM-based human annotations (Lommel et al., 2014).

text: Proposing a dependency parsing approach to the full task of SSA, Barnes et al. (2021) show that it leads to strong improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Peng et al. (2021) propose a sparse fuzzy attention mechanism to deal with the sparseness of dependency arcs in the models from Barnes et al. (2021) and show further improvements. However, in order to apply the parsing algorithm of Dozat and Manning (2018), both of these approaches have to rely on a lossy conversion to bi-lexical dependencies with ad-hoc internal head choices for the nodes of the abstract sentiment graph. This lossy behaviour is caused by nested text spans in the sentiment graphs, as illustrated by Figure , which are ambiguous in their bi-lexical dependency encoding (see Section A in the Appendix). More generally, decoding structured graph information from text has sparked a lot of interest in recent years, especially for parsing meaning representation graphs (Oepen et al., 2020). There has been tremendous progress in developing complex transition-based and graph-based parsers (Hershcovich et al., 2017;McDonald and Pereira, 2006;Dozat and Manning, 2018). Recent work on general graph parsing and structured prediction spans a spectrum of models and resources without a unifying perspective, including transition-based AMR parsers that leverage stack-pointer networks (Zhang et al., 2019), biaffine graph parsers for semantic dependencies (Dozat and Manning, 2018; Dozat and Manning, 2017), neural encoders for UCCA and MRP with cross-framework evaluation (Hershcovich et al., 2017; Oepen et al., 2020), and pretrained language model adaptations such as BERT-based semantic parsers for AMR 2.0 and AMR 3.0 (Cai and Lam, 2020; Bevilacqua et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020). In this paper, we adopt PERIN (Samuel and Straka, 2020), a state-of-theart graph-based parser capable of modeling a superset of graph features needed for our task. We focus on sentiment structure analysis (SSA) where graph nodes may correspond to nested spans, operators, and roles that exceed bi-lexical formalisms. Prior work has often reduced these structures to trees or bilexical arcs, sacrificing expressivity when dealing with discontinuities and reentrancies. Our formulation treats SSA as a typed, labeled graph prediction problem over spans and anchors with constraints inspired by meaning representation parsing. PERIN provides a natural foundation as it supports multi-head edges, latent anchors, and edge reentrancies. We extend PERIN with span-level representations derived from contextual encoders to better handle nested sentiment constituents. Additionally, we introduce a graph decoding constraint set that preserves well-formedness while allowing multiple overlapping spans. To evaluate these modeling choices, we compare against dependency-based baselines and conversion pipelines on established SSA benchmarks. We report results across standard precision, recall, and F1 for nodes, edges, and role labels under exact and partial span matching. Our experiments further analyze error types related to nested spans, discontinuities, and operator-role confusion. Finally, we discuss implications for downstream sentiment summarization and controllable opinion generation.

text: The works that are most similar to ours strive to gain diversity using controlled-paraphrase generation, by exposing control mechanisms that are manipulated to produce either lexically (Zeng et al., 2019;Thompson and Post, 2020) or syntactically Goyal and Durrett, 2020) diverse paraphrases. One approach is to use an exemplar sentence for guiding the syntax of the generated paraphrase Bao et al., 2019). An alternative is to directly employ constituency tree as the syntax guidance (Iyyer et al., 2018;Li and Choi, 2020). Goyal and Durrett (2020) promote syntactic diversity by conditioning over possible syntactic rearrangements of the input. Zeng et al. (2019) use keywords as lexical guidance for the generation process. The broader landscape of controllable text generation has also included style transfer (Shen et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2018;Lample et al., 2019), controllable summarization (Fan et al., 2018;He et al., 2020;Schumann et al., 2020), attribute-conditioned generation (Hu et al., 2017;Keskar et al., 2019;Dathathri et al., 2020;Krause et al., 2020), and syntactic control via parse templates or structured encoders (Iyyer et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2021;Yang and Klein, 2021), along with benchmarking efforts on paraphrase corpora such as Quora Question Pairs, MRPC, and ParaNMT (Dolan and Brockett, 2005;Iyer et al., 2017;Wieting and Gimpel, 2018). Here we introduce a simple model for jointly controlling the lexical, syntactic and semantic aspects of the generated paraphrases.

text: Various benchmarks were proposed to measure models' temporal reasoning abilities. The bAbI suite contains a task that requires reasoning about the order of time expressions (Weston et al., 2015). MC-TACO is a reading comprehension task pertaining to ordering, duration, stationarity, frequency, and typical times of events (Zhou et al., 2019). TI-MEDIAL (Qin et al., 2021) is a dialogue QA task focusing on temporal commonsense. Zhou et al. (2021) and Thukral et al. (2021) both cast the temporal ordering task as an NLI task. In another line of work, tracking state changes in procedural text is also related to temporal ordering (Dalvi et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020). Despite the success of pre-trained LMs on language understanding tasks, their performance on these benchmarks is limited, maybe due to the fact that many temporal relations are not explicitly stated in text (Davis and Marcus, 2015). A promising direction is to train LMs explicitly on temporal knowledge (Zhou et al., 2020). Recent advances in temporal commonsense also include methods and resources that emphasize structured temporal knowledge and probing of pre-trained models without explicitly relating these strands to a unifying objective, such as CaTeRS for event relations (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), TimeQA for temporally-aware question answering (Chen et al., 2021), TEA-GNN architectures for temporal event graphs (Ning et al., 2019), temporal probing suites for LMs (Zhou et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2020), and hybrid neural-symbolic temporal reasoning frameworks (Lee et al., 2020), alongside evaluations on TimeBank-Dense and MATRES (Cassidy et al., 2014;Ning et al., 2018).

text: Several other works (Guu et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Qu et al., 2020;Lu et al., 2020) proposed representing the queries and documents as vectors (as opposed to a vector per token), and using dot product as the interaction block. While this ranker architecture approach is simple (and can also be used for the retrieval step via an approximate nearest neighbor search such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017) or ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020)), the overall ranking quality is generally lower compared to methods that employ a query-document cross-attention interaction. Recently, several lines of work in neural ranking and retrieval have explored architectural simplifications, efficiency-oriented interaction designs, and dense retrieval objectives without cross-attention, including ANCE (Xiong et al., 2021), DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), COIL (Gao et al., 2021), ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022), SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021), and RocketQA (Qu et al., 2021), as well as approximate nearest neighbor toolkits such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017) and ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020), and compression-oriented methods like product quantization (Jegou et al., 2011) and scalar quantization baselines (Gong et al., 2014).

text: Patient-Specific Literature Retrieval. Since 2014, the Text REtrieval Conference (TREC) has organized a series of challenges to advance research in this area. The TREC Clinical Decision Support (CDS) tracks focused on evaluating systems on the task of retrieving biomedical articles relevant for answering generic clinical questions about patient medical records (e.g., identifying potential diagnoses, treatments, and tests) (Simpson et al., 2014;Roberts et al., 2015Roberts et al., , 2016). TREC CDS 2014 and 2015 used short case reports as idealized representations of medical records due to the lack of available de-identified records. TREC 2016 shifted to using real-world medical records from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) database (Johnson et al., 2016). In our work, our focus is on predicting clinical outcomes using ICU admission notes and patient-specific retrieved literature. Ueda et al. (2021) use contextualized representations on more structured retrieval tasks not involving clinical notes (Voorhees et al., 2021), leaving open the question of how large pretrained language models would fare on long, noisy EHR text. We explore this by experimenting with language models for retrieval based on EHR text. Recent retrieval-oriented modeling for clinical text has also drawn from general-domain neural IR and biomedical QA, including dense retrievers and late-interaction models (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), biomedical sentence selection for evidence gathering (Wiese et al., 2017;Beltagy et al., 2019), clinical concept linking with UMLS-aware encoders (Mullenbach et al., 2018;Peng et al., 2020), and large biomedical language models for document ranking and re-ranking (Lee et al., 2020;Gururangan et al., 2020;Gu et al., 2021;Singhal et al., 2023). Clinical Outcome Prediction. The idea of using automated outcome prediction for assisting clinical triage, workflow optimization, and hospital resource management has received much interest recently, especially given the conditions of the COVID-19 pandemic. Predictive models based on structured and unstructured information have been built for key clinical outcomes including mortality (Jain et al., 2019;Feng et al., 2020), length of hospital stay (van Aken et al., 2021), readmission (Jain et al., 2019), sepsis (Feng et al., 2020), prolonged mechanical ventilation, and diagnostic coding (Jain et al., 2019;van Aken et al., 2021). Increasingly, models have leveraged unstructured text from notes since they can contain key information for outcome prediction (Boag et al., 2018;Jin et al., 2018). Most recently, van Aken et al. (2021) attempted this using large pretrained language models. Our work compares the performance of a broader range of state-of-the-art pretrained language models on outcome prediction tasks.

text: We focus on modeling dependencies that span thousands of tokens in practical settings such as legal and scientific corpora. Prior work shows that architectural inductive biases significantly affect the ability to capture long-range structure under fixed memory budgets. Recent surveys catalog numerous memory-augmented and sparse-attention variants, including Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020), BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020), Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), Routing Transformer (Roy et al., 2021), ETC (Ainslie et al., 2020), and Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al., 2022), alongside benchmarks such as NarrativeQA (Kočiský et al., 2018), GovReport (Huang et al., 2021), Qasper (Dasigi et al., 2021), and Long Range Arena (Tay et al., 2020), as well as training methods like gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., 2016), mixed-precision (Micikevicius et al., 2018), and sequence packing (Kundu et al., 2021). However, the interaction between positional encodings and block-sparse routing remains underexplored in domain-specific settings.

text: Vision-language few-shot learning. Recently, several few-shot learners on vision-language tasks were proposed including GPT (Radford et al., 2019;Brown et al., 2020), Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021), PICa (Yang et al., 2022), SimVLM (Wang et al., 2021), OFA (Wang et al., 2022), BLIP (Li et al., 2022), and Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022), with related advances in multimodal prompting and retrieval-augmented modeling (Jia et al., 2021;Khandelwal et al., 2021;Li et al., 2023;Yu et al., 2022). Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021) is a large language model based on GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), and is transformed into a multimodal few-shot learner by extending the soft prompting to incorporate a set of images and text. Their approach shows the fewshot capability on visual question answering and image classification tasks. Similarly, PICa uses GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) to solve VQA tasks in a few-shot manner by providing a few in-context VQA examples. It converts images into textual descriptions so that GPT-3 can understand the images. SimVLM is trained with prefix language modeling on weakly-supervised datasets. It demonstrates its effectiveness on a zero-shot captioning task. While these models achieve improvement on few-shot tasks, they are impractical to use in real-world applications due to their model sizes.

text: Language model prompting. Providing prompts or task descriptions play an vital role in improving pre-trained language models in many tasks (Radford et al., 2021;Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b;Brown et al., 2020). Among them, GPT models (Radford et al., 2019;Brown et al., 2020) achieved great success in prompting or task demonstrations in NLP tasks. In light of this direction, prompt-based approaches improve small pre-trained models in few-shot text classification tasks (Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b). CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) also explores prompt templates for image classification which affect zero-shot performance. Prompting strategies span manual templates (Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b;Petroni et al., 2019), automatic template search (Gao et al., 2021;Shin et al., 2020), soft or continuous prompts (Lester et al., 2021;Li and Liang, 2021;Hambardzumyan et al., 2021), instruction tuning and in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020;Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022), and multimodal prompt tuning for CLIP-like models (Radford et al., 2021;Zhou et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2021;Lu et al., 2022), alongside calibration and selection methods for few-shot settings (Zhao et al., 2021;Rubin et al., 2022;Holtzman et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022). We follow these core ideas so we aim to improve zero-shot and few-shot performance using prompts in visionlanguage tasks. We pretrain FEWVLM with masked language modeling (MaskedLM) and prefix language modeling (Pre-fixLM).

text: Sequence Ordering. Story sequencing test is a popular way of examining children's abilities on sequential reasoning which is shown evident for procedural understanding (Tomkins, 1952;Baron-Cohen et al., 1986;Loucks et al., 2017). In NLP, existing works attempt the sequencing task as sorting a series of unordered sentences Cui et al., 2018;Logeswaran et al., 2018;Oh et al., 2019;Lee et al., 2020;Calizzano et al., 2021) from paper abstracts or short paragraphs, and related efforts on commonsense and narrative ordering draw on ROCStories (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), Story Cloze Test (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), and narrative coherence modeling (Barzilay and Lapata, 2008; Li and Hovy, 2014; Chen et al., 2019) alongside discourse-based methods (Pitler et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2011; Ji and Eisenstein, 2014) and pretraining with sentence order prediction (Lan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Conneau and Lample, 2019). While certain prior work also attempts to extend it to incorporate multimodality , the dataset used, Visual StoryTelling , features album images that were not intended to be procedural nor supply unstated details to complement the texts. In computer vision, existing work leverages shuffle frame prediction for learning video representations (Lee et al., 2017;Xu et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020;Li et al., 2020) as well as cycle consistency constraints for learning temporal dynamics (Epstein et al., 2021). text: Recent work on temporal robustness in NLP and vision has cataloged a range of dataset shifts and evaluation protocols across time without converging on consistent mitigation strategies, including approaches for domain adaptation under time-stamped distributions (Rabanser et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2021), retrospective calibration and reweighting (Ovadia et al., 2019;Ashukha et al., 2020), continual and lifelong learning to address non-stationarity (Parisi et al., 2019;Delange et al., 2021), evaluation frameworks for robustness under distribution shift (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019;Taori et al., 2020), and language drift analyses measuring token- and discourse-level changes over decades (Hamilton et al., 2016;Rosenfeld and Erk, 2018;Shoemark et al., 2019;Gururangan et al., 2020). This line of research underscores the breadth of temporal phenomena encountered by modern models. However, its implications for multi-label classification under skew remain underexplored in practice.

text: Early approaches to OTD relied primarily upon dictionaries like hatebase 3 to lookup offensive words and phrases. The creation of OTD datasets enabled the development of ML-based approaches utilizing simple features, such as bag-of-word representations. With the advent of social media platforms, many resources have been developed for identifying toxic comments in web text (Waseem and Hovy, 2016;, including a number of deep learning-based methods (Pitsilis et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2018b;Casula et al., 2020;Yasaswini et al., 2021;Djandji et al., 2020;Badjatiya et al., 2017;Park and Fung, 2017;Founta et al., 2018;Davidson et al., 2017). Notably, all of these methods can be described as building a contextual representation of a sentence (whether trained end-to-end or on top of existing pre-trained language models), and making a classification based on this representation. However, the generalization challenges posed by domain shift across platforms and time have motivated research into robustness and calibration for toxicity classifiers. Prior work has explored subword modeling and character-level cues to mitigate spelling variation and adversarial obfuscation while preserving recall on colloquial forms. Complementary efforts have examined metadata and conversational context, showing that user- and thread-level signals can reduce false positives arising from reappropriated slurs and quoted speech. Beyond architecture, dataset construction practices—such as annotator guidelines, multi-label taxonomies, and adversarially curated negatives—have been shown to influence measurement of both fairness and utility. Cross-lingual and code-switching scenarios further complicate the landscape, as direct translation of lexicons or labels often fails to capture pragmatic force and sociolinguistic nuance. Recent studies have therefore combined translation with culture-specific reannotation, yielding improved agreement but at higher curation cost. In parallel, pre-training on large-scale web corpora has enabled transfer to rare toxicity categories, yet raises questions about spurious correlations inherited from upstream data. Evaluations increasingly adopt stress tests and counterfactual augmentations to separate performance on identity terms from true detection of abusive intent. Despite these advances, a consistent gap remains in systematically disentangling toxicity from legitimate expressions of identity, irony, and reclaimed language. Addressing this gap requires methods that couple representation learning with semantically grounded constraints and auditable decision rationales. Our work contributes to this direction by formalizing a framework that partitions lexical, pragmatic, and contextual evidence and by introducing diagnostics that quantify overreliance on identity markers. We further present a modular training regimen that integrates counterfactual supervision with distributionally robust objectives to stabilize performance under domain shift. Finally, we release evaluation suites aligned with these objectives to promote reproducible assessment of robustness, fairness, and interpretability in OTD models.

text: Fair machine learning The literature on inducing approximately fair models from biased data is rapidly growing. See Mehrabi et al. (2021) for a recent survey. We rely on this literature in how we define fairness, and for the algorithms that we compare in our experiments below. As already discussed, we adopt a capability-centered approach to fairness and define fairness in terms of performance parity (Hashimoto et al., 2018) or equal risk (Donini et al., 2018). The fairness-promoting learning algorithms we evaluate are discussed in detail in §4. Some of these -Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (Sagawa et al., 2020) and Invariant Risk Minimization (Arjovsky et al., 2020) -have previously been evaluated for fairness in the context of hate speech (Koh et al., 2021). Foundational approaches to algorithmic fairness span pre-processing adjustments that rebalance datasets (Kamiran and Calders, 2012; Feldman et al., 2015; Calmon et al., 2017), in-processing constraints that regularize or constrain models during training (Zafar et al., 2017; Agarwal et al., 2018; Cotter et al., 2019; Celis et al., 2019), and post-processing techniques that modify decision thresholds to equalize error rates or acceptance rates across groups (Hardt et al., 2016; Pleiss et al., 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2017; Corbett-Davies and Goel, 2018). We focus on supervised classification and structured prediction where sensitive attributes may be observed or only weakly inferred. Our scope includes group fairness criteria that trade off utility with parity constraints and individual fairness notions grounded in similarity metrics. We also consider the practicalities of limited labels and resource constraints in high-stakes domains. A substantial body of work debates the compatibility of fairness metrics, emphasizing impossibility theorems and calibration trade-offs. These discussions motivate careful selection of evaluation criteria aligned with deployment goals. We build on these insights to construct robust benchmarks and ablations. We detail our datasets, metrics, and model classes in the following section. In particular, we highlight settings with pronounced subgroup heterogeneity and label imbalance. We further examine the stability of fairness metrics under resampling and perturbation. Our analysis emphasizes reproducibility and transparent reporting of group-specific outcomes. We also report cost-sensitive metrics relevant to clinical and judicial use cases. We now turn to historical precedents that illustrate societal risks from predictive systems. This background informs our emphasis on distribution shift and equity. has a limited history. In a classic study, Angwin et al. (2016) analyzed the performance of the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) system, which was used for parole risk assessment (recidivism prediction) in the US. The system relied on 137 features from questionnaires and criminal records. Angwin et al. (2016) found that blacks were almost twice as likely as whites to be mislabeled as high risk (of re-offending), revealing a severe racial bias in the system. The system was later compared to crowdworkers in Dressel and Farid (2018). Subsequent critiques expanded the discussion to measurement error and construct validity in recidivism labels. These examples underscore challenges in defining harm and accountability. Beyond criminal justice, similar concerns arise in credit scoring and hiring. We include tasks from these domains to stress-test fairness claims. We finally connect to robustness and generalization under distribution shift. Our experiments probe worst-case risk across predefined groups and latent clusters. We complement aggregate metrics with subgroup-conditioned calibration analysis. This design reflects practical deployment constraints. Recent work in robustness and distribution shift connects to fairness through worst-group risk and spurious correlation mitigation, including techniques such as domain-adversarial training (Ganin et al., 2016), group-DRO and its variants (Sagawa et al., 2020; Hashimoto et al., 2018), invariant predictors from causal perspectives (Peters et al., 2016; Arjovsky et al., 2020; Rosenfeld et al., 2021), and calibration-aware or conformal methods for reliable uncertainty under shift (Guo et al., 2017; Kuleshov et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2020; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). We implement strong baselines and identify failure modes under reweighting and data augmentation. We conclude by outlining the criteria used to interpret fairness-utility trade-offs.

text: Recent efforts on knowledge-grounded dialogue and document-grounded response generation have surveyed and advanced a broad set of techniques spanning retrieval-augmented generation, graph-enhanced reasoning, and memory-augmented architectures, including retrieval-then-read pipelines for conversational grounding (Dinan et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Komeili et al., 2022), graph neural models that encode structured commonsense for response planning (Zhou et al., 2018b;Liu et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2022), memory networks and differentiable knowledge access for task-oriented settings (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015;Madotto et al., 2018;Eric et al., 2017), and pre-training strategies tailored to knowledge selection with topic or entity supervision (Lian et al., 2019;Zhao et al., 2020a;Kim et al., 2020).

text: Most human languages contain ways of expressing generalized quantifiers, and their semantics exhibit striking similarities across languages (Matthewson, 2004;Fintel and Matthewson, 2008;Steinert-Threlkeld, 2019). At the same time, generalized quantifiers can be instantiated very differently across languages due to pragmatic considerations (Grice, 1989) or cognitive economy and cost-benefit optimisation in the exchange of information (Sperber and Wilson, 1986;Levinson et al., 2000). Quantifier words also exhibit syntactic differences, e.g., with some languages having specialized words to express quantity, while others rely on metaphorical usage of common nouns (Katsos et al., 2012). In English, most is a determiner, but Spanish and French express the same concept through common nouns, la mayoría and la majorité. The relative stability of the core semantics of quantifiers makes a cross-linguistic comparison possible, but the syntactic and pragmatic variation associated with the expression of generalized quantifiers poses a challenge for multilingual NLU. We consult quantifier taxonomy studies (Keenan and Westerståhl, 1997;Peters and Westerståhl, 2006;Szymanik and Thorne, 2015;Szymanik, 2016) and derive a categorization set for quantifier analysis in NLU benchmarks. In Table , we list the 11way quantifier categorization set and their logical denotation based on set theory.

text: While other foci of formal linguistics have attracted the attention of NLP researchers—including coreference (Ogrodniczuk et al., 2019;Ogrodniczuk et al., 2020), negation (Hossain et al., 2020;Hartmann et al., 2021), and consistency (Li et al., 2019;Ribeiro et al., 2019;Asai and Hajishirzi, 2020)—there has been little work on generalized quantifiers as a source of error in NLU, let alone in multilingual NLU. Researchers have explored compositional semantics in neural models (Lake and Baroni, 2018;Li et al., 2019;Keysers et al., 2020;Hupkes et al., 2020;Goodwin et al., 2020), evaluated monotonicity reasoning (Icard and Moss, 2014;Hu and Liang, 2018;Yanaka et al., 2019;Geiger et al., 2020), and examined cross-lingual entailment and QA benchmarks (Conneau et al., 2018;Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019;Xue et al., 2021;Lewis et al., 2020), alongside resources targeting scalar implicature and pragmatics (Potts, 2015;Talmor et al., 2020;Jeretic et al., 2020;Ruis et al., 2020). It remains an open problem whether LMs represent the semantics of quantifiers words adequately, or if they provide a basis for resolving scopal ambiguities.

text: Another direction of research has shown impressive results using extremely large models (Radford et al., 2019;Devlin et al., 2019). Using these as a basis for experiments could be an interesting direction, but fine-tuning models in low data settings is known to be difficult and highly variable (Dodge et al., 2020). Similar transformer models have been used for controlled generation. Zellers et al. (2019) developed a model for news generation that conditioned on meta-data including domain, date, authors, and headline. No ablation is performed, and though it would be interesting to compare to a transformer method that conditions on authors alone, we opted for a model that is faster and cheaper to train (Grover-Mega from Zellers et al. (2019) was trained for two weeks and cost around 25k USD). Additionally, when fine-tuning models for new users, little data is available. Contextualized embedding models often require a large amount of data to train effectively, though this type of comparison would be an interesting future direction to explore. Variations of the LSTM have consistently achieved state-of-the-art performance without massive compute resources and thus we chose this architecture for our experiments (Merity et al., 2018a;Melis et al., 2019;Merity, 2019;Li et al., 2020). Another direction of research has shown impressive results using extremely large models (Radford et al., 2019;Devlin et al., 2019), and related lines have explored prompt-based conditioning and domain control for generation (Keskar et al., 2019;Dathathri et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020;Gururangan et al., 2020;Lester et al., 2021;Scao and Rush, 2021), controlled news and story generation (Zellers et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2018;See et al., 2019;Holtzman et al., 2020), parameter-efficient adaptation methods (Houlsby et al., 2019;Li and Liang, 2021;Hu et al., 2022;Ben Zaken et al., 2022), and personalization signals from user or social attributes (Bamman et al., 2014;Hovy, 2015;Li et al., 2016;Khalifa et al., 2021).

text: Efficient Pre-training for NLP. Recently, researchers find that the performance of PLMs can be simply improved by increasing the model size, data size and training steps Raffel et al., 2019;Kaplan et al., 2020), sparking a wave of training ever-larger PLMs. However, larger models require greater computational demands (Patterson et al., 2021). To this end, researchers propose to accelerate pre-training by mixed-precision training (Shoeybi et al., 2019), distributed training (Shoeybi et al., 2019;Huang et al., 2019), large batch optimization (You et al., 2020) and architecture innovation (Lan et al., 2020). Recent work spans scaling laws, optimization, and systems, including Raffel et al. (2019), Kaplan et al. (2020), Brown et al. (2020), Chowdhery et al. (2022), Hoffmann et al. (2022), Smith et al. (2022), Narayanan et al. (2021), and Patterson et al. (2021), alongside pre-training data studies such as C4 (Raffel et al., 2019), The Pile (Gao et al., 2020), ROOTS (Laurençon et al., 2022), and RefinedWeb (Penedo et al., 2023), as well as architecture lines including BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), T5 (Raffel et al., 2019), and ELECTRA (Clark et al., 2020), and training efficiency techniques like ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al., 2020), DeepSpeed (Rasley et al., 2020), Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019), and FSDP (Zhao et al., 2023), with complementary studies on curriculum learning (Gururangan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020), tokenization (Bostrom and Durrett, 2020; Xue et al., 2021), and data quality filtering (Kreutzer et al., 2022; Dodge et al., 2021).

text: Knowledge Distillation for PLMs. Knowledge Distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015) aims to compress a large model into a fast-to-execute one. KD has renewed a surge of interest in PLMs recently. Some explore KD at different training phases, e.g., pre-training (Sanh et al., 2019), downstream finetuning (Sun et al., 2019;Krishna et al., 2020), or both of them (Jiao et al., 2020); others explore distilling not only the final logits output by the large PLM, but also the intermediate hidden representations (Sanh et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2020). Conventional KD presumes that teacher models play pivotal roles in mastering knowledge, and student models generally cannot match their teachers in performance. When it comes to the scenario of KI, since student models have larger capacities, the performance of teacher models is no longer an "upper bound" of student models. Prior work on knowledge distillation and related compression-transfer paradigms encompasses foundational formulations and PLM adaptations (Hinton et al., 2015; Buciluǎ et al., 2006; Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), layer- and feature-level transfer (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2017; Park et al., 2019; Passban et al., 2021), logit matching and temperature scaling variants (Ba and Caruana, 2014; Furlanello et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2020), self- and born-again distillation (Furlanello et al., 2018; Xu and Liu, 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2023), online and mutual learning (Zhang et al., 2018; Anil et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021), multi-teacher and ensemble distillation (You et al., 2017; Hinton et al., 2015; Gou et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022), and efficient student architectures for NLP (Sanh et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019; Turc et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). Based on the prior explorations, in this paper, we investigate the application of reversed KD in pre-training and conduct a series of empirical studies under various settings.

text: Despite the effort in putting forward challenging sets of data to test WSD capabilities of NMT models, to the best of our knowledge, only a few approaches (Gonzales et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2018) have been proposed to mitigate this issue, and none of them are effective with modern Transformerbased architectures. Furthermore, while parallel corpora have been exploited to produce sense annotations in the past (Bonansinga and Bond, 2016;Delli Bovi et al., 2017), they have been built by utilizing outdated disambiguation approaches that have been recently surpassed by more advanced neural architectures. Indeed, the Word Sense Disambiguation field has received much attention in the most recent years, with several supervised approaches (Conia and Navigli, 2021;Blevins and Zettlemoyer, 2020; and sense embedding models (Loureiro and Jorge, 2019;Scarlini et al., 2020a,b;Wang et al., 2020) performing close to the upper bound limit of the inter-annotator agreement, which finally makes them feasible for inclusion in other downstream tasks, e.g., Machine Translation. Recent neural approaches to semantics and translation have explored contextualized representations and sense-aware modeling from multiple angles (Peters et al., 2018;Devlin et al., 2019;Conneau and Lample, 2019;Loureiro and Jorge, 2019;Scarlini et al., 2020a;Wang et al., 2020;Kepler et al., 2019;Nguyen et al., 2018;Pu et al., 2018), as well as evaluation resources designed to probe semantic fidelity (Gonzales et al., 2017;Raganato et al., 2019;Emelin et al., 2020;Navigli and Ponzetto, 2012).

text: In this section, we firstly discuss the background of OpenQA retrieval, then our methodology and training framework. Recent advances further explore unsupervised or weakly supervised objectives for dense retrieval across heterogeneous corpora, including contrastive pre-training with in-batch negatives (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021), generative pre-training that aligns encoder representations via query reformulation (Lewis et al., 2020;Sachan et al., 2021), domain-adaptive pre-training on web-scale mixtures (Ni et al., 2021;Gao and Callan, 2021), and supervised distillation from cross-encoders or rerankers (Hofstätter et al., 2021;Qu et al., 2021), as well as evaluation on BEIR, MS MARCO, and Natural Questions benchmarks (Thakur et al., 2021;Bajaj et al., 2018;Kwiatkowski et al., 2019). To situate HLP within OpenQA, we consider retrieval as mapping a natural-language question to a distribution over passages under a bi-encoder architecture. We adopt a standard dual-encoder with late interaction and train it with negative sampling strategies tailored to hyperlink structure. Our pre-training corpus is constructed from Wikipedia snapshots, where anchor-target pairs serve as weak supervision for building question-passage affinities. We design curriculum schedules that interleave hyperlink-local negatives with cross-article hard negatives mined by BM25. The training framework integrates in-batch negatives and temperature-scaled contrastive loss with momentum encoders to stabilize optimization. We then fine-tune on OpenQA datasets using a multi-task objective that blends retrieval and marginal likelihood over answer-bearing passages. Implementation details, including batch size, learning rates, and document encoders, follow standard settings to facilitate reproducibility. Finally, we report results under zero-shot and few-shot regimes to probe generalization across out-of-domain corpora. We also ablate the impact of hyperlink density, anchor text length, and target page popularity on retrieval effectiveness. For completeness, we analyze failure cases where anchors are ambiguous or referentially underspecified. The discussion highlights practical considerations for scaling hyperlink-induced supervision to larger and noisier web graphs.

text: Short-text Representations: Multiple NLP areas involve very short texts with some unique characteristics. Several methods have been developed for tweets (e.g., (Nguyen et al., 2020)). Tweets pose the added challenge of containing many non-standard colloquial expressions and contain non-language text like URLs. Still, Wang et al. (2020) present a similar finding to ours: massively pre-trained encoders do not always perform well. Search queries are also short, with an average of three terms (Taghavi et al., 2012). Unlike to-dos, information such as click logs (Zhang et al., 2019) can be used as an indicator of user intent. Another key difference is that search queries are written with the goal of having a machine interpret them. Prior work on short-text and task-oriented representations has explored diverse approaches, including doc2vec and sent2vec adaptations for brief inputs (Le and Mikolov, 2014;Pagliardini et al., 2018), character- and subword-level encoders for robustness to noise (Sennrich et al., 2016;Bojanowski et al., 2017), domain-adaptive pretraining for specialized intent spaces (Gururangan et al., 2020;Howard and Ruder, 2018), and supervised intent classification benchmarks and methods in conversational AI and personal assistants (Hemphill et al., 1990;Larson et al., 2019;Casanueva et al., 2020;Schuster et al., 2019).

text: Prompt-based Language Models. Prompt-based learning is a way of leveraging PLMs by prepending task-specific instructions to the task input when feeding into PLMs. Early approaches mainly utilized hand-crafted prompts to adapt to different generation tasks (Brown et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020;Zou et al., 2021). However, manually designed prompts are not flexible and cannot be applied to more kinds of tasks. Thus, recent works have focused on automating the learning of discrete prompts (Shin et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2020). However, learning prompts over discrete space is hard to optimize and likely to be sub-optimal. To address these problems, many works proposed to optimize continuous prompts (Liu et al., 2021c;Li and Liang, 2021), which are more flexible to any kinds of tasks. Among these studies, prefix-tuning (Li and Liang, 2021) prepended a sequence of vectors to the input for text generation tasks. By contrast, we utilize soft prompts to investigate transfer learning for text generation and demonstrate that generation tasks can often help each other via prompt transfer.

text: Transferability of Natural Language Processing. We are also closely related to existing works on transferability of NLP tasks (Jeong et al., 2020;Wiese et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2019). Prior studies have shown that cross-task transfer can address the data scarcity issue (Wiese et al., 2017), enhance the ability to complex reasoning and inference (Jeong et al., 2020), or learn effective word representations (Liu et al., 2019). Efforts to transfer prompts for addressing NLU tasks have also been developed (Vu et al., 2021;Su et al., 2021). Beyond single-task setups, researchers have explored cross-domain and cross-format transfer signals in prompt-based and non-prompt paradigms, including multi-task pretraining (Sanh et al., 2022;Aghajanyan et al., 2021), adapter-based transfer (Houlsby et al., 2019;Pfeiffer et al., 2021), meta-learning for few-shot generalization (Finn et al., 2017;Bansal et al., 2020), cross-lingual prompting and translation-based transfer (Winata et al., 2021;Ponti et al., 2020), curriculum or task-routing schedulers (Rosenfeld et al., 2020;Tay et al., 2023), and instruction tuning corpora and methods (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022;Longpre et al., 2023). In prompt-centric literature, transfer has been examined via prompt ensembling (Zhou et al., 2022), prompt composition (Schick and Schütze, 2021), prompt calibration (Zhao et al., 2021), and prompt parameter sharing across tasks (Lester et al., 2021;He et al., 2022), with extensions to controllable generation and safety constraints (Keskar et al., 2019;Askell et al., 2021). Yet related datasets for generation and understanding tasks span SuperGLUE, XSum, CNN/DailyMail, CoNLL03, TyDiQA, and XNLI, among others, and evaluation has leveraged standard automatic metrics and human judgments. As an representative work, Vu et al. (2021) used the learned prompt to directly initialize the prompt for a target task while not considered the specific input. Our work focuses on the challenging text generation tasks by utilizing prompts to extract implicit taskrelated knowledge and considering specific model inputs for the most useful knowledge transfer.

text: Several approaches exist in the literature to capture interdependence of arcs in SDP, which often derive from proposals made for DP. One is to use a higher-order graph-based parser. Wang et al. (2019) achieve state-of-the-art results (without pretrained LM) by using second-order factors to score the graphs, yet at the cost of a O(n 3 ) complexity. Recent neural graph parsers leverage pretrained encoders, structured inference, and learning-to-search variants in diverse ways across formalisms and languages, including higher-order CRF-style models and global decoders for semantic graphs (Zhang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Dozat and Manning, 2018; He and Choi, 2020; Fernández-González and Gómez-Rodríguez, 2020; Kurita and Søgaard, 2019; Oepen et al., 2015; Dozat and Manning, 2017).

text: The breadth of these contributions underscores a shared concern with establishing reliable, well-calibrated knowledge about model behavior. The debate around hype and overclaiming is not purely rhetorical; it shapes incentives for data curation, reporting standards, and the interpretation of benchmark results. Evaluation methodology, in particular, has emerged as a pivot point linking safety, robustness, and deployment readiness. Prior work on adversarial and contrastive testing shows that small perturbations can expose brittle shortcuts, calling for metrics that go beyond average-case accuracy. At the same time, alignment-oriented analyses caution that naively scaling models does not resolve specification gaps and can entrench opaque failure modes. Recent surveys and position papers chart complementary territory across model evaluation, alignment, robustness, and societal impact without integrating these strands into a unifying perspective, including Bommasani et al. (2021), Bender and Koller (2020), Raji et al. (2021), Jin et al. (2021), Rogers (2021), Morris et al. (2020), Hauser et al. (2021), and Welty et al. (2019). These observations motivate a closer look at how claims are operationalized within experimental designs.

Recent advancements introduce doubly robust estimators, targeted maximum likelihood estimation, outcome regression with machine learning, and balancing approaches such as entropy balancing and kernel mean matching (Bang and Robins, 2005; van der Laan and Rubin, 2006; Athey et al., 2018; Hainmueller, 2012; Gretton et al., 2009), as well as modern causal forests, Bayesian propensity score models, deep representation learning for deconfounding, and semiparametric efficiency frameworks (Wager and Athey, 2018; McCandless et al., 2009; Johansson et al., 2016; Robins et al., 1994). Yet these techniques rely on correct model specification, overlap, and careful diagnostics to mitigate bias.

text: More importantly, Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. ( 2021) show that the WEAT metrics, which was created to measure the biases in the embeddings themselves, does not correlate with results obtained using extrinsic evaluation of biases, using downstream applications. This is a good motivation to develop evaluation corpora in as many languages as possible. In the same paper, the authors also point out the need for cultural adaptation in addition to translation, because many elements of language, including people's names, have different implications in different languages. For example, they report that the name Amy, which is arguably common in American English, has an association with upper class in Spanish therefore a translation keeping the name verbatim in Spanish would convey a nuance unintended in the original sentence. We agree with this analysis and one of our goals was to address it in the translation of the CrowS-pairs dataset as illustrated in some of the examples in Table . Zhao et al. (2020) study gender bias in a multilingual context. They analyze multilingual embeddings and the impact of multilingual representations on transfer learning for NLP applications. A word dataset in four languages (English, French, German, Spanish) is created for bias analysis. Related evaluations of social bias in multilingual or cross-lingual settings appear in StereoSet (Nadeem et al., 2021), Multilingual LIWC-based analyses (Pennebaker et al., 2015), bias measures for contextualized embeddings (May et al., 2019; Kurita et al., 2019), and transfer-oriented debiasing approaches leveraging XLM-R and mBERT (Conneau et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020; Prost et al., 2019), alongside corpus-level resources that facilitate demographic attribute probing across languages (Bhardwaj et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2018; Swinger et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020).

text: Early works cast event factuality prediction (EFP) as a classification or regression problem and have employed rule-based (Nairn et al., 2006; Lotan et al., 2013) or machine learning approaches (Diab et al., 2009; Rudinger et al., 2018) using hand-engineered features and local lexical cues. Subsequent research incorporated compositional semantics to handle negation, modality, and source attribution, showing that clausal structure and scope profoundly affect factuality judgments. Datasets such as FactBank, MEANTIME, and UW have standardized evaluation and highlighted the importance of consistent annotation schemes across genres. Cross-lingual studies further revealed that morphosyntactic markers of evidentiality and modality vary, complicating transfer and necessitating careful typological consideration. Neural architectures leveraging contextual encoders improved robustness to lexical variation while still struggling with nested scope and long-distance dependencies. Recent neural formulations explore contextual embeddings and graph structures for EFP and related semantics, including span-based models and graph neural networks for factuality and uncertainty (Lee et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020; Rudinger et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2022), dependency-based causal and modal reasoning frameworks (Kwon et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Pyatkin et al., 2021), prompt-tuned encoders for information extraction (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023), and instruction-following large language models for event semantics (Brown et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022; Touvron et al., 2023). These advances coincide with a shift from purely sentence-level modeling to discourse-aware frameworks that propagate beliefs across mentions and documents. Prior document-level EFP systems often rely on pipeline architectures that separately detect events, sources, and cues before attributing factuality. While pipelines can modularize the task, they incur cascading errors and require extensive feature engineering or auxiliary components. Joint models mitigate error propagation but can be brittle when supervision is sparse or annotation schemas diverge. Probabilistic formulations that encode scope constraints offer principled inference yet tend to be computationally intensive for large corpora. Our work is most closely related to that of Yao et al. (2021), which casts EFP as modal dependency parsing. However, they first extract events and conceivers and then build the MDS by ranking the candidate parents for each event. In contrast, we perform modal dependency parsing by constructing a prompt with the event to predict its conceiver parent, simplifying the pipeline. We further reduce reliance on task-specific labels through in-context formulations that allow the model to condition on exemplars rather than fixed classifiers. This approach aims to couple source attribution with factuality inference via a unified decoding problem. To evaluate, we consider both sentence- and document-level settings to assess generalization under distribution shift. We adopt standard metrics for factuality and parent assignment, ensuring comparability with prior reports. Our training objective balances correctness of parent selection with calibration of factuality scores. We also analyze error types associated with cue detection, implicit sources, and conflicting attributions across a document. Our ablations test sensitivity to prompt format, context window size, and negative sampling of distractor parents. We evaluate data efficiency by progressively subsampling supervision and measuring degradation in attribution accuracy. To facilitate reproducibility, we release code, prompts, and processed datasets aligned with prior benchmarks. Finally, we discuss implications for downstream event analytics where provenance-aware factuality supports trustworthy summarization and forecasting. Our prompt-based approach also bears resemblance to works applying prompt-based learning to other NLP tasks, such as event extraction (Liu et al., 2020; Fincke et al., 2021), relation extraction, named entity recognition, and coreference resolution. We conclude by outlining open challenges in modeling nested modality and capturing multi-source disagreement under limited supervision.

text: Table  summarizes existing datasets for Hate and Counter-hate detection. Most of them do not include context information. In other words, the preceding comments are not provided when annotating Targets. Context does affect human judgments and has been taken into account for Hate detection (Gao and Huang, 2017;Vidgen et al., 2021;Pavlopoulos et al., 2020;Menini et al., 2021). Gao and Huang (2017) annotate hateful comments in the nested structures of 10 Fox News discussion threads. Vidgen et al. To our knowledge, we are the first to investigate the role of context in Hate and Counter-hate detection.

text: Model Robustness to Entity Substitution. It is non-trivial for NLP models to be able to properly handle the large space of named entities. Previous works use entity substitution to audit or improve model robustness on different tasks like NER (Agarwal et al., 2020;Lin et al., 2021), Natural Language Inference (Mitra et al., 2020). Recent studies on robustness-enhancing strategies in MRC and related tasks span data augmentation with adversarial triggers and paraphrases (Jia and Liang, 2017; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Si et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021), calibration and uncertainty-aware decoding (Kadavath et al., 2022; Desai and Durrett, 2020; Minderer et al., 2021; Jagannatha et al., 2020), robust pretraining and domain generalization (Hendrycks et al., 2020; Arjovsky et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Sagawa et al., 2020), and entity-aware modeling or substitution protocols (Agarwal et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021; Zmigrod et al., 2019; Balasubramanian et al., 2020), but the literature has also explored counterfactual data augmentation and invariance testing across benchmarks (Kaushik et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020; Khashabi et al., 2020; Talmor et al., 2020). Despite these efforts, entity substitution in MRC poses distinct challenges because answer spans, coreference chains, and world knowledge interact, creating failure modes that differ from token-level paraphrases.

text: Introduction Textual EL has matured with robust benchmarks and methods, yet entity-centric applications increasingly involve images and text together in the wild. There is vast prior research on textual entity linking. Multiple datasets have been proposed over the years including the manuallyannotated high-quality datasets like AIDA (Hoffart et al., 2011), automatically-annotated large-scale datasets like CWEB (Guo and Barbosa, 2018) and zero-shot datasets like Zeshel (Logeswaran et al., 2019). To evaluate the EL models' performance, it is usual to train on the AIDA-train dataset, and test on the datasets of AIDA-test, MSNBC (Cucerzan, 2007), AQUAINT (Milne and Witten, 2008), DBpedia Spotlight (Daiber et al., 2013), TAC-KBP EL (Ji et al., 2010), and WNED (Guo and Barbosa, 2018). Recent neural models span local-collective graph approaches (Ganea and Hofmann, 2017), bi-encoder and cross-encoder retrievers (Gillick et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020), span-based disambiguation with pre-trained transformers (Yamada et al., 2020), and end-to-end EL pipelines over Wikipedia/Wikidata (Kolitsas et al., 2018; Broscheit, 2019). Additional resources include Wikipedia hyperlinks (Spitkovsky et al., 2012), Wikidata descriptions (Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014), and cross-lingual corpora such as Mewsli-9 (Botha et al., 2020). However, as mentioned in (Cao et al., 2021), many methods have achieved high and similar results within recent three years. One possible explanation is that it may simply be near the ceiling of what can be achieved for these datasets, and it is difficult to conduct further research based on them. This observation motivates a closer look at settings where textual context alone is insufficient for disambiguation.

text: Background and Motivation Multimodal EL aims to ground mentions in text to a knowledge base while leveraging complementary visual cues to reduce ambiguity. In recent years, the growing trend towards multimodality requires to extend the research of EL from monomodality to multimodality. Moon et al. (2018), Zhang et al. (2020), Chen et al. (2021), and Peng (2021) propose three MEL datasets, which are built from Weibo, Wikipedia, and Richpedia information and use CNDBpedia, Wikidata, and Richpedia as the corresponding KBs, alongside related benchmarks such as XMEL (Zhang et al., 2022), WikiDiverse-MEL (Liu et al., 2023), and WebQSP-Vis (Huang et al., 2022). Methods range from visual-semantic alignment via multimodal transformers (Lu et al., 2019; Tan and Bansal, 2019), cross-modal contrastive pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021), entity-aware visual grounding (Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), and fusion-based disambiguation with region features (Anderson et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019). Datasets for related tasks include entity-centric image-caption corpora (Biten et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2020), multimodal NER (Lu et al., 2018; Arshad et al., 2021), and multimodal relation extraction (Zheng et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). However, using Wikipedia as the target dataset may lead to the data leakage problem as many language models are pretrained on it. Prior work has also noted that noisy social media images and informal text present new failure modes for canonical EL pipelines.
