text: Prior work on OpenIE spans rule-based extractors (Banko et al., 2007; Fader et al., 2011), clause-based and dependency-driven systems (Del Corro and Gemulla, 2013; Angeli et al., 2015), neural sequence labeling and tagging approaches (Stanovsky et al., 2018; Kolluru et al., 2020), encoder–decoder models with constrained decoding (Cui et al., 2018; Roy et al., 2019), calibration and confidence estimation methods (He et al., 2015; Jiang and Marquez, 2016), and standardized benchmarks such as OIE2016, CaRB, MinIE, and WiRe57, as well as downstream uses in QA and KB population (Etzioni et al., 2011; Mausam, 2016). Recent analyses emphasize the ambiguity in gold annotations across benchmarks, where minimal vs. context-rich tuples are scored differently under token-level and tuple-level metrics. Concurrently, there has been movement toward models that jointly segment, label, and canonicalize extractions, with constraints that penalize overlapping arguments and hallucinated predicates. These developments raise the question of how to evaluate tuple integrity when multiple semantically equivalent forms exist for a single sentence.

text: Recent studies on robustness and safety span a broad set of techniques and perspectives, including gradient-based word substitutions and paraphrase generation for adversarial crafting (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Alzantot et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019; Jin et al., 2020), certified and provable defenses for text classifiers (Jia et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Ye et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2021), robustness benchmarks that target semantic invariances and perturbation resilience (Ribeiro et al., 2018; Gardner et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Goel et al., 2021), and safety evaluations for toxicity and bias in dialogue and language models (Gehman et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2020; Welbl et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021). Building on the observation that imperceptible perturbations are especially harmful in open-domain dialogue, we focus on the intersection of adversarial methods and safety metrics.

text: We evaluate on open-domain conversational datasets using both pretrained and safety-aligned dialogue models. Our experiments compare attack success, toxicity elevation, and perceptual indistinguishability under constrained budgets. We further ablate lexicon-sensitive versus semantic-invariance attacks to disentangle surface perturbations from meaning-preserving transformations. Parallel threads examine prompt-based and instruction-tuned models under adversarial prompting and safety interventions, covering red teaming protocols (Perez et al., 2022; Ganguli et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Perez et al., 2023), jailbreak taxonomies and defenses (Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023), toxicity and harassment benchmarks for conversational systems (Gehman et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021; Vidgen et al., 2021), and multilingual robustness datasets and methods (Xu et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2023; Leong et al., 2023). Finally, we discuss implications for safe deployment and identify open challenges in certifying robustness for conversational safety.

text: Hierarchical solutions. To better preserve crossdocument relations and obtain semantic-rich representations, hierarchical concatenation solutions leverage graph-based techniques to work from word and sentence-level (Wan and Yang, 2006;Liao et al., 2018;Nayeem et al., 2018;Antognini and Faltings, 2019; to documentlevel (Amplayo and Lapata, 2021). Other hierarchical approaches include multi-head pooling and inter-paragraph attention architectures (Liu and Lapata, 2019a), attention models with Maximal Marginal Relevance (Fabbri et al., 2019), and attention across different granularity representations (Jin et al., 2020). Such models are often datasetspecific because of the custom architecture, so they struggle to adapt to other datasets and effectively leverage pre-trained state-of-the-art transformers.

text: Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding. Knowledge graph embedding learning (Bordes et al., 2013;Yang et al., 2014;Trouillon et al., 2016;Dettmers et al., 2018;Shang et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2019;Ji et al., 2021) has been an active research area with applications directly in knowledge base completion and relation extractions. Recently, there are several works that extended the static KG embedding models to temporal KGs. Jiang et al. (2016) first attempt to extend TransE (Bordes et al., 2013)   (Lacroix et al., 2020) extends the ComplEx with time based on the canonical decomposition of tensors of order 4. Building on these foundational efforts, subsequent temporal KGE approaches diversify along representation choices and training signals, including diachronic embeddings (Trivedi et al., 2017;Goel et al., 2020), time-aware scoring functions such as TNTComplEx and TuckER-Bi (Lacroix et al., 2020;Balazevic et al., 2019), event-centric formulations treating time as first-class entities (García-Durán et al., 2018;HyTE, Dasgupta et al., 2018), and neural encoders that parameterize temporal evolution with recurrent or attention-based dynamics (Sarkar et al., 2020;Xu et al., 2020), alongside evaluation on standard temporal benchmarks like ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, YAGO11k, and WIKIDATA12k.

text: In this paper, we use the advanced encoderdecoder framework, Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), to introduce the language generation models. To simplify the process, we simply format the main self-attention network (SAN) module and do not involve other modules (e.g., positional encoding, multiple stacked layers, and so on). Encoder represents the source input X={x 1 , • • • , x J } as the source representation H= {h 1 , • • • , h J } using SANs. Decoder then generates the target sentence word-by-word based on H with attention mechanism and the generated target fragment. Specifically, given a sequence of word vectors in the generated target fragment {E is the embedding matrix of the target language vocabulary), they are packed into keyvalue matrices K i−1 and V i−1 at the i-th time-step. At each decoding step, we form the query from the current state and retrieve information through scaled dot-product attention. The attention weights over K i−1 and V i−1 are normalized with softmax to ensure a convex combination of values. where the function M(•) packs a sequence of word vectors into a matrix. Another SelfATT s module is then used to learn the target representation s i. We regularize SelfATT s with dropout and share projections across heads to control parameter growth. where c i−1 ∈R d model is the previous context vector and d model is the dimension of language generation model. s i is then fed into another SelfATT c to compute the dependent-time context vector c i. We interleave SelfATT s and SelfATT c to balance autoregressive target modeling and source conditioning. where K e and V e are key and value matrices, respectively, that are transformed from the source representation H according to Eq.(1). The probability distribution P g (y i |y <i , X) is then computed using the MLP layer. Finally, we apply layer normalization before the output projection to stabilize training dynamics. (4) y i with the maximum probability is selected as the output of decoder at the i-th time-step. Prior work on neural sequence generation spans recurrent encoder–decoders with attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015;Luong et al., 2015), convolutional sequence models (Gehring et al., 2017), the original Transformer and its scaled variants (Vaswani et al., 2017;Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020), and training refinements such as label smoothing, scheduled sampling, and minimum risk training (Szegedy et al., 2016;Bengio et al., 2015;Shen et al., 2016), as well as evaluation datasets like WMT14 En–De, IWSLT14 De–En, and OpenSubtitles. We adopt standard teacher forcing during training and switch to greedy decoding for clarity in exposition. To obtain the language generation model θ, the training objective maximizes the conditional generation probability over the training dataset {[X, Y]}: J (θ) = P g (Y|X; θ). We optimize J (θ) with Adam and employ inverse-sqrt learning rate decay with warmup. For completeness, we clip gradients to avoid exploding updates in early training. During evaluation, we compute sequence-level scores and also report per-token cross-entropy as a diagnostic. We ablate the contribution of SelfATT s and SelfATT c to quantify their respective roles. Implementation details, including tokenization and batching, are provided in the appendix for reproducibility.

text: While there are various tasks and datasets, the underlying associations between language and visual concepts are often common across different tasks (Lu et al., 2020). Therefore, we use CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) to study the TARA dataset in this paper. CLIP is a recently released state-ofthe-art image representation model, and has shown impressive performance on various tasks through pre-training on 400 million image and captions pairs collected from the internet. Recent literature surveys cover broad vision-language grounding and retrieval formulations and list a variety of benchmarks and methods without unifying perspective or explicit linkage to any particular research agenda, including ViLBERT (Lu et al., 2019), UNITER (Chen et al., 2020), VisualBERT (Li et al., 2019), OSCAR (Li et al., 2020), LXMERT (Tan and Bansal, 2019), VQA v2 (Goyal et al., 2017), Flickr30k Entities (Plummer et al., 2015), RefCOCO/RefCOCO+ (Yu et al., 2016), and WebQA (Chang et al., 2022). Spatio-temporal IE from Texts There has been extensive work on identifying temporal expressions and their associations with events in texts. Uz-Zaman et al. (2013); Ning et al. (2018) focus on temporal information extraction within the local contexts, and Zhou et al. (2020Zhou et al. ( , 2021 further extends the scope to consider contextual information from external texts. The NLP community has also investigated spacial information extraction, with geocoding (Gritta et al., 2018;Kulkarni et al., 2020), which maps mentions to geological coordinates, being closest to our scope.

text: BERT Benchmarks An integral part involved in developing various PLMs is providing NLU multitask benchmarks used to demonstrate the linguistic abilities of new models and approaches. English BERT models are evaluated on 3 standard major benchmarks. The Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) is used to test paragraph level reading comprehension abilities. Wang et al. (2018) selected a diverse and relatively hard set of sentence and sentence-pair tasks which comprise the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. The SWAG (Situations With Adversarial Generations) dataset (Zellers et al., 2018) presents models with partial description of grounded situations to see if they can consistently predict relevant scenarios that come next thus indicating the ability for commonsense reasoning. When evaluating Hebrew PLMs, one of the key pitfalls is that there are no Hebrew versions for these benchmarks. Furthermore, none of the suggested benchmarks account for examining the capacity of PLMs. In particular, currently there is no standard accepted way for evaluating the word-internal morphological structures which are inherent for MRLs and for the Hebrew language. BERT Devlin et al. (2019) produced 2 BERT models for English and Chinese. To support other languages they trained a multilingual BERT (mBERT) model combining texts covering over 100 languages. They hoped to benefit low resourced languages with the linguistic information obtained from other languages with large dataset sizes. In reality however mBERT performance on specific languages have not been as successful as English. A parallel literature has explored alternatives and extensions to BERT and mBERT across pretraining objectives, architectures, and evaluation suites, including XLNet with permutation language modeling (Yang et al., 2019), RoBERTa with larger batch training and dynamic masking (Liu et al., 2019), XLM and XLM-R for cross-lingual pretraining at scale (Conneau and Lample, 2019; Conneau et al., 2020), ELECTRA with replaced token detection (Clark et al., 2020), ALBERT with parameter sharing (Lan et al., 2020), T5 and mT5 as text-to-text transformers for multilingual tasks (Raffel et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021), and evaluation resources such as SuperGLUE (Wang et al., 2019), XTREME and XTREME-R (Hu et al., 2020; Ruder et al., 2021), and TyDi QA for typologically diverse question answering (Clark et al., 2020b).

text: What is worse, for an LM-based chatbot, its training conversations are prone to include more private attributes than other commonly-used corpora for language modeling like BooksCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015) and Wikipedia. Tigunova et al. (2019) proposed Hidden Attribute Model (HAM) to extract professions and genders of speakers from various dialog datasets.  further applied Attribute Extractor to generate speakers' attribute triplets flexibly and suggested downstream tasks based on the triplets. Pan et al. (2020) exploited embeddings of language models to recover inputs' digits and keywords. Additional efforts on privacy in conversational AI include membership inference against dialogue models (Shokri et al., 2017), exposure measurement in generative models (Carlini et al., 2019), privacy-preserving training via differential privacy (Abadi et al., 2016), and representation-level attacks leveraging gradient leakage (Zhu et al., 2019), alongside defenses such as PATE (Papernot et al., 2017) and federated learning with secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al., 2017). Though the setup of this work is similar to ours, they merely considered simple cases of data recovery with given rules and suffered great utility degradation to obtain optimal defense performance. For our work, there is no fixed pattern or rule for the model input. Instead of finding keywords or recovering digits, we aim to infer more complicated private attributes from such embeddings. Moreover, our proposed defenses have almost no influence on the utility.

text: Prior work on negation spans data resources, rule-based parsing, and neural modeling, including BioScope (Vincze et al., 2008), ConanDoyle-Neg (Morante and Daelemans, 2012), PB-FOC (Blanco and Moldovan, 2011), SFU Review Corpus (Konstantinova et al., 2012), CoNLL 2010 shared task datasets (Farkas et al., 2010), dependency-based scope detectors (Councill et al., 2010;Morante and Blanco, 2012), neural sequence labeling approaches (Zou et al., 2019;Khandelwal and Sawant, 2020), and cross-lingual negation resources (Rosenthal et al., 2015). More related to the work presented here, Sarabi et al. (2019) present a corpus of negations and their underlying affirmative interpretations (they call them positive interpretations). We are inspired by them but bypass several of their limitations. First, they only work with negations from Simple Wikipedia, a site devoted to English learners. As a result, their corpus uses (relatively) unsophisticated vocabulary and grammar. Second, they impose several restrictions on the negations they work with (e.g., negation cue modifies root verb, sentences between 6 and 25 tokens and not including certain tokens (because, until, etc.)). Third, their affirmative interpretations are restricted to a rephrasing of the statement containing negation with only one change: an argument of the negated predicate. In contrast, we barely impose restrictions on the negations we work with (no questions and no auxiliary verbs). More importantly, we introduce a questiondriven approach that allow us to obtain multiple affirmative interpretations with increasing degrees of complexity (see examples in Table ).

text: Non-autoregressive generation is originally proposed for machine translation (Gu et al., 2018). Recently, Jia et al. (2021) apply non-autoregressive models to extractive document-level summarization; Su et al. (2021) stack a non-autoregressive BERT model with a conditional random field (CRF) for abstractive summarization; since the summary is shorter than the input text, their approach puts multiple end-to-sequence (EOS) tokens at the end of the sentence, and thus is unable to utilize the strong input-output correspondence in the summarization task. Yang et al. (2021) apply auxiliary part-of-speech (POS) loss and  explore pretraining strategies for encoder-decoder non-autoregressive summarization; their length is given by POS tag/EOS predictions. Recently, Jia et al. (2021) apply non-autoregressive models to extractive document-level summarization; Su et al. (2021) stack a non-autoregressive BERT with a CRF for abstractive summarization; Yang et al. (2021) explore auxiliary POS losses and pretraining strategies; related advances in length-aware decoding and constrained generation appear in Kikuchi et al. (2016), Fan et al. (2018), Liu et al. (2022), and Xu et al. (2023). All these studies concern supervised summarization, and none can explicitly control the output length. By contrast, our paper focuses on unsupervised summarization. We adopt CTC training in our encoderonly architecture, allowing blank tokens to better align input and output words, which is more appropriate for summarization. We further propose a dynamic programming algorithm to control the summary length.

text: Seed-Guided Topic Discovery. Seed-guided topic models aim to leverage user-provided seeds to discover underlying topics according to users' interests. Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning. For example, Andrzejewski et al. (2009) consider must-link and cannot-link constraints among seeds as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed relevant information. Subsequent work also explores user interaction, posterior regularization, and semi-supervision in related formulations (Ramage et al., 2009; Mei et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2013). Recent studies start to utilize embedding techniques to learn better word semantics. For example, CatE (Meng et al., 2020) explicitly encourages distinction among retrieved topics via categoryname guided embedding learning. However, all these models require the provided seeds to be invocabulary, mainly because they focus on the input corpus only and are not equipped with general knowledge of PLMs.

text: Embedding-Based Topic Discovery. A number of studies extend LDA to involve word embedding. The common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), and CGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). Some other studies think out of the LDA backbone. For example, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings. CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling and word embedding by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word-topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings (e.g., word2vec or BERT) also generates good topics; Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not. These models are unsupervised and hard to be applied to seed-guided settings. In contrast, our SEETOPIC framework joint leverages PLMs, word embeddings, and seed information.

text: Other work has focused on creating automated cloze tests by controlling aspects of the proposed gaps so that they correlate with a target proficiency level. , for example, manipulate the difficulty of C-tests (open cloze tests with hints, Grotjahn et al. (2002)) by varying the position and word length of the gaps. A similar concept is presented by Settles et al. (2020) and McCarthy et al. (2021), although difficulty is predicted using a machine-learning model that correlates with CEFR levels. In these cases, tests are dynamically adapted to the examinee's proficiency level during the test session. From a different perspective, Felice and Buttery (2019) show that controlling gap entropy can be useful for designing open cloze tests at different CEFR levels. The work we present in this paper, however, aims to model the more complex task of predicting a full set of gaps at the paragraph level that comply with design and testing principles and is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to employ and adapt transformer-based models for this task.

text: Recent studies catalog a variety of mitigation strategies spanning constrained decoding and calibration (Kumar and Talukdar, 2021;Nie et al., 2021), post-hoc factuality ranking (Kryściński et al., 2020;Goyal and Durrett, 2021), retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021), instruction tuning and preference optimization (Ouyang et al., 2022;Rafailov et al., 2023), and automatic verification with external knowledge bases or tool use (Thorne et al., 2018;Schick et al., 2023;Creswell et al., 2022). However, the interaction between these interventions and domain shift, prompt sensitivity, and input noise is not yet fully characterized by standardized stress-testing.

text: Recent studies present a range of compression and acceleration strategies for pre-trained Transformers across tasks and modalities, including layer dropping and head pruning in encoder-only models (Voita et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019), width/depth scaling for efficient pre-training and fine-tuning (Turc et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2022), structured sparsity and block-wise pruning for deployment efficiency (Lagunas et al., 2021; Frantar and Alistarh, 2023; Mao et al., 2020), low-bit quantization with post-training and quantization-aware variants (Zafrir et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Dettmers et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021), and retrieval-augmented or mixture-of-experts architectures that trade parameter count for conditional computation (Lewis et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2021; Du et al., 2022; Artetxe et al., 2021).

text: The scope of peer-review text analysis has broadened to include aspects such as rating prediction, calibration, and meta-review synthesis. Several studies investigate score rationales by linking textual evidence to score justifications, while others examine disagreement patterns across reviewers and the effect of rebuttals on final decisions. Recent efforts also leverage large-scale datasets and modeling resources that explore review helpfulness, score calibration, and rebuttal dynamics without a unified perspective on how these strands relate to one another or converge on design principles (Kang et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022; Ghosal et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020; Miguel et al., 2021). In parallel, domain adaptation and cross-venue analyses have revealed differences in reviewing norms that complicate direct model transfer.

text: Parameter-Efficient Tuning of PLMs. As it is increasingly infeasible to train and store full copies of large PLMs for various downstream tasks, how to efficiently tune the PLMs with few trainable parameters becomes critical. Existing PELT methods can be largely divided into two categories based on whether new trainable parameters are introduced. Specifically, one may either train a subset of the model parameters such as the prediction head or inject small modules that modulate frozen backbones. Classic full fine-tuning offers strong task performance but scales poorly in memory and deployment cost. Adapters insert small bottlenecks per layer to reduce the number of updated weights while preserving frozen parameters. Low-rank updates such as LoRA reduce memory and compute by constraining update matrices to be low rank. Prompt-based techniques optimize task-specific continuous prompts or prefixes that steer the model without updating core weights. BitFit constrains updates to biases, and mask-based schemes select a sparse set of parameters to train. Quantization-aware parameter-efficient tuning further reduces memory by combining low-bit storage with lightweight adaptation. Recent literature has explored adapters that insert lightweight bottleneck layers between transformer blocks (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021; He et al., 2022), low-rank adaptation that decomposes weight updates into rank-constrained matrices (Hu et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023), prompt- and prefix-tuning that condition the model via learned continuous vectors (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner, 2021; Liu et al., 2023), as well as reparameterization strategies including BitFit and bias-only tuning (Ben-Zaken et al., 2022) and sparse masking approaches (Sung et al., 2021; Ansell et al., 2022), along with quantization-aware PEFT that adapts low-bit backbones (Frantar et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Despite numerous advances, open questions remain regarding trade-offs among capacity, stability, and transfer across tasks. Empirically, parameter-efficient methods can approach full fine-tuning on many classification and generation tasks, yet systematic regressions appear under distribution shift. The interplay between adaptation placement, optimizer choice, and initialization often dictates convergence speed and final accuracy. From a systems perspective, PEFT facilitates multi-tenant serving by sharing a frozen backbone across many lightweight adapters. Storage and I/O costs are dominated by the base model, while swapping small deltas amortizes deployment overhead. In multilingual and multi-domain settings, PEFT variants can selectively capture domain idiosyncrasies without catastrophic interference. However, the design space is large, and best practices vary with model size and task complexity. Robust evaluation therefore needs to cover diverse tasks, metrics, and data regimes. For sequence-to-sequence and instruction-following tasks, careful prompt formatting and stabilization tricks mitigate optimization brittleness. When data are scarce, strong regularization and calibration of prompt length or rank improve reliability. Finally, reproducibility demands transparent reporting of hyperparameters, data preprocessing, and model variants. We now present our framework that unifies adapter placement with rank-constrained updates and stable prompt initialization. Our experiments target both low-resource and cross-domain generalization benchmarks. We quantify memory-accuracy Pareto frontiers under realistic serving constraints. We also ablate architectural and optimization choices to isolate their effects. Results indicate consistent gains in stability without sacrificing parameter efficiency. We release code and configuration files to facilitate community adoption.

text: In this section, we first briefly introduce a mainstream NMT framework, Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), with a focus on how to generate prediction probabilities. We describe how token-level probabilities are produced by the decoder through attention-mediated context fusion and softmax normalization over the vocabulary. We then review standard training objectives, including cross-entropy with teacher forcing, and discuss how label smoothing alters the target distribution. Next, we summarize how beam search converts local token probabilities into sequence-level hypotheses under length and coverage normalizations. We also outline how exposure bias and search heuristics interact with probability estimates at inference time. Building on these preliminaries, we turn to the problem of confidence estimation and calibration in neural machine translation. Recent advances in calibration and uncertainty for sequence models report diverse strategies across architectures and tasks without a unified perspective (Guo et al., 2017;Kumar et al., 2019;Minderer et al., 2021;Mejia et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2021;Desai and Durrett, 2020;Kong et al., 2020;Ott et al., 2018), spanning temperature scaling, label smoothing, focal losses, Bayesian approximations, and post-hoc mapping functions. We next quantify miscalibration by measuring Expected Calibration Error at both token- and sequence-level granularities. Specifically, we compute reliability diagrams for predicted probabilities, examining overconfidence in high-frequency tokens and underconfidence in rare constructions. We additionally assess segment-level confidence using minimum Bayes risk decoding with utility-weighted calibration metrics. Our analysis reveals systematic deviations between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy across domains and language pairs. We find that domain shift exacerbates miscalibration, particularly when training data underrepresents morphology-rich targets. Furthermore, we observe that length normalization can mask severe token-level overconfidence in long outputs. These findings motivate approaches that adjust probabilities with structure-aware post-hoc transforms. We therefore investigate calibration mechanisms that couple token contexts with sequence constraints. Finally, we discuss practical implications for risk-sensitive applications such as interactive translation and quality estimation. We conclude by outlining evaluation protocols to ensure fair comparisons across calibration methods.

text: 2.1 Cognitively Inspired NLP Using NLP Representations for Brain Activity Prediction Since the pioneering work (Mitchell et al., 2008), connecting statistical NLP representations with cognition has attracted widespread attention. A substantial body of research has explored how distributed word and sentence representations correlate with neural signals measured via fMRI, EEG, MEG, and ECoG across a range of stimuli and tasks. Recent efforts span representational similarity analysis linking embeddings to fMRI (Huth et al., 2016; Caucheteux and King, 2022), MEG decoding with transformer layers (Toneva and Wehbe, 2019; Jain and Huth, 2018), EEG alignment to surprisal and entropy (Frank et al., 2015; Heilbron et al., 2022), probing semantic vectors with intracranial recordings (Pereira et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020), cross-modal alignment with CLIP-style pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022), and task-driven analyses of language areas using fine-tuned LMs (Schrimpf et al., 2021; Caucheteux et al., 2023), alongside benchmark datasets such as Pereira2018, Narratives, and BOLD5000. Collectively, this literature underscores shared structure between linguistic computation and brain activity while raising open questions about temporal dynamics and causal mechanistic explanations. Parallel strands in cognitive modeling evaluate how inductive biases and training curricula shape the emergence of linguistic abstractions under capacity limitations. Work on multi-task and transfer learning indicates that auxiliary supervision can bias representations toward features beneficial for generalization across tasks and domains. In representation learning, contrastive objectives and masked language modeling have been examined as implicit curricula that align with human-like predictive processing constraints. The intersection of these threads suggests a framework in which neural language models provide testable hypotheses about representational geometry and processing costs in the brain. Within NLP, task transfer methods exploit shared substructures to improve sample efficiency and robustness under distribution shift. Modular approaches further decompose learning into reusable components that can be recombined across tasks with minimal adaptation. Recent benchmarks have emphasized low-resource and cross-domain generalization to stress-test the reliability of transfer methods. Methodologically, progress relies on precise evaluation protocols that disentangle gains from data scale, architecture, and supervision types. Finally, we highlight the need for standards that bridge cognitive plausibility with engineering desiderata, enabling cumulative progress on both scientific and applied fronts.

text: Zero-shot methods for relation extraction have explored a wide array of formulations and resources, including slot filling with reading comprehension templates (Levy et al., 2017), natural language inference casts of relation labels (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018;Yin et al., 2019;Soares et al., 2019), semantic matching with description encoders (Broscheit, 2019;Chen and Li, 2021;Han et al., 2018), and concept-level generalization with knowledge-graph text corpora (Xiong et al., 2018;Baldini Soares et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020). Parallel advances combine meta-learning with episodic training over relation descriptions (Geng et al., 2021;Bansal et al., 2020) and use large pretrained encoders to align entity mentions and label semantics (Wu et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2021;Ye et al., 2022). Recent benchmarks and resources provide open-domain settings for evaluating unseen relations (Levy et al., 2017;TACRED-ZS;FewRel;Wiki-ZSL).

text: Iterative Text Revision Datasets. While some prior works have constructed iterative text revision datasets, they are limited to singular writing domains, such as Wikipedia-style articles (Anthonio et al., 2020), academic essays (Zhang et al., 2017 or news articles (Spangher and May, 2021). In this work, we develop a unified taxonomy to analyze the characteristics of iterative text revision behaviors across different domains and collect large scale text revisions of human writings from multiple domains. Beyond revision-specific research, related strands include document-level rewriting and controllable editing in general, where approaches range from sequence-to-sequence editing with learned operation tags to plan-based or constraint-driven revision pipelines (Dong et al., 2019; Malmi et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Reid and Neubig, 2022; Kumar et al., 2022; Panthaplackel et al., 2021; Krishna et al., 2023). text: It was first introduced in (Hu et al., 2016a), where they generate the referent's segmentation mask by directly concatenating visual features from CNN with tiled language features from LSTM.  generates refined segmentation masks by incorporating multi-scale semantic information from the image. Since each word in expression makes a different contribution in identifying the desired object, (Shi et al., 2018) model visual context for each word separately using query attention. (Ye et al., 2019) uses a self-attention mechanism to capture long-range correlations between visual and textual modalities while improving feature aggregation. Recent extensions consider compositional reasoning and cross-modal alignment with graph structures, transformers, and multi-stage fusion, reporting gains on standard benchmarks and datasets without detailing implications for downstream RIS or REC design (Liu et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Kamath et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022; Krishna et al., 2017; Kazemzadeh et al., 2014; Mao et al., 2016; Plummer et al., 2015; Pont-Tuset et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2016b; Rohrbach et al., 2016; Plummer et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2019). Despite these advances, challenges remain in segmenting small or heavily occluded referents and in resolving ambiguous expressions that require fine-grained relational cues. In this work, we build upon dense pixel-level multi-modal alignment to better capture fine structures while maintaining robustness to distractors. We adopt a modular design that disentangles language grounding, visual refinement, and cross-scale fusion, allowing the model to adapt to expressions of varying granularity. Our approach leverages proposal-free backbones to avoid biases induced by detection anchors and to preserve spatial precision. We further incorporate soft linguistic priors that modulate feature propagation across scales to favor regions consistent with the expression semantics. Finally, we evaluate on multiple benchmarks to assess generalization across domains and expression styles, and we analyze the contributions of each component through targeted ablations.

text: Related directions span a broad space including bias mitigation in NLP (Zhao et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Barocas et al., 2019), parameter-efficient transfer methods such as adapters and LoRA (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021), calibration and logit adjustment for imbalanced learning (Menon et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2019; Gong et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2017), and output-layer modeling in sequence tasks (Press and Wolf, 2017; Yang et al., 2018; Shazeer, 2019; He et al., 2021). These strands highlight tooling that touches either the output distribution or the efficiency of adaptation. Yet the specific mechanics of bias vectors remain comparatively opaque. Prior reports often treat biases as incidental offsets rather than controllable levers. Moreover, evaluation typically emphasizes accuracy without decomposing calibration or margin sensitivity. This obscures when and why bias-only updates help. A clearer taxonomy would separate initialization, constraint, and regularization schemes for bias parameters. It would also align measurement with hypothesized causal pathways.

text: Comparable resources span explanation-augmented datasets such as E-SNLI (Camburu et al., 2018), CoS-E (Rajani et al., 2019), e-SNLI-VE (Kayser et al., 2021), and ECQA (Aggarwal et al., 2021), alongside rationale-centric corpora like ERASER (DeYoung et al., 2020), MultiRC rationales (Khashabi et al., 2018), HotpotQA supporting facts (Yang et al., 2018), and FEVER evidence (Thorne et al., 2018), as well as program-of-thought and chain-of-thought style collections derived from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), StrategyQA (Geva et al., 2021), AQuA-RAT (Ling et al., 2017), and OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018). In parallel, automatic short-answer grading (ASAG) research has built benchmarks including ASAP-SAS (Kaggle/ASAP, 2012), Mohler et al. (2011), SemEval-2013 STS student response corpora (Agirre et al., 2013), Beetle/Beetle2 (Dzikovska et al., 2012; Dzikovska et al., 2013), SciEntsBank (Dzikovska et al., 2013), and CREG (Ott et al., 2012), while related evaluation-oriented datasets cover BEA grammatical error corpora (Bryant et al., 2019), MACE/H-Swag style annotation aggregation resources (Hovy et al., 2013; Zellers et al., 2019), and rubric-aligned assessment sets such as ASAP-Reader variants, RACE (Lai et al., 2017), and SQuAD rationales (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), together with explanation-trained models like BART-Large (Lewis et al., 2020), T5-11B (Raffel et al., 2020), DeBERTaV3 (He et al., 2021), and Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), and classic similarity methods including BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009), SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), TF–IDF, and Word Mover’s Distance (Kusner et al., 2015), as well as counterfactual and perturbation datasets such as CheckList (Ribeiro et al., 2020), ANLI (Nie et al., 2020), and AdvGLUE (Wang et al., 2021). These corpora and methods collectively delineate a diverse landscape of explanation-bearing resources and assessment tools. Yet the relationship between these assets and content-focused elaborated feedback for short answers remains to be clarified in terms of task-specific requirements, alignment with rubrics, and the granularity of feedback. Consequently, we next outline the operational characteristics of SAF and its annotation protocol to situate it within the broader ecosystem of explanatory and assessment datasets. We emphasize aspects of content validity, evidence localization, and pedagogical actionability that differentiate feedback-oriented annotation from mere justification text. We also discuss licensing, data splits, and quality control procedures relevant to reproducible evaluation. Finally, we sketch anticipated usage scenarios for formative assessment, model critique, and teacher-in-the-loop workflows.

text: Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning. Recently, thanks to the rapid development of multilingual pre-trained language models such as multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), a number of approaches have been proposed for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning on various downstream tasks, including semantic parsing (Sherborne and Lapata, 2021), natural language generation (Shen et al., 2018) and understanding Lauscher et al., 2020). In this work, we claim our method is zeroshot because no non-Chinese CSRL annotations are seen during the CSRL training stage. For decoding, we directly use the cross-lingual CSRL model trained on Chinese CSRL data to analyze conversations in other languages. To our best knowledge, our work is the first step to cross-lingual CSRL. Recent work on cross-lingual generalization also surveys multilingual adapters (Pfeiffer et al., 2020;Ansell et al., 2021), translation-based transfer with knowledge distillation (Kim et al., 2020;Tang et al., 2020), task-adaptive pretraining across languages (Gururangan et al., 2020;Eisenschlos et al., 2019), multilingual prompts and prefix-tuning (Lester et al., 2021;Zhong et al., 2021;Minixhofer et al., 2022), evaluation suites such as XTREME and XGLUE (Hu et al., 2020;Liang et al., 2020), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning frameworks like BitFit and LoRA (Zaken et al., 2022;Hu et al., 2022).

text: Visual Question Answering. The current dominant framework for VQA consists of an image encoder, a question encoder, multimodal fusion, and an answer predictor (Agrawal et al., 2015). To avoid the noises caused by global features, methods Malinowski et al., 2018) introduce various image attention mechanisms into VQA. Instead of directly using visual features from CNN-based feature extractors, to improve the performance of model, BUTD (Anderson et al., 2018) adopts Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) to obtain candidate regional features while Pythia (Jiang et al., 2018) integrates the regional feature with grid-level features. Meanwhile, Lu et al. (2016); Nam et al. (2017) put more attention on learning better question representations. To merge information from different modalities sufficiently, MFB (Yu et al., 2017), MUTAN (Ben-younes et al., 2017), MLB (Kim et al., 2016), BLOCK (Ben-Younes et al., 2019), and MFH (Yu et al., 2018) explored higher-order fusion methods, while SAN (Yang et al., 2016), HAN (Lu et al., 2016), UpDn (Anderson et al., 2018), and ViLBERT (Lu et al., 2019) represent notable alternatives that rely on distinct attention or co-attention formulations without a unifying perspective on their comparative trade-offs. Further, BAN (Kim et al., 2018) and DCN(Nguyen and Okatani, 2018) propose dense co-attention model which directly establish interaction between different modalities with word-level and regional features. Moreover, with the proposal of Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), MCAN and DFAF (Gao et al., 2019) adopt self-attention mechanism to fully excavate the fine-grained information contained in text and image. Meanwhile, to fully cover the holistic scene in an image, MuREL (Cadène et al., 2019) and ReGAT (Li et al., 2019) explicitly incorporate relations between regions into the interaction process. Selvaraju et al. ( 2020) also introduces sub questions into their work, the distinctness between us is that it constructs a Sub-VQA dataset for the subset of reasoning questions in VQA dataset to evaluate consistency of VQA models while we adopt sub questions to achieve task-dividing. Visual Dialogue. Different from VQA, Visual dialogue(VD) is a continuous conversation for images. Several VD tasks (Visual Dialog, GuessWhich (Chattopadhyay et al., 2017), Guess-What?! (de Vries et al., 2017), MMD (Saha et al., 2018)) have been proposed. GuessWhat?!, as a goal-directed dialogue task, requires both players to continuously clarify the reference object through dialogue. The Oracle provides the Questioner with relevant information about the target object by constantly answering yes/no questions raised by the Questioner, and the Guesser generates the final answer based on the historical dialogue. Following the setting, our Co-VQA framework consists of three components, in which Questioner raises SQs, and Oracle answers them one-by-one, finally, Answerer obtains the answer to the original question.

text: The authors of BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) provided the first Chinese BERT model which was trained on Chinese Wikipedia data. On top of that, Cui et al. (2019) trained RoBERTa-wwm-ext with WWM on extended data. Cui et al. (2020) further trained a Chinese ELECTRA model and MacBERT, both of which did not have [MASK] tokens. ELEC-TRA was trained with a token-level binary classification task, which determined whether a token was the original one or artificially replaced. In MacBERT, [MASK] tokens were replaced with synonyms and the model was trained with WWM and ngram masking. ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) was trained with entity masking, similar to WWM yet tokens corresponding to an entity were masked at once. Language features are considered in more recent works. For example, AMBERT and Lattice-BERT (Lai et al., 2021) both take word information into consideration, Chinese-BERT (Sun et al., 2021) utilizes pinyin and glyph of characters, ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) performs entity-level masking, RoBERTa-wwm-ext (Cui et al., 2019) adopts whole-word masking, and MacBERT (Cui et al., 2020) replaces [MASK] with near-synonyms. Chinese-BERT (Sun et al., 2021) utilizes pinyin and glyph of characters to enrich sub-character features. These developments highlight the variety of pretraining objectives and input representations explored for Chinese.

text: In the early stages, , , (Moon et al., 2018) and Arshad et al. (2019) propose to encode the text through RNN and the whole image through CNN, then designing implicit interaction to model information between two modalities to explore multimodal NER tasks. Recently, ;  propose to leverage regional image features to represent objects in the image to exploit fine-grained semantic correspondences based on Transformer and visual backbones. Representative approaches span visual grounding with attention over object regions (Yu et al., 2020; Zhang and Lu, 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023), contrastive pretraining with CLIP-style objectives (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2022), multimodal transformers for token-level alignment (Sun et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023), and graph-based fusion that links detected entities and visual objects (Wang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2022). These lines of work collectively illustrate the rapid maturation of multimodal architectures for fine-grained understanding.

text: Recent advances leveraging pre-trained transformers have explored diverse strategies across domains including sequence labeling and document classification, with notable systems such as RoBERTa-based span classifiers (Liu et al., 2019), ELECTRA discriminators for efficient pre-training (Clark et al., 2020), SpanBERT for span-level representations (Joshi et al., 2020), ALBERT for parameter-efficient scaling (Lan et al., 2020), and multitask fine-tuning regimes on GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks (Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020), alongside task-specific augmentations like back-translation (Edunov et al., 2018), mixup for text (Guo et al., 2020), curriculum learning schedules (Bengio et al., 2009), and contrastive objectives for sentence embeddings (Gao et al., 2021).

text: More recent research has been focusing on improving the memory and computation efficiency of transformer models (Tay et al., 2020b(Tay et al., , 2021 for handling long input. One type of such approaches is using non-full attention patterns to restrict the attention field range, so that it reduces the attention complexity from O(n 2 ) to O(nlogn) or O(n), including Sinkhorn (Tay et al., 2020a), Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), ETC (Ainslie et al., 2020), and BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020a). Another type of approaches is leveraging the low-rank approximation of the attention matrix, such as Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021, Random Feature Attention (Peng et al., 2021), and LUNA (Ma et al., 2021). Recent efforts also explore retrieval-augmented generation and memory-augmented pretraining for scaling context, with retrieval-augmented language models (Guu et al., 2020;Lewis et al., 2020b), kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020), retrofitted pretraining via RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022), and parametric–nonparametric hybrids like ATLAS (Izacard et al., 2022), alongside architectural modifications such as Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020), Routing Transformers (Roy et al., 2021), Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al., 2022), and state-space models like S4 and Mamba (Gu et al., 2021;Gu and Dao, 2023). Despite these advances, a clear understanding of how pretraining objectives interact with sparse or low-rank attention under extreme sequence lengths remains limited. We specifically revisit span corruption under long-context constraints and analyze its behavior when coupled with block-sparse routing and kernelized attention.

text: Interactive evaluation systems attract increasing attention lately. Ghandeharioun et al. (2019) and Deriu and Cieliebak (2019) use dialogues between a bot and itself, which is called self-talk, to evaluate the bot in a more automatic manner. But it often leads to a lot of repeated chat context. Deriu et al. (2020) designed Spot The Bot, a framework that enables a group of bots to chat with each other and then asks humans to annotate if the bots talk more like a human or more like a bot. Recent advances emphasize learned evaluators and task-specific testbeds for dialogue quality, including learned reward models fine-tuned from human feedback and preference data (Stiennon et al., 2020; Bai et al., 2022), reference-free metrics that predict coherence and engagingness (Zhang et al., 2020; Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020), adversarial and stress-test protocols for safety and robustness (Dinan et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021), multi-turn consistency checks (Welleck et al., 2019; Roller et al., 2021), and open-domain benchmarks leveraging human-bot conversations such as ConvAI2, DSTC, and FED (Zhang et al., 2018; Gunasekara et al., 2019; Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020). Prior to our work, there was still no interactive and automatic evaluation framework that works without any participation of human annotators. Our work fills this gap and moreover, it's very flexible since more complex metrics or algorithms can be plugged in as scoring functions. Our results also show that there is a strong correlation between automatic evaluation results and human judgments.

text: Meta-Learning. Meta-Learning aims to improve the learning algorithm itself based on the previously learned experience (Thrun and Pratt, 1998;Hospedales et al., 2021). In general, there are three categories of meta-learning methods: model-based methods, (Santoro et al., 2016;Obamuyide et al., 2019) which depend on the particular model design to facilitate fast learning; metric-based methods, (Vinyals et al., 2016;Snell et al., 2017;Geng et al., 2019) which encode samples into an embedding space and classify them based on the learned distance metric; optimization-based methods (Finn et al., 2017;Mi et al., 2019) that learn a wellgeneralized model initialization which allows for fast adaptation to new tasks. For low-resource scenarios in NLP, optimization-based meta-learning methods achieved promising results on tasks such as personalized dialog generation (Madotto et al., 2019;Song et al., 2020), low-resource machine translation (Gu et al., 2018;Sharaf et al., 2020), few-shot slot tagging (Wang et al., 2021). Recent advances include neural episodic controllers and differentiable neural computers for rapid adaptation (Graves et al., 2016; Pritzel et al., 2017), memory-based meta-learners for one-shot prediction (Santoro et al., 2016; Munkhdalai and Yu, 2017), hierarchical Bayesian formulations of meta-learning (Grant et al., 2018; Ravi and Beatson, 2019), gradient-based formulations and their variants (Finn et al., 2017; Nichol et al., 2018; Rusu et al., 2019), and memory-augmented metric learning approaches (Vinyals et al., 2016; Snell et al., 2017; Oreshkin et al., 2018).

text: There are a number of existing NLP specific detection approaches. For character level attacks, detection approaches have exploited the grammatical (Sakaguchi et al., 2017) and spelling (Mays et al., 1991;Islam and Inkpen, 2009) inconsistencies to identify and detect the adversarial samples. However, these character level attacks are unlikely to be employed in practice due to the simplicity with which they can be detected. Therefore, detection approaches for the more difficult semantically similar attack samples are of greater interest, where the meaning of the textual input is maintained without compromising the spelling or gram-matical integrity. To tackle such word-level, semantically similar examples,  designed a discriminator to classify each token representation as part of an adversarial perturbation or not, which is then used to 'correct' the perturbation. Other detection approaches (Raina et al., 2020;Han et al., 2020;Minervini and Riedel, 2018) have shown some success in using perplexity to identify adversarial textual examples. Recent text robustness literature has produced a wide array of defenses and detectors grounded in language modeling, representation learning, and edit-based heuristics, including adversarial training with semantically constrained perturbations (Jin et al., 2020; Morris et al., 2020), likelihood-ratio or perplexity-based scoring over pretrained LMs (Zhu et al., 2020; Salazar et al., 2020), token-level saliency regularization and attribution smoothing (Shao et al., 2021; Si et al., 2021), and contrastive or consistency-driven objectives for stability under paraphrase (Xie et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). Most recently, (Mozes et al., 2020) achieved state of the art performance with the Frequency Guided Word Substitution (FGWS) detector, where a change in model prediction after substituting out low frequency words is revealing of adversarial samples.

text: Lexically Constrained Translation Existing translation methods impose lexical constraints during either inference or training. At training time, constrained MT models include code-switching data augmentation (Dinu et al., 2019;Song et al., 2019; and training with auxiliary tasks such as token or span-level mask-prediction (Ailem et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2021). At inference time, autoregressive constrained decoding algorithms include utilizing placeholder tag (Luong et al., 2015;Crego et al., 2016), grid beam search (Hokamp and Liu, 2017;Post and Vilar, 2018) and alignment-enhanced decoding (Alkhouli et al., 2018;Song et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2021). For the purpose of efficiency, recent studies also focus on non-autoregressive constrained translation. Susanto et al. (2020) proposes to modify the inference procedure of Levenshtein Transformer (Gu et al., 2019) where they disallow the deletion of constraint words during iterative editing. Xu and Carpuat (2021) further develops this idea and introduces a reposition operation that can reorder the constraint tokens. Recently, researchers have also explored constraint satisfaction through lexically aware prompting, constrained attention masks, bilingual lexicon constraints derived from alignment, and terminology-constrained datasets, including placeholder-based alignment (Luong et al., 2015; Crego et al., 2016), grid beam and lexically guided search (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018), alignment-enhanced decoding and lexicon injection (Alkhouli et al., 2018; Song et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021), and terminology-driven constraints from curated resources such as IATE, JRC-Acquis, and OPUS. Our work absorbs the idea of both lines of work. Based on NAT methods, we brings alignment information by terminologies to help learn the contextual information for lexical constraints, especially the rare ones.

text: With the rise of social media and hate speech forums online (Phadke and Mitra, 2020;Szendro, 2021) offensive language detection has become more important that ever before. Several recent works focus on characterizing various types of offensive language detection (Fortuna and Nunes, 2018;Shushkevich and Cardiff, 2019;Mishra et al., 2019;Parekh and Patel, 2017), and additional studies examine hate speech typologies and multilingual toxicity benchmarks (Waseem and Hovy, 2016;Davidson et al., 2017;Founta et al., 2018;Rosenthal et al., 2020), while concurrent lines of research investigate abusive language in specific domains such as gaming and news comments (Chung et al., 2019;Gao and Huang, 2017;Zampieri et al., 2019;Kumar et al., 2018), and method-oriented work reports advances using contextual encoders and data augmentation (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Wei and Zou, 2019;Xie et al., 2020). But, works that focus solely on Stereotype Detection in English language are scarce. This is partly because stereotypes tend to be subtler offenses in comparison to other types are offensive languages and hence receive less immediate focus, and in part due to the challenge of requiring the knowledge of the stereotype's existence in society to reliably annotate data for the task. We approach this problem by breaking down various aspects of stereotypical text and crowd-sourcing annotations only for aspects that require linguistic understanding rather than world-knowledge. Few recent works have focused solely on stereotypes, some proposing pioneering diagnostic datasets (Nadeem et al., 2020;Nangia et al., 2020) while others worked on knowledge-based and semi-supervised learning based models (Fraser et al., 2021;Badjatiya et al., 2019) for identifying stereotypical text. Computational model based 1. Ethiopians like stew (Explicit Stereotype) 2. The lawyer misrepresented the situation and tricked the person (Implicit Stereotypical Association) 3. Jews spend money frivolously (Anti-Stereotypes) 4. There is an Asian family that lives down the street (Non-Stereotypes) works either use datasets meant for other tasks such as hate speech detection etc, or focus mainly on the available diagnostic datasets modified for classification task. But, diagnostic datasets suffer from lack of sufficient coverage of naturally occurring text due to their crowd-sourced construction procedure (Blodgett et al., 2021b). We address these issues in our work by collecting natural text data from social forum Reddit, by mining specific subreddits that contain mainly subtle stereotypical text.

text: Given the low-resource setting on Stereotype Detection task, semi-supervised data annotation is one plausible solution for the problem. Several recent works have also been focusing on reinforcementlearning guided semi-supervision (Ye et al., 2020;Konyushkova et al., 2020;Laskin et al., 2020). Ye et al. (2020), in particular, work with a singletask and unsupervised data to generate automatedannotations for new examples. In contrast, we use the data from neighboring tasks with different labels for multi-task learning and apply an RL agent to select examples for training the neighboring task in such a way that benefits the target task the most. Related efforts on stereotype-sensitive modeling survey diagnostic probing sets and bias evaluations (Caliskan et al., 2017;May et al., 2019;Kurita et al., 2019;Nangia et al., 2020), resource creation initiatives target social commonsense and demographic attributes (Sap et al., 2020;Hwang et al., 2021;Emami et al., 2021;Bhatt et al., 2022), representation learning approaches adapt debiasing or counterfactual data augmentation (Zhao et al., 2018;Hall Maudslay et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2018;Liang et al., 2020), and evaluation protocols cover fairness, calibration, and robustness across datasets (Blodgett et al., 2020;Barocas et al., 2019;Garg et al., 2018;Röttger et al., 2021).

text: Prompt Learning The concept of prompt-based learning starts from the GPT3 model (Brown et al., 2020), which can complete various zero-shot or few-shot tasks with natural language instruction (i.e., prompts). Previous works design different prompts to query language models to extract knowledge triples (Petroni et al., 2019) or classify sentences into pre-defined categories (Schick and Schütze, 2021) in the few-shot setting. They con-struct various discrete prompts manually for these tasks. To reduce the human effort in this selection process, (Gao et al., 2021) proposes to expand prompts using pre-trained language models. However, the selection of discrete prompts is still an independent process and cannot be optimized together with the downstream tasks in an end-to-end manner. To solve this issue, (Lester et al., 2021;Li and Liang, 2021) propose to use soft prompts, which are sets of trainable vectors, in the frozen pretrained language models. Unlike the hard prompts, these vectors do not correspond to any real words. It allows the optimization with the downstream tasks in an end-to-end manner. As shown in Li and Liang (2021), PLMs with Soft Prompts can often perform better in the low-resource setting. Recent studies explore prompt tuning, prefix-tuning, and instruction tuning with large decoder-only or encoder-decoder models across classification, extraction, and generation benchmarks without unifying assumptions about when discrete prompts suffice or how soft prompts interact with model scale (Brown et al., 2020; Schick and Schütze, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023).

text: Different from LM-BFF that uses a single demonstration per label, our work uses multiple demonstrations which are provided for automatically generated label phrases. In addition, inspired by the method of soft prompting, we use soft demonstration memory based on globally shared soft vectors for prompt tokens, without using hard tokens of the similar context. We also examine how memory size and sharing schemes affect stability under distribution shift. We report mean (and standard deviation) performance over 5 different splits. Majority: majority class "GPT-3" in-context learning: using the in-context learning proposed in (Brown et al., 2020) with RoBERTa-large (no parameter updates); man: manual prompt; LM-BFF & DART: we report the performance in (Gao et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021); PET (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b); AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020); Null Prompts (Logan et al., 2021); soft prompting (Lester et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2021); and demonstration-aware prompts such as LM-BFF (Gao et al., 2021). We ensure comparable hyperparameters across baselines to isolate the effect of demonstrations. Our method is evaluated on diverse classification benchmarks spanning sentiment, topic, and natural language inference tasks. We adopt standard preprocessing and use development sets for early stopping. The proposed memory is initialized randomly and trained jointly with task objectives. Ablations examine the contribution of memory sharing versus task-specific slots. Finally, we release code and configuration files to facilitate reproducibility and future research in prompt-based few-shot learning.

text: Motivated by the desire to reduce compute while retaining strong accuracy, recent work explores alternatives that modify only a small subset of parameters. Adapters introduce task-specific modules inserted between transformer layers to enable efficient multi-task or continual learning with minimal interference across tasks. Prompt tuning learns continuous embeddings that steer a frozen backbone toward a target objective without changing core weights. Low-rank adaptation applies compact updates that approximate full fine-tuning in a constrained subspace, often yielding favorable trade-offs under memory limits. Beyond layer-freezing strategies, related methods span parameter-efficient tuning and representation reuse, including adapter modules that insert small bottleneck layers without updating the backbone (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Rücklé et al., 2021; He et al., 2022), prompt-based tuning that conditions frozen models via discrete or continuous prompts (Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Scao and Rush, 2021), low-rank updates of weight matrices that constrain trainable degrees of freedom (Hu et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023; Frantar and Alistarh, 2023; Ben Zaken et al., 2022), and feature reuse through task-specific probes or linear heads over frozen representations (Alain and Bengio, 2017; Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Pimentel et al., 2020; Voita and Titov, 2020). These directions highlight a spectrum of design choices that trade off trainable parameters, wall-clock time, and deployment constraints in resource-limited settings.

text: A core task in this area has been legal judgment prediction (forecasting), where the goal is to predict the outcome (verdict) of a court case. In this direction, there have been at least three lines of work. The first one (Aletras et al., 2016;Chalkidis et al., 2019a;Medvedeva et al., 2020Medvedeva et al., , 2021) predicts violations of human rights in cases of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). The second line of work (Luo et al., 2017;Zhong et al., 2018;Yang et al., 2019) considers Chinese criminal cases where the goal is to predict relevant law articles, criminal charges, and the term of the penalty. The third line of work (Ruger et al., 2004;Katz et al., 2017;Kaufman et al., 2019) includes methods for predicting the outcomes of cases of the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS).

text: Legal Question Answering (QA) is another task of interest in legal NLP, where the goal is to train models for answering legal questions (Kim et al., 2015;Ravichander et al., 2019;Kien et al., 2020;Zhong et al., 2020a,c). Not only is this task interesting for researchers but it could support efforts to help laypeople better understand their legal rights. In the general task setting, this requires identifying relevant legislation, case law, or other legal documents, and extracting elements of those documents that answer a particular question. A notable venue for legal QA has been the Competition on Legal Information Extraction and Entailment (COLIEE) (Kim et al., 2016;Kano et al., 2017Kano et al., , 2018). Recent studies explore retrieval-augmented readers, entailment-oriented ranking, and domain-specific adaptations of pre-trained encoders (Rabelo et al., 2020;Shinoda and Aoki, 2019;Kornilova and Eidelman, 2019;Zheng et al., 2021;Xiao et al., 2021), alongside datasets such as LEDGAR, LexGLUE, and JEC-QA that support varied formulations of the task.

text: Majority of the work in the legal domain has focused on the higher court (Malik et al., 2021;Strickson and De La Iglesia, 2020;Zhong et al., 2020b); however, the lower courts handle the maximum number of cases. We try to address this gap by releasing a large corpus of district court level legal documents. The literature on multilingual legal-NLP includes benchmarks and shared tasks that enumerate resources without a unifying outlook, including the Competition on Legal Information Extraction/Entailment (COLIEE) corpora and tasks (Rabelo et al., 2019;Rabelo et al., 2020), the LeSicIL shared tasks for Italian legal text processing (Cecchini et al., 2020), the CUAD contract understanding dataset for clause extraction (Hendrycks et al., 2021), the MultiLegalPile corpus for multilingual pretraining (Alemany et al., 2023), the CaseHOLD dataset for legal multiple-choice question answering (Zheng et al., 2021), and the EUR-Lex and ECHR datasets used for European legislation and case-law analysis (Mencia and Fürnkranz, 2007;Chalkidis et al., 2019).  et al., 2019, 2017) have published legal data in Japanese, along with their English translation. The competition had two sub-tasks, a legal information retrieval task and an entailment identification task between law articles and queries. Multiple datasets in Chinese have been released for different tasks, namely Reading Comprehension (Duan et al., 2019), Similar Case Matching (Xiao et al., 2019), Question Answering (Zhong et al., 2020b). Duan et al. (2019) proposed Chinese judicial reading comprehension (CJRC) dataset with about 10K documents and almost 50K questions with answers. Zhong et al. (2020b) presented JEC-QA, a legal question answering dataset collected from the National Judicial Examination of China with about 26K multiple-choice questions. They augment the dataset with a database containing the legal knowledge required to answer the questions and also assign meta information to each of the questions for in-depth analysis. Xiao et al. (2019) proposed CAIL2019-SCM, a dataset containing 8,964 triplets of the case document, with the objective to identify which two cases are more similar in the triplets. Similar case matching has a crucial application as it helps to identify comparable historical cases. A historical case with similar facts often serves as a legal precedent and influences the judgement. Such historical information can be used to make the legal judgement prediction models more robust. Kleinberg et al. (2017) proposed bail decision prediction as a good proxy to gauge if machine learning can improve human decision making. A large number of bail documents along with the binary decision (granted or denied) makes it an ideal task for automation. In this paper, we also propose the bail prediction task using the HLDC corpus.

text: Recent work on persuasion and social influence in dialogue also documents varied settings and supervision signals without connecting them, including persuasion-as-debate with stance shifts (Wang et al., 2019), argument quality estimation for convincingness (Habernal and Gurevych, 2016; Gretz et al., 2020), goal-directed motivational interviewing corpora (Rollnick and Miller, 1995; Tanana et al., 2016), large-scale Reddit negotiations and bargaining (He et al., 2018; Lewis et al., 2017), and scripted campaign persuasion datasets (Durmus and Cardie, 2018; Yang et al., 2019). These lines of work further include controlled generation with style and politeness transfer (Rao and Tetreault, 2018; Niu and Bansal, 2018), persona-grounded persuasion (Zhang et al., 2018; Mazaré et al., 2018), and interactive tutoring systems emphasizing scaffolding over direct recommendation (Graesser et al., 2004; Nye et al., 2014).

text: Beyond recommendation and persuasion, dialogue data creation has drawn from task-oriented benchmarks such as MultiWOZ (Budzianowski et al., 2018), Schema-Guided Dialogue (Rastogi et al., 2020), Taskmaster (Byrne et al., 2019), and MetalWOZ (Lee et al., 2019), as well as open-domain corpora like DailyDialog (Li et al., 2017), BlendedSkillTalk (Smith et al., 2020), ConvAI2 (Zhang et al., 2019), and Topical-Chat (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2019). Methods include self-play simulation (Shah et al., 2018; Takanobu et al., 2020), knowledge-grounded prompting (Dinan et al., 2019; Komeili et al., 2022), and instruction-tuned data mixtures (Sanh et al., 2022; Longpre et al., 2023), alongside alignment techniques using human preference data (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022).

text: ARA is traditionally treated as a classification problem in NLP research, although there are some exceptions. Heilman et al. (2008) compared linear, ordinal, and logistic regression and concluded that ordinal with a combination of lexical and grammatical features worked the best for ARA, although subsequent research was still dominated by classification approaches. There is some past work that considered ARA as a pairwise ranking problem, using SVM/SVM rank and hand crafted linguistic features (Pitler and Nenkova, 2008;Tanaka-Ishii et al., 2010;Ma et al., 2012;Mesgar and Strube, 2015;Ambati et al., 2016;Howcroft and Demberg, 2017). While Tanaka-Ishii et al. (2010) and Ma et al. (2012) showed that ranking performs better than traditional features and classification/regression respectively, Xia et al. (2016) did not find ranking to be consistently better across the board. In this background, we take a fresh look at the application of ranking for ARA, by proposing a new neural pairwise ranking model. Recent multilingual transfer work in NLP provides several avenues that appear relevant to readability assessment across languages, including multilingual masked language models and sentence encoders as general-purpose backbones and evaluation targets, with studies on cross-lingual zero-shot classification and regression, cross-lingual sentence retrieval and similarity, and language-agnostic sentence embeddings learned via translation ranking or contrastive alignment (Devlin et al., 2019;Conneau et al., 2020;Reimers and Gurevych, 2020;Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019;Feng et al., 2020).

text: There has been a growing body of research studying the inner workings of BERT and trying to quantify what it learns in various scenarios, dubbed "BERTology" (Rogers et al., 2020). Of particular interest to this paper is work that analyzes BERT's output embeddings. Prior analyses of contextual representations have examined anisotropy reduction techniques (Mu and Viswanath, 2018), geometry of embedding spaces (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019), probing-based diagnostics (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Tenney et al., 2019), and sense-specific clustering behavior across layers and models (Peters et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Reif et al., 2019), as well as cross-lingual alignment and multilingual transfer in contextual encoders (Conneau et al., 2020; Pires et al., 2019), contextual subspace methods (Kovaleva et al., 2019; Voita et al., 2019), and layer-wise information flow measured via mutual information or CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019; Raghu et al., 2017). Recent studies have found that embeddings created from the final layer of BERT tend to cluster according to word senses (Wiedemann et al., 2019), though this varies somewhat based on the position of a word in a sentence (Mickus et al., 2020). The final BERT layers also produce more contextualized word embeddings than the earlier layers (Ethayarajh, 2019), a finding we revisit using paraphrases in Section 3.3. To situate our analysis, we next delineate the operational definition of sense separation adopted in this study. We define sense separation as the degree to which examples of a polysemous lemma partition into distinct regions of the embedding space. We operationalize regions using density-based clustering applied to contextual tokens sampled from balanced corpora. We complement clustering with a nearest-neighbor sense attribution protocol based on lexicographic sense inventories. We then evaluate stability across paraphrase-preserving rewrites and across syntactic alternations. We also compare layer-wise trends between BERT base and large configurations. We assess the role of subword segmentation by conditioning on wordpiece length. We distinguish positional effects by stratifying contexts according to sentence-internal orderings. We compute layer similarity profiles using CKA to relate sense separation to representational drift. We measure anisotropy and apply common normalization techniques before clustering. We estimate uncertainty via bootstrap resampling to quantify variability in cluster counts. We further examine cross-domain robustness using newswire, Wikipedia, and conversational corpora. We finally report statistical significance using permutation tests with multiple-comparison control. Collectively, these components form a comprehensive framework for analyzing embedding behavior under controlled paraphrase variation. The ensuing sections detail datasets, preprocessing, and evaluation metrics. Section 3 presents empirical findings with ablations and sensitivity analyses. Section 4 discusses implications for contextual meaning representation and outlines limitations. Section 5 concludes with directions for scalable diagnostics and downstream integration.

text: Pretrained generative LLMs (Raffel et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020) have enable framing NLP tasks as seq2seq problems. Some DST papers (Zhao et al., 2021a;Feng et al., 2021) look at settings with no train-test discrepancy. Many studies explore the efficacy of task-specific prompts (Jiang et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2021). Madotto et al. (2020) prime LMs with examples for dialogue tasks, but without finetuning. Wei et al. (2021) fine-tune language models to understand prompts for a different task. A broader line of work examines prompt-based and instruction-tuned approaches across diverse NLP tasks without restricting to dialogue state tracking, including pattern-exploiting training and automatic prompt search (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021), calibration and template engineering for zero-shot classification (Zhao et al., 2021b; Holtzman et al., 2021), chain-of-thought prompting and rationale-augmented decoding (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023), in-context learning with retrieval or demonstration selection (Rubin et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022), and instruction tuning with mixtures of datasets such as FLAN, T0, and Super-NaturalInstructions (Sanh et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).

text: Recent efforts to mitigate these issues have emphasized scalable schema definitions, crowd-driven corrections, and programmatic consistency checks. Benchmarks now increasingly include out-of-distribution slots, unseen goal compositions, and cross-domain goal transfers to probe generalization. Recent efforts also expanded beyond English and single-domain settings, including cross-lingual and multi-domain corpora and benchmarks that emphasize schema diversity and compositional generalization (Bapna et al., 2017;Schuster et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020;Ponti et al., 2020;Lai et al., 2021;FitzGerald et al., 2022;Hudeček and Dušek, 2023). At the same time, dataset creators have incorporated richer dialog phenomena such as corrections, hesitations, and ellipses to better approximate real user behavior. The introduction of standardized slot ontologies and interface layers has further facilitated adapter-based reuse across domains.
