text: Sparse attention mechanism The full attention mechanism has a quadratic memory cost. Prior research works have proposed different sparse attention mechanisms to reduce the memory cost. Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) uses a dilated sliding window of blocks and global attention patterns. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) employs sliding window and random blocks. Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) uses the locality-sensitive hashing. In addition to optimizing the encoder self-attention, Huang et al. (2021) proposes head-wise positional strides to reduce the cost of the encoder-decoder attention. Recent efforts further broaden this landscape with block-sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019), routing-based sparsity in Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), linearized attention kernels such as Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), kernelized low-rank projections in Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), and long-context pretraining strategies exemplified by LED (Beltagy et al., 2020) and UL2 (Tay et al., 2023). However, sparse attention diminishes the benefits of pretraining and sacrifices parts of the receptive field.

text: Sentence rewriting IUR can be considered to be similar to the sentence rewriting task (Xu and Veeramachaneni, 2021;Lin et al., 2021;Chen and Bansal, 2018;Cao et al., 2018), and related advances also include controllable paraphrasing (Iyyer et al., 2018;Krishna et al., 2020), style transfer for text (Shen et al., 2017;Li et al., 2018), edit-based revision (Guu et al., 2018;Dong et al., 2019), and constrained decoding with lexical control (Hu et al., 2019;Post and Vilar, 2018). Recent studies have been addressed the IUR task with various sophisticated methods. Text generation IUR can be formulated as text generation by using the seq2seq model (Pan et al., 2019;Huang et al., 2021). For the generation, several well-known pre-trained models have been applied (Lewis et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020) with promising results. We employ the T5 model (Raffel et al., 2020) as the main component to rewrite utterances. To address the problem of missing important tokens in model's rewriting, we enhance T5 by introducing a Picker and two labeling methods (Section 3.2). The learning of Θ is composed by only using utterance generation (the generator) or the combination of two tasks: important token identification (the picker) and utterance generation (the generator). To situate IUR within broader dialog modeling, prior work has explored context-aware rewriting for ASR repair and disfluency removal (Rao et al., 2020;Cho et al., 2021), user-intent preserving paraphrase generation (Zhang et al., 2020), and slot-focused reformulation in task-oriented systems (Elgohary et al., 2019). Compared to classification-style IUR approaches that detect and tag utterance issues (Kim et al., 2021), our focus remains on direct generation with explicit token guidance. We assume access to dialogue context and system schema, and we condition the generator on these signals to improve factual retention. The picker identifies salient tokens that must be preserved or emphasized during rewriting, thereby reducing omissions of entity names, slot values, and negations. We further introduce two supervision strategies for the picker, one derived from alignment heuristics and one from gradient-based salience, to balance precision and coverage. The generator is a T5-based encoder–decoder with constrained copy bias, while the picker is a lightweight token scorer that outputs hard and soft masks. Training proceeds in two stages, starting with generator pretraining on synthetic rewrites and followed by joint finetuning with picker guidance. Inference uses a constrained beam search that respects hard masks and prioritizes soft-mask tokens through a modified length-normalized score. We evaluate on multi-domain dialog benchmarks with entity-rich utterances and report improvements in content preservation and factuality over strong pretrained baselines. Ablations demonstrate that both picker supervision strategies are complementary and that the constrained decoding contributes most to recall of critical tokens.

text: In its baseline form, the word segmentation process is fully unsupervised, and the only training material is a set of transcribed sentences (see Fig.). Prior work has emphasized that purely unsupervised models benefit from simple priors when data are scarce. Recent neural and probabilistic approaches to unsupervised word and morpheme segmentation span Bayesian models with hierarchical priors (Goldwater et al., 2009;Mochihashi et al., 2009;Teh, 2006b), heuristic or constraint-based algorithms evaluated on morph-rich languages (Creutz and Lagus, 2005;Virpioja et al., 2013), subword modeling for ASR and MT using BPE and unigram LM segmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016;Kudo, 2018), and evaluation on benchmark corpora such as Brent and CHILDES for English as well as Mboshi and Japhug for low-resource settings (Brent, 1999;MacWhinney, 2000;Boito et al., 2018;Jacques, 2016). This landscape motivates a closer examination of probabilistic assumptions under limited supervision.

text: Several works have since shifted focus toward the more challenging phoneme discovery problem by formulating it as a self-supervised learning problem where the semantics of the speech are known, such as from translation, phonemelevel language models or other sensory modalities such as vision. (Jansen, 2013) has studied the use of pairwise word identity labels for training phoneme discovery models based on Gaussian mixture models (GMM); (Harwath and Glass, 2019) analyzes the hidden layers of a two-branch neural network trained to retrieve spoken captions with semantically related images and finds strong correlation between segment representation and phoneme boundaries. (Harwath et al., 2020) adds hierarchical vector quantization (VQ) layers in the same retrieval network and is able to find a much smaller codebook than the unsupervised neural approach (Baevski et al., 2020), and achieve high correlation with the phoneme inventory. (Godard et al., 2018;Boito et al., 2019) has studied the possibility of learning semantic units using an attention-based speech-to-text translation system, though the units appear to correlate more with words. Works on unsupervised speech recognition  attempt to learn to recognize phonemes by leveraging the semantic information from a phoneme language model unpaired with the speech, typically by matching the empirical prior and posterior distributions of phonemes either using cross entropy (Yeh et al., 2019) or adversarial loss Baevski et al., 2021). Throughout the paper, we use P{•} to denote probability. We use capital letters to denote random variables and lower-case letters to represent samples of random variables. We use P X := P{X = x} to denote both probability mass and density functions of random variable X, depending on whether it is continuous or discrete. Further, denote P Y |X (y|x) := P{Y = y|X = x} as the true conditional probability distribution of random variable Y = y given random variable X = x. The probability simplex in R d is denoted as ∆ d .

text: Discrete Prompts The release of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) has led to interest in prompting, a new way to leverage pretrained language models (PLM). Brown et al. (2020) proposes an intuitive in-context learning paradigm by concatenating a few input and output examples and feeding them to the language model and let the model autoregressively generate answers for new examples. Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019;Davison et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020) design prompts to probe the factual and commonsense knowledge encoded within a PLM. Recent works (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b;Gao et al., 2021) demonstrate that even smaller PLMs have similar few-shot learning capacity. Le Scao and Rush (2021) analyzes the effect of prompting and concludes that a single prompt may be worth 100 training examples in fine-tuning. In parallel, studies on cloze-style prompting and calibration report sensitivity to template wording and verbalizers (Zhao et al., 2021;Holtzman et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022). Additional lines of work examine prompt transfer across tasks and domains (Vu et al., 2021;Logan IV et al., 2022;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023). Efforts on prompt ensembling and selection explore stability and robustness (Shin et al., 2020;Ben-David et al., 2023;Zhong et al., 2021;Rubin et al., 2022).

text: While much of the literature in NLP recognizes that idioms share a cluster of properties, including semantic idiosyncrasy, syntactic inflexibility, and institutionalization (e.g., Sag et al., 2002;Fazly and Stevenson, 2006;Fazly et al., 2009), our approach is novel in attempting to characterize idioms along two orthogonal dimensions that correspond to specific proposals from the cognitive science literature. To situate these choices, we first review recent work that operationalizes idiomaticity within neural language models. Recent neural methods for idiom and multiword expression processing span contextualized representation learning and task-specific architectures, including sequence tagging with BiLSTMs and CRFs (Ma and Hovy, 2016;Gharbieh et al., 2016), transformer-based encoders fine-tuned for idiom token identification (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Reddy et al., 2021), probing studies of idiomaticity in BERT-like models (Nivre et al., 2020;Ettinger, 2020;Liu et al., 2022), and contrastive learning frameworks for compositionality (Wu et al., 2020;Chiang et al., 2022;Zeng and Bansal, 2023); complementary resources include PARSEME MWE corpora (Ramisch et al., 2018;Baldwin and Kim, 2010), the VNC-Tokens dataset (Cook et al., 2008), and idiom lexica such as IDIX and SemEval-2013 Task 5 (Korkontzelos et al., 2013). In Section 4 we describe how we instantiate our dimensions in a model-agnostic scoring pipeline. We also clarify how our dataset selection controls for lexical frequency and topical confounds. Our measures may offer a new avenue for tackling the problem of automatic idiom detection. We report empirical results on three benchmarks to quantify the contribution of each dimension. Finally, we outline limitations and opportunities for broader generalization beyond English idioms. We conclude by discussing implications for cognitively informed representations in NLP.

text: Besides modeling optimization, techniques like data augmentation (Zhao and Wang, 2020;Tang et al., 2021) and model ensemble (Hinson et al., 2020) have also been proved very useful for CGEC. Across both EGEC and CGEC, prior studies have explored diverse modeling and evaluation setups without a unifying perspective, including neural sequence-to-sequence architectures with attention (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015;Luong et al., 2015), Transformer-based encoders and decoders (Vaswani et al., 2017;Zhao and Wang, 2020;Tang et al., 2021), sequence editing frameworks such as LaserTagger and GECToR (Malmi et al., 2019;Omelianchuk et al., 2020;Liang et al., 2020), pretrained language models adapted to grammatical error correction (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020), and evaluation protocols spanning M2, ERRANT, and span-based F-scores (Dahlmeier and Ng, 2012;Bryant et al., 2017;Felice et al., 2016).

text: There also exists a wide range of prior modeling work on CS in ASR models, for a variety of strategies (Lyu et al., 2006;Ahmed and Tan, 2012;Seki et al., 2018;Luo et al., 2018;Lu et al., 2020;Du et al., 2021). However, the recently introduced large multilingual models for speech, such as Wav2Vec, Wav2Vec 2.0, Schneider et al. (2019); Baevski et al. (2020) and HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021), are still underexplored with regards to their CS performance. Recent efforts also examine multilingual pre-training and adaptation for code-switching using a variety of corpora and methods without a unified framing of objectives (Conneau et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2020;Xue et al., 2021;Pires et al., 2019;Artetxe et al., 2020;Pratap et al., 2020;Zhou et al., 2021;Rijhwani et al., 2017).

text: Existing methods (Tseng et al., 2016;Serdyuk et al., 2018;Su and Fung, 2020) focus on optimizing each module in a two-stage manner, where errors in the ASR module would result in severe performance loss. Recent advances in multimodal QA and speech-language modeling provide a broad context for this direction, with works on end-to-end SQA pipelines (Haghani et al., 2018; Lugosch et al., 2019), joint speech-text pre-training (Baevski et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2021), conversational QA over text (Reddy et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018), and robustness to ASR noise via data augmentation and confidence modeling (Khurana et al., 2021; Parthasarathi and Strom, 2019) all illustrating complementary threads without explicit unification. SpeechBERT (Chuang et al., 2019) cascaded the BERT-based models as a unified model, and then trained it in a joint manner of audio and text. However, the existing SQA methods aimed at solving a single question given the related passage, without building and maintaining the connections of different questions in the human conversations. In addition, we compare our Spoken-CoQA with existing SQA datasets (See Table ). Unlike existing SQA datasets, Spoken-CoQA is a multi-turn conversational SQA dataset, which is more challenging than single-turn benchmarks.

text: On the other hand, a line of studies measure the "human rationales alignment" (Paranjape et al., 2020), which compares how well the model generated rationales are agreeing with human grounded annotations (DeYoung et al., 2019). There are also studies involving human-in-the-loop to evaluate the explanations, such as asking humans to choose a better model Ribeiro et al. (2016). However, there is a lack of human evaluations on validating the effect of rationale length on human understanding. Beyond these, prior work has examined extractive sufficiency losses (Jain et al., 2020), post-hoc faithfulness diagnostics (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020), counterfactual sufficiency and comprehensiveness tests (DeYoung et al., 2020), perturbation-based rationale generators (Chang et al., 2020), and prompt-driven attribution methods for large language models (Sun et al., 2022; Wiegreffe et al., 2022), as well as datasets with human-marked evidence spans such as ERASER, FEVER, MultiRC, and e-SNLI, and modeling recipes including sparsity-inducing selectors, entropy regularization, and confidence calibration. In this work, we conduct a human-subject study to directly test how rationale length influences comprehension and trust. We design a controlled annotation task where participants answer questions with or without model-provided rationales of varying lengths. Our study measures task accuracy, response time, perceived clarity, and perceived helpfulness as primary outcomes. We further analyze whether rationale length interacts with instance difficulty and annotator expertise. To isolate length from content quality, we normalize for semantic coverage using matched-span paraphrases. We also assess downstream calibration by comparing confidence reports to correctness across length conditions. Finally, we discuss implications for constructing explanation policies that trade off brevity and informativeness in applied settings.

text: Early measurement efforts emphasized word-level associations using distributional semantics and embedding geometry. Subsequent work extended these paradigms to sentence encoders and contextual models, revealing that debiasing techniques often reduce measured associations without improving downstream fairness. Dataset construction has therefore shifted toward templates and minimal pairs to stress-test group contrasts while controlling for lexical content. Crowdsourced annotations and synthetic generation techniques have been combined to probe both localized bias triggers and broader discourse effects. Beyond intrinsic evaluations, researchers have introduced a range of extrinsic and diagnostic protocols spanning sentiment analysis debiasing benchmarks (Kiritchenko and Mohammad, 2018), toxicity and hate speech classification audits (Waseem and Hovy, 2016;Davidson et al., 2017;Sap et al., 2019), counterfactual fairness test suites (Garg et al., 2019;Maudslay et al., 2019), representational association probes such as WEAT and SEAT (Caliskan et al., 2017;May et al., 2019), and dataset-level diversity assessments including BOLD, CrowS-Pairs, and StereoSet (Dhamala et al., 2021;Nangia et al., 2020;Nadeem et al., 2021). These tools vary in their operationalization of bias, coverage of protected attributes, and sensitivity to distributional shifts. However, methodological choices about context, label space, and calibration can confound interpretation of results across settings.

text: The game of Mafia is particularly well-suited for the goal of determining whether the deceptive participants in a conversation can be identified from the contents of their utterances. In Mafia, speakers have asymmetric access to the ground truth, strategically manage information over multiple rounds, and face incentives to mislead without contradicting shared public evidence. These properties create a natural laboratory for studying deception in interactive, high-stakes, and adversarial settings. Prior work in deception detection has largely focused on monologic statements or dyadic interviews, leaving open questions about group interaction and evolving strategies. Prior work spans several strands, including deception detection from linguistic cues using lexical and psycholinguistic markers (Bond and DePaulo, 2006; Ott et al., 2011; Newman et al., 2003; Mihalcea and Strapparava, 2009), multimodal analyses that integrate prosody and facial dynamics (Perez-Rosas et al., 2015; Krishnamurthy et al., 2018; Carriero et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022), conversational games as testbeds such as Werewolf and Diplomacy (Kashima et al., 2015; Niculae and Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil, 2016; Bakhtin et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2023), and computational pragmatics for modeling implicature and belief states (Goodman and Frank, 2016; Potts, 2012; Andreas and Klein, 2016; Fried et al., 2018). However, debates persist over whether deception is primarily signaled by surface-level markers (e.g., pronoun shifts, hedging) or by higher-order discourse moves that manipulate common ground. In interactive games like Mafia, utterances must be interpreted relative to dynamically updated beliefs and publicly observable votes, complicating the modeling assumptions of static classifiers. Recent advances in conversational representation learning enable modeling of speaker roles, turn-taking structure, and temporal dependencies over long horizons. At the same time, the availability of large language models suggests opportunities to infer latent intentions from contextualized evidence. The combination of structured game mechanics and rich linguistic behavior provides leverage for causal probing of deception cues. We consider how public commitments, contradictions, and justificatory burden interact with role knowledge to alter predictive signals. By aligning utterances to event timelines (e.g., accusations, defenses, and votes), we can test whether patterns of framing, entailment, and uncertainty correlate with deceptive roles. We further explore whether deception cues are stable across players or heavily individualized. Our empirical setting draws on annotated multi-session Mafia transcripts with role labels and turn-level metadata. The dataset supports both discriminative analyses of cue prevalence and generative analyses of strategy adaptation across days. We additionally discuss methodological controls to avoid overfitting to idiosyncratic game jargon or community norms. Finally, we outline evaluation protocols that emphasize generalization across groups and sessions rather than in-sample accuracy.

text: Relation Extraction. Relation extraction aims at extracting relation between entities within a given sentence. Many relation extraction methods (Qian et al., 2008;Zeng et al., 2014;Zhou et al., 2016) are supervised model. Recently, some studies focus on pre-training language model (Devlin et al., 2019;Lan et al., 2020) because of its powerful capability of semantic representation. Wu and He (2019) propose R-BERT that uses BERT to extract relation features and incorporates entity information to perform relation extraction. Soares et al. (2019) propose a relation representation learning method based on BERT and have shown promising results. However, these models require labeled data. Unsupervised relation extraction (Yu et al., 2017;Saha et al., 2018;Stanovsky et al., 2018) seeks to discover relations without annotated pairs by clustering or leveraging patterns from large corpora. Distant supervision (Mintz et al., 2009) alleviates annotation costs by aligning text with knowledge bases but introduces label noise. Noise-robust training and multi-instance learning have been developed to mitigate misalignment issues in distant supervision (Surdeanu et al., 2012;Riedel et al., 2010;Lin et al., 2016). Contextualized encoders further improve extraction by modeling entity-aware representations and capturing long-range dependencies across sentences (Zhang et al., 2017;Wang et al., 2019). Prior distant supervision and open information extraction lines also offer alternatives, including Mintz et al. (2009), Hoffmann et al. (2011), Riedel et al. (2010), Angeli et al. (2015), OpenIE (Banko et al., 2007; Stanovsky and Dagan, 2016), and TACRED and SemEval datasets (Zhang et al., 2017; Hendrickx et al., 2010), as well as neural architectures such as PCNN (Zeng et al., 2015), multi-instance learning with attention (Lin et al., 2016), and span-based transformers for relation classification (Baldini Soares et al., 2019). Despite these advances, cross-domain generalization remains a central challenge due to vocabulary shift and schema mismatch between source and target corpora (Alt et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2021). Recent work explores domain-adaptive pretraining and instance reweighting to improve robustness under domain shift (Gururangan et al., 2020;Jiang and Zhai, 2007). Zero-shot and few-shot RE further reduce annotation requirements by exploiting descriptions of relations or external knowledge (Levy et al., 2017;Huang et al., 2022). Prompt-based and instruction-tuned language models offer a promising alternative by mapping natural language prompts to relation labels (Gao et al., 2021;Wei et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2023). Nevertheless, prompt brittleness and label verbalization ambiguity can degrade transfer performance when prompts are underspecified (Scao and Rush, 2021;Min et al., 2022). In parallel, multi-sentence and document-level RE investigate reasoning across multiple evidence sentences, often integrating coreference and discourse cues (Yao et al., 2019;Nan et al., 2020). Knowledge-augmented approaches enrich representations with graph structures and typed constraints to improve factual consistency (Yao et al., 2019;Zhu et al., 2019). Evaluation remains challenging due to label noise, partial matches, and the need to assess calibration in low-resource regimes (Bekoulis et al., 2018;Zhou and Chen, 2022). To address reliability, some studies measure confidence estimates and selective prediction for relation predictions under distribution shift (Kamath et al., 2020;Lei et al., 2022).

text: More recently, Moon et al. (2019) propose a neural coherence model to exploit both local and structural aspects. They evaluate their model on an artificial task only, the shuffle test, which determines whether sentences in a document are shuffled or not. However, recent studies (Pishdad et al., 2020) claim that this artificial task is not suitable to evaluate coherence models. Lai and Tetreault (2018) show that the neural coherence models, which achieve the best performance on this task, do not outperform non-neural models on downstream tasks. More recently, Mohiuddin et al. (2021) find a weak correlation between the model performance in artificial tasks and downstream tasks. Neural coherence research has also expanded beyond entity-centric views to include discourse relations, attention-based sequence encoders, and pre-trained representations (Li and Hovy, 2014; Li and Jurafsky, 2017; BERTScore, Zhang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020; Mohiuddin et al., 2021; Moon et al., 2019; Mesgar and Strube, 2018; Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019), with additional benchmarks and evaluation protocols appearing in work on sentence ordering and summary coherence (Barzilay and Lee, 2004; Logeswaran et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2019). In our evaluation, we compare Moon et al. (2019) with ours in an artificial task as well as in three downstream tasks. Moon et al. (2019) perform the best in the artificial task, but do not outperform our model in three downstream tasks (Section 4).

text: Learning self-supervised tasks on large-scale multilingual texts has proven to be effective for pretraining cross-lingual language models. Masked language modeling (MLM; Devlin et al. 2019) is typically used to learn cross-lingual encoders such as multilingual BERT (mBERT; Devlin et al. 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020). The crosslingual language models can be further improved by introducing external pre-training tasks using parallel corpora. XLM (Conneau and Lample, 2019) introduces the translation language modeling (TLM) task that predicts masked tokens from concatenated translation pairs. ALM utilizes translation pairs to construct codeswitched sequences as input. InfoXLM (Chi et al., 2021b) considers an input translation pair as crosslingual views of the same meaning, and proposes a cross-lingual contrastive learning task. Several pre-training tasks utilize the token-level alignments in parallel data to improve cross-lingual language models (Cao et al., 2020;Zhao et al., 2021;Hu et al., 2020a;Chi et al., 2021c). Prior work has also explored multilingual denoising autoencoding, multilingual machine translation pretraining, and retrieval-augmented cross-lingual objectives in diverse settings, including mBART (Liu et al., 2020), MASS (Song et al., 2019), m2m-100 (Fan et al., 2021), mBART50 (Tang et al., 2021), and mRAG-style approaches (Lewis et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2021), along with alignment-enhanced variants such as ERNIE-M (Ouyang et al., 2021) and LaBSE (Feng et al., 2020), as well as multilingual adapters (Pfeiffer et al., 2020) and parameter-efficient finetuning methods like LoRA (Hu et al., 2022).

text: Rule-based DA relies on handcrafted heuristics and transformation templates such as synonym replacement, back-translation pipelines, and paraphrase rules (Zhang et al., 2015; Sennrich et al., 2016; Wei and Zou, 2019; Xie et al., 2020), interpolation-based DA constructs synthetic examples in representation or input space via mixup, manifold mixup, and vicinal risk methods (Zhang et al., 2018; Verma et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020), and model-based DA leverages pretrained generators, masked language modeling, and conditional text synthesis, including EDA variants, back-translation with neural MT, contextual augmentation with BERT-style models, and prompt-based sampling (Kobayashi, 2018; Edunov et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020; Schick and Schütze, 2021).

text: Recent studies on leveraging large pretrained language models for structure induction span a broad set of techniques and tasks, including masked-language-model probing for part-of-speech discovery (Peters et al., 2018;Devlin et al., 2019;Tenney et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019), attention-based syntax induction from Transformers (Clark et al., 2019;Manning et al., 2020;Hewitt and Manning, 2019;Goldberg, 2019), cross-lingual transfer of token-level categories via multilingual encoders (Pires et al., 2019;Wu and Dredze, 2019;Conneau et al., 2020;Artetxe et al., 2020), and unsupervised constituency or dependency parsing driven by representational geometry (Shen et al., 2018;Kim et al., 2020;Cao et al., 2020;Wu et al., 2020).

text: Recent neural MT architectures and training strategies span a wide range of paradigms, including transformer-based sequence modeling (Vaswani et al., 2017), non-autoregressive decoding for efficiency (Gu et al., 2018; Ghazvininejad et al., 2019), minimum risk and margin-based objectives to align training with evaluation metrics (Shen et al., 2016; Edunov et al., 2018), and auxiliary losses such as bag-of-words or future n-gram prediction to enrich target-side supervision (Zhou et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Du and Ji, 2019).

text: Adapter modules Adapters have proven to be very efficient for multi-task NLP (Houlsby et al., 2019;Bapna and Firat, 2019;Pham et al., 2020;Pfeiffer et al., 2020). In a nutshell, this technique consists in plugging several so-called adapter modules to the intermediate layers of a pretrained Transformer and finetuning these adapters on the downstream tasks. Adapters can also be trained without supervision for multilingual translation (Philip et al., 2020). However, the hard-coded separation between the domains of different tasks may lead to a catastrophic forgetting effect (Pfeiffer et al., 2021), which is a common problem in multi-task modeling using neural networks (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989). In multidomain translation, Pham et al. (2021) recently demonstrated the brittleness of adapters against fuzzy domain separations, outof-domain distributions, and erroneous domain tags. Several subsequent studies have aimed to mitigate this weakness through a mixture of expert mechanism (e.g. (Pfeiffer et al., 2021)). Zhang et al. (2021) propose to learn to route between shared and language-specific representations with a conditional language-specific routing while training the parameters of the underlying Transformer. This method is related to the Fusion-Adapters of Pfeiffer et al. (2021). Both approaches aim to select between shared and task-specific representations. The proximity between tasks is not taken into account in the routing mechanism. We propose a different approach to the problem of multi-task routing in the underlying network.

text: We organize the literature into three clusters that map to our evaluation axes. First, general narrative comprehension datasets emphasize story-level inference, long-range dependencies, and discourse cohesion. Second, character-centered tasks emphasize tracking entities, modeling intentions, and attributing beliefs under partial observability. Third, hybrid benchmarks combine plot understanding with fine-grained social reasoning signals. Recent narrative comprehension benchmarks span commonsense story understanding and plot inference (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016;Roemmele et al., 2011;Lai et al., 2017;Bhagavatula et al., 2020), multi-hop narrative reasoning (Yang et al., 2018;Welbl et al., 2018;Khashabi et al., 2018), temporal and causal coherence (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008;Rashkin et al., 2018;Do et al., 2011;Zhou et al., 2020), and long-form reading with discourse phenomena (Kočiský et al., 2018;Hermann et al., 2015;Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019;Zhu et al., 2015). Additional datasets consider character-centric annotations such as coreference and entity tracking (Pradhan et al., 2012;Clark and Manning, 2016;Bamman et al., 2014;Liu et al., 2019), dialogic and social dynamics in stories (Iyyer et al., 2016;Choi et al., 2014;Zhou and Wang, 2019;Sap et al., 2019), and narrative question answering or cloze tests (NarrativeQA, Kočiský et al., 2018;StoryCloze, Mostafazadeh et al., 2016;RACE, Lai et al., 2017;MCTest, Richardson et al., 2013). To situate character-centered prediction, we next review modeling approaches that interface with these benchmarks.

text: Abstractive Related Work Generation. Recently, Xing et al. (2020) extend the pointergenerator (See et al., 2017) to take two text inputs, allowing them to recover a masked citation sentence given its neighboring context sentences. Ge et al. (2021) encode the citation context, cited paper's abstract, and citation network and train their model with multiple objectives: sentence salience score regression of the cited paper's abstract, functional role classification of the citation sentence, and citation sentence generation. Chen et al. (2021) propose a relation-aware, multi-document encoder to generate a related work paragraph given a set of cited papers. Luu et al. (2021) fine-tune GPT2 (Radford et al., 2019) on scientific texts and explore several techniques for representing documents, such as using extracted named entities. Early neural and graph-based models for scientific document understanding and generation have explored citation intent classification, keyphrase extraction, and multi-document summarization without shared formulations (Cohan et al., 2018; Kardas et al., 2020; Yasunaga et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Collins et al., 2017; DeYoung et al., 2021; Fabbri et al., 2021). Work on leveraging heterogeneous citation graphs for content planning emphasizes structural signals and influence propagation (Liu et al., 2020; Sachan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2020). Pretrained language models have been adapted to scientific discourse with domain-specific corpora and objectives (Beltagy et al., 2019; Gururangan et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2020; Phang et al., 2020; Cohan et al., 2020). Prompting and controllable generation techniques have been examined for scholarly text drafting and reference-aware summarization (Shin et al., 2020; Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Dou et al., 2022; Goyal et al., 2022).

text: All of the works described above focus on the generation aspect, while neglecting dataset collection; their datasets are mostly extracted automatically. Moreover, the datasets are not reused, though they are publicly available, because these works all use slightly different problem definitions, and thus the models are not directly comparable (Li and Ouyang, 2022). Concurrent efforts have cataloged datasets for citation recommendation, scientific summarization, and long-context language modeling, including SciCite, TLDR, S2ORC, arXivSumm, and LongSumm, alongside methods such as LED, Longformer, BigBird, PEGASUS, and BART (Cohan et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2020; Cachola et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2022). Evaluations frequently rely on ROUGE, METEOR, and BERTScore with occasional human assessments for coherence and factuality (Lin, 2004; Banerjee and Lavie, 2005; Zhang et al., 2019). Several studies also consider content planning and discourse coherence via rhetorical structure and section-aware decoding (Li et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022; Iso et al., 2020; Goyal and Durrett, 2021). In this work, we focus on collecting a dataset that is widely applicable to various related work generation settings, rather than proposing another incomparable approach.

text: Language Model Evaluation. Many efforts have studied the evaluation on language model performance. Liu et al. (2019a) evaluate BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), GPT (Radford et al., 2018), and ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) on a variety of linguistics tasks. Their results suggest that the features generated by PLMs are sufficient for high performance on a board set of tasks but fail on tasks requiring fine-grained linguistics knowledge. Tenney et al. ( 2019) evaluate similar models on a variety of sub-sentence linguistic analysis tasks, showing that PLMs encode both syntax and semantics into parameters. Zhou et al. ( 2020) is in line in the sense that PLMs can learn rich knowledge but focus on evaluating the commonsense. However, these work just focus on one dimension of PLMs ability evaluation. Other work such GLUE (Wang et al., 2019b) and CLUE (Liang Xu, 2020) just consider a simple mixture of multiple tasks lacking comprehensive evaluation. Recent studies catalog a broad spectrum of evaluation perspectives and resources for PLMs, including probing tasks for syntax and semantics (Tenney et al., 2019;Hewitt and Manning, 2019;Liu et al., 2019a), commonsense and world knowledge benchmarks (Zhou et al., 2020;Talmor et al., 2019;Sap et al., 2019), general-purpose leaderboards such as GLUE, SuperGLUE, and CLUE (Wang et al., 2019b;Wang et al., 2019a;Liang Xu, 2020), multilingual and cross-lingual suites (Conneau et al., 2018;Hu et al., 2020;Ruder et al., 2021), as well as robustness and adversarial stress tests (Ettinger, 2020;Nie et al., 2020;Ribeiro et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2021). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically evaluate PLMs by defining various kinds of ability and performing extensive comparison.

text: Prior studies have examined extreme multi-label classification with thousands to millions of labels under severe class imbalance, including one-vs-rest linear models (Babbar and Schölkopf, 2017), tree-based partitioning methods (Jain et al., 2019), embedding-based approaches such as SLEEC and AnnexML (Bhatia et al., 2015; Tagami, 2017), deep architectures like XML-CNN, AttentionXML, and XR-Transformer (Liu et al., 2017; You et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020), and benchmark datasets including Wikipedia-500K, Amazon-670K, and Amazon-3M (McAuley et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2015; Dahiya et al., 2021).

text: Pretraining for Retrieval first propose to pretrain a bi-encoder retriever with an Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), which constructs a training pair by randomly selecting a sentence from a passage as the query and leaving the rest as the document. Subsequently, several studies propose two pretraining tasks for Wikipedia and attempt to combine them with ICT and masked language modeling (MLM). Guu et al. (2020) pretrain a retriever and a reader together for end-to-end question answering (QA). Pretraining for information retrieval has explored diverse objectives and resources across both supervised and unsupervised regimes, including ICT for pseudo-query construction (Lee et al., 2019), Wikipedia-specific pretraining with hyperlink prediction and section-aware tasks (Chang et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2021), end-to-end retriever–reader pretraining for open-domain QA (Guu et al., 2020), contrastive representation learning frameworks adapted from vision such as MoCo and SimCLR (He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020), and large-scale synthetic QA generation for domain matching and coverage (Lewis et al., 2021; Oguz et al., 2021).

text: For pragmatic purposes, a "loose" variant of sentence intersection is desired, since redundant content is most likely salient, yet additional important but non-overlapping information may be relevant for a final summarized sentence. For this reason, our extended dataset follows the fusion as "loose" intersection approach applied by Barzilay andMcKeown (2005), McKeown et al. (2010) and Thadani and McKeown (2013). The latter comprises templates that prioritize content units repeatedly expressed across inputs while allowing the inclusion of ancillary facts when they contribute to informativeness. We construct our resources by annotating sentence sets with varying degrees of lexical overlap and by supplying references that demonstrate conservative merging with limited abstraction. We further operationalize this design by instructing annotators to avoid speculative paraphrase unless it is licensed by explicit cross-sentence entailments. Our sampling procedure targets news and encyclopedic domains to capture both event-centric and definitional fusion. Prior work spans a wide range of modeling and data perspectives in fusion, including graph-based compression and lattice methods for multi-sentence compression (Filippova, 2010; Filippova and Altun, 2013), integer linear programming for fusion and summarization (Woodsend and Lapata, 2012; Thadani and McKeown, 2013), neural encoder-decoder approaches leveraging copy and coverage mechanisms (See et al., 2017; Nallapati et al., 2016; Lebanoff et al., 2019), discourse-informed and RST-guided fusion strategies (Marsi and Krahmer, 2005; Louis et al., 2010; Hirao et al., 2013), datasets for disparate and union-style fusion (Elsner and Santhanam, 2011; Geva et al., 2019; Lebanoff et al., 2020; Bingel and Søgaard, 2016), and recent pretraining-based formulations that cast fusion as conditional generation with content planning (Zhu et al., 2021; Iso et al., 2020; Goyal and Durrett, 2020; Laban et al., 2020). We also include inter-annotator agreement protocols that quantify the stability of loose-intersection references under synonymy and ordering variations.

text: Neural text ranking. A number of so-called cross-attention models concatenate a query and a candidate document into a string and feed it into the model (Han et al., 2020;, which allows the attention mechanism of the model to capture interactions across query and document terms. However, deploying such models to millions or billions of documents is usually intractable due to the exorbitant computational cost. To combat this cost, other studies have explored more efficient models, e.g., dual-encoder models (Karpukhin et al., 2020;, BERT with late interaction (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), or using contextual language models to improve term weighting in traditional inverted indexes Dai and Callan, 2020;. Neural text ranking has also been explored through a variety of retriever–reader pipelines, sparse–dense hybrids, and prompt-augmented retrievers that aim to balance effectiveness and efficiency across large corpora, with studies examining dense dual-encoders trained with in-batch negatives (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Hofstätter et al., 2021), late-interaction schemes for token-level matching (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020;Santhanam et al., 2021;Formal et al., 2021), sparse lexical models derived from pretrained transformers (Formal et al., 2021;Mallia et al., 2021;Zhuang and Zuccon, 2021), and retrieval-augmented generation frameworks that treat ranking as conditional text generation or scoring via language model likelihoods (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021;Wang et al., 2022;Ni et al., 2021).

text: There are a couple of other efficient model structures, such as early exiting (Soldaini and Moschitti, 2020;Xin et al., 2020), Transformer-Kernel (TK) model (Hofstätter et al., 2020), and contextualized offline relevance weighting (Chen et al., 2021b). Beyond architecture design, efficiency-focused work in neural IR has emphasized approximate nearest neighbor indexing for dense vectors (Johnson et al., 2019;Dou et al., 2022;Gao et al., 2021), dynamic routing or token pruning to reduce per-query computation (Kaya et al., 2019;Kim and Cho, 2021;Yu et al., 2022), quantization and product quantization for compact embeddings (Jegou et al., 2011;Mao et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2020), and mixed-precision or sparsity-inducing training to lower inference latency (Micikevicius et al., 2018;Narang et al., 2017;Lagunas et al., 2021;Frantar and Alistarh, 2023). In terms of storage cost, Cohen et al. (2021) proposed the succinct document representation which reduces the dimension of token representation to compress document representations. These techniques are orthogonal to our study and can be combined with our work to further improve the time and storage efficiency.

text: Our task is to produce an embedding z ∈ R d of any document x ∈ X such that any single sentence s i ∈ x is indistinguishable with every other sentence s i ∈ S\s i . That is, if one were to replace any single sentence in the document s i ∈ x with any other sentence s i ∈ S\s i , the probability of producing a given embedding z is similar. Prior work on document embeddings spans distributed representations for sentences and paragraphs (Le and Mikolov, 2014; Kiros et al., 2015; Pagliardini et al., 2018), privacy-preserving encodings via randomized mechanisms and differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006; Abadi et al., 2016; Erlingsson et al., 2014), contrastive and self-supervised objectives for text (Logeswaran and Lee, 2018; Gao et al., 2021; Oord et al., 2018), and task-specific encoders fine-tuned from large language models (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020). To achieve this, we propose a randomized embedding function (the embedding mechanism) M : X → R d , that generates a private embedding z = M(x) that is useful for downstream tasks.

text: Biases in Contextualised Embeddings: May et al. (2019) extended WEAT to sentence encoders by creating artificial sentences using templates and used cosine similarity between the sentence embeddings as the association metric. Recent work examines bias and fairness in contextualized representations through template-based probes, perturbation tests, and counterfactual evaluations across a variety of encoders and tasks (Kurita et al., 2019; Tan and Celis, 2019; Basta et al., 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; Nangia et al., 2020; Kurita et al., 2020; De-Arteaga et al., 2019), alongside benchmark datasets and diagnostic suites that target social dimensions such as gender, race, and occupation (Zhao et al., 2018; Rudinger et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2018; Parrish et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021), and methodological extensions including counterfactual data augmentation and causal framing for bias measurement (Maudslay et al., 2019; Garg et al., 2018; Gonen and Goldberg, 2019; Vig et al., 2020), as well as evaluation protocols that incorporate calibration, threshold-agnostic metrics, and distributional shift analyses (Narayanan et al., 2018; Dixon et al., 2018; Blodgett et al., 2020; Barocas et al., 2019).

text: There is limited literature available for adversarial attacking on structured prediction tasks. Despite growing interest in model robustness, most advances have centered on single-label classification, leaving gaps in understanding how structured outputs react to adversarial perturbations across decoding horizons. Prior work spans several paradigms, including gradient-based perturbations and search over discrete edits for text classification (Liang et al., 2018; Alzantot et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2020), sequence-to-sequence attacks for machine translation (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2020a; Michel et al., 2019), adversarial robustness in dialogue systems with goal-oriented and open-domain setups (Cheng et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2019), and extensions to structured prediction via token substitutions or constraint-aware perturbations (Zheng et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). However, structured prediction introduces specific challenges such as label interdependency, sequence-level losses, and constrained decoding, which may limit the transferability of instance-level attack strategies.

text: The feasibility of using answer-aware neural QG in an educational setting was investigated by Wang et al. (2018), who used a BiLSTM encoder (Zhang et al., 2015) to encode C and A and a unidirectional LSTM decoder to generate Q. They trained on the SQuAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) and evaluated on textbooks from various domains (history, sociology, biology). They showed that generated questions were largely grammatical, relevant, and had high n-gram overlap with humanauthored questions. However, given that we may not always have a convenient list of key terms to use as answer spans for an input passage, there is a desire to move past answer-aware QG models and evaluate the feasibility of answer-unaware models for use in education. Neural question generation has also been explored through sequence-to-sequence architectures with attention, pointer-generator mechanisms, and copy-augmented decoders, along with pre-trained language models adapted for QG (Du et al., 2017;Zhou et al., 2017;Song et al., 2018;Zhang and Bansal, 2019;Dong et al., 2019;Kumar et al., 2019;Scialom et al., 2019;Chan and Fan, 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020;Fabbri et al., 2020), and work on controllable QG introduces mechanisms for difficulty conditioning and answer type control (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016;Hu et al., 2018;Subramanian et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020), while domain transfer and robustness have been studied using multi-domain training and adversarial objectives (Jia and Liang, 2017;Dua et al., 2019;Sugawara et al., 2018;Bartolo et al., 2020).

text: These and other works (Zhang et al., 2019) state that sparsity in the weights of attention produces more interpretable patterns. However, Meister et al. (2021) questioned this claim and were unable to find clear evidence to support it. Therefore, in this work, we focused on the application of α-ReLU to the output of the transformer model, and not to the mechanism of attention, but at the same time we do not deny the possibility of studying the latter. Recent approaches explore sparsity through pruning, low-rank factorization, and attention bottlenecks across vision and language, including Lottery Ticket Hypothesis-style pruning (Frankle and Carbin, 2019), movement pruning for transformer-based models (Sanh et al., 2020), magnitudebased and structured pruning in BERT-like encoders (Michel et al., 2019; Gordon et al., 2020), sparse mixture-of-experts routing (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2021), sparse attention patterns such as Longformer and BigBird (Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020), routing via Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), N:M sparsity constraints (Gale et al., 2020), and variational sparsification with L0 regularization (Louizos et al., 2018), while concurrent work on entmax-style alternatives considers adaptive sparsity in sequence labeling and parsing (Peters et al., 2019; Correia et al., 2019; Niculae and Blondel, 2017), and separate lines examine calibrated confidence under sparse outputs (Guo et al., 2017; Minderer et al., 2021).

text: Past work has shown that using in-domain text can provide additional gains over general-domain language models (Gu et al., 2020). Therefore, recent work (BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020), SciB-ERT (Beltagy et al., 2019)) addressed biomedical NEL, focusing on pre-training models on scientific/medical text. Liu et al. (2021) developed Sap-BERT, a pre-training scheme which exploits the graph structure of the UMLS ontology and aims at learning an encoding of medical mentions that can align with synonym relations in the UMLS graph. Combining the SapBERT objective with pre-training on biomedical text of PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2020) boosts results on NEL. Experimental results demonstrated that SapBERT outperforms many domain-specific BERT-based variants (BioBERT and SciBERT) on the BC5CDR dataset. Although our model focuses on cross-lingual NEL, it also applies to English documents. We compare our results to these approaches on BC5CDR and MedMentions (Tables ).

text: Extending on previous works, Wang et al. (2019b) attempted to couple tree structures and transformers. We instead embed the tree structure of RST into transformers through constrained attention in a separate RST embedding dimension. Recent work on more explicit steering further broadens the space of controls by leveraging plug-and-play discriminators (Dathathri et al., 2020), attribute-conditioned decoders (Keskar et al., 2019), controllable rewriting and editing interfaces (Reif et al., 2021; Madaan et al., 2022), prefix-tuning and prompt-tuning methods (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021), and controllable decoding heuristics including nucleus sampling and contrastive search variants (Holtzman et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022), alongside constraint-aware decoding for lexical targets (Anderson et al., 2017; Hokamp and Liu, 2017).

text: Prior works related to this task can be categorized into two groups: (i) Toxicity Detection: These works aim to classify a piece of text as toxic or nontoxic (Wulczyn et al., 2017;Borkan et al., 2019;Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017;Pavlopoulos et al., 2017aPavlopoulos et al., ,b, 2019Zampieri et al., 2019). The main limitation of these works is that they cannot recognize the spans in the text that are responsible for the toxicity of the text. (ii) Opinion Word Extraction: In this group of prior works, models perform a sequence labeling task to identify the spans in the text that convey the sentiment (Liu et al., 2015;Xu et al., 2018;Yin et al., 2016;Wang et al., 2016Wang et al., , 2017Li and Lam, 2017;Mao et al., 2021). The major limitation of all these models is that they require the existence of the target opinion (i.e., the word or phrase that the text has a sentiment polarity toward it). Despite these advances, span-level identification of harmful language remains underexplored compared to sentence-level toxicity classification. Prior datasets typically annotate at the comment or sentence level, which obscures which specific tokens contribute to harm. This limitation has motivated research into explainability, attribution, and fine-grained supervision. Beyond these categories, related efforts include span-based rationalization for classification (Lei et al., 2016;Jain et al., 2020), token-attribution methods such as Integrated Gradients and LIME (Sundararajan et al., 2017;Ribeiro et al., 2016), contextual toxicity datasets with bias annotations (Dixon et al., 2018;Sap et al., 2019;Kennedy et al., 2020), span-level offensive language corpora and benchmarks (Ross et al., 2017;Zampieri et al., 2020;Hartvigsen et al., 2022), and prompt-based large language model approaches to moderation (Gehman et al., 2020;Kirk et al., 2021;Ganguli et al., 2022). However, identifying toxic spans introduces challenges distinct from sentiment targets, including context-dependent slurs, reclaimed language, and multi-token expressions. Sequence labeling models must also contend with label sparsity and long-range dependencies in conversational threads. Another line of work studies data augmentation and counterfactual rewriting to mitigate spurious correlations in toxicity detection. These techniques often reduce unintended bias but may dilute signal at the span level when edits remove lexical cues. From a modeling perspective, pre-trained encoders benefit from auxiliary objectives aligned with token-level supervision. Joint learning with span extraction and classification has been shown to improve calibration for sensitive categories. Evaluation further complicates the landscape because multiple spans can be equivalently toxic, requiring tolerant matching metrics. Recent benchmarks propose partial-overlap F1 and character-level alignment to handle boundary ambiguity. Finally, practitioners emphasize transparency and annotator well-being, recommending protocols that capture uncertainty and context notes during span annotation.

text: Visual Question Answering. Existing visual question answering (VQA) datasets can be categorized along two dimensions. The first dimension is the type of visual data, which includes either real world images (Malinowski and Fritz, 2014; Ren et al., 2015; Antol et al., 2015) and synthetic images (Johnson et al., 2017; Yi et al., 2019) as well as videos (Lei et al., 2018; Zellers et al., 2021). Recent benchmarks span general-domain photographs and web images (Malinowski and Fritz, 2014; Antol et al., 2015; Goyal et al., 2017), diagram and chart understanding corpora (Kafle et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Mathew et al., 2021), synthetic scene-composition datasets emphasizing compositionality (Johnson et al., 2017; Hudson and Manning, 2019; Yi et al., 2019), and video-based QA suites that introduce temporal reasoning (Tapaswi et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2018; Zellers et al., 2021), alongside functionally grounded causal-counterfactual evaluations such as CLEVR-HYP and CRAFT (Santoro et al., 2017; Atzmon et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2023). The second dimension is the type of question, which ranges from descriptive queries about objects and attributes to causal and counterfactual reasoning tasks. Descriptive questions often assess recognition, counting, and spatial relations, while causal questions require modeling interventions and implications under changes to the scene. Counterfactual prompts test whether models can predict outcomes if particular elements are altered or removed. Across these settings, annotation quality and distributional biases can strongly influence measured performance. In particular, language priors and answer frequency effects can yield inflated scores without genuine visual reasoning. To mitigate these issues, several works advocate balanced splits, adversarial filtering, and compositional generalization protocols. Synthetic datasets offer controllable environments to probe fine-grained reasoning skills. However, bridging from synthetic control to real-world complexity remains difficult. Video-based VQA further introduces temporal dependencies and partial observability. As a result, evaluation must consider not only static recognition but also dynamics and causality over time. Recent methods integrate graph neural modules and structured causal abstractions to better capture interactions. Others rely on large pretrained multimodal transformers with alignment objectives. Despite advances, robust generalization to out-of-distribution compositions is still an open challenge. Moreover, causal-counterfactual queries demand explicit modeling of interventions rather than pattern matching. Standard metrics such as accuracy may obscure nuanced failures in reasoning. Emerging protocols emphasize disentangled reporting across perception, grounding, and causal inference. Together, these considerations motivate benchmarks that stress both compositionality and intervention-aware evaluation. We build on these insights to articulate requirements for datasets that disentangle perception from reasoning and test intervention consistency.

text: Pre-processing steps can substantially alter the results of the LDA models even in languages with good tokenization heuristics such as English (Schofield and Mimno, 2016;May et al., 2016). We believe that languages that do not have clear tokenization standards deserve investigation into what kind of processing is appropriate. Many works recognize that LDA results can be improved when input are including phrases (Lindsey et al., 2012;Lau et al., 2013;Yu et al., 2013;El-Kishky et al., 2014;Wang et al., 2016;Bin et al., 2018;Li et al., 2018). We consider it valuable to specifically assess approaches to determining these phrases. Prior work on phrase-aware topic modeling spans a range of techniques and resources, including noun-phrase chunking with POS patterns (Lindsey et al., 2012), PMI- and NPMI-based phrase discovery (Lau et al., 2013; Bouma, 2009), statistically driven segmentation and phrase mining (El-Kishky et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016), data-dependent n-gram LDA variants (Yu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018), and large-scale collocation extraction pipelines evaluated on English, Chinese, and Arabic corpora (Mimno et al., 2011; Bin et al., 2018; May et al., 2016), as well as domain-specific adaptations for scientific text and social media streams (Schofield and Mimno, 2016; Lau et al., 2014; Wallach et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2009). We consider it valuable to specifically assess approaches to determining these phrases in non-segmented languages, where segmentation decisions and phrase boundaries interact with topic distributions. Despite their popularity in analyzing large amounts of text data, LDA models are notoriously complex to evaluate. One must evaluate both the statistical fit of a model and the human-registered thematic coherence of the words found to arise in the high-probability words, or keys, of a topic, which may not correlate (Chang et al., 2009). Analyses often combine evaluations of fit (Wallach et al., 2009) and automated approximations of human judgments of coherence (Bouma, 2009;Mimno et al., 2011) based on mutual information, even with the expectation these may only somewhat correlate with true human judgments (Lau et al., 2014). A limitation of these existing approaches, however, is that they expect the vocabulary and tokenization to remain constant between two models. This assumption becomes problematic when phrase mining or alternative segmentation modifies the unit of analysis, thereby altering the effective vocabulary and the conditional likelihood landscape across competing models. Moreover, coherence metrics grounded in pointwise or normalized PMI are sensitive to phrase boundary choices that shift co-occurrence windows and frequency counts in nontrivial ways. These sensitivities can obscure whether observed differences are due to improved topic structure or merely artifacts of tokenization change. Consequently, evaluation protocols must be adjusted to disentangle modeling improvements from preprocessing effects in multilingual or non-standardized settings. For our evaluation, we use a normalized log likelihood approach to capture fit while accounting for changes in vocabulary (Schofield and Mimno, 2016). We then complement this with human assessments that explicitly control for phrase availability to reduce confounds arising from segmentation variability. Together, these choices allow a more faithful comparison of models that differ in phrase inclusion while maintaining interpretability of resulting topics. Finally, we outline how these adjustments generalize to corpora where token boundaries are uncertain, ensuring consistent evaluation across languages and domains.

text: Dense retrievers have emerged as a dominant paradigm for open-domain and web-scale search because they learn compact representations that enable efficient approximate nearest neighbor lookup while preserving semantic relevance. Despite steady progress, robustness to limited supervision and distribution shift remains a central concern for practical deployment in high-variance domains such as news, forums, and scientific literature. Recent work on pre-trained encoders and dual-encoder architectures has reported strong performance for large-scale passage retrieval, in particular DPR and its variants (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Sachan et al., 2021;Izacard et al., 2021), momentum-contrast and late-interaction schemes (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020;Luan et al., 2021;Hofstätter et al., 2021;Santhanam et al., 2022), as well as multi-vector retrieval with ColBERTv2 and SPLADE-like sparse expansions (Formal et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021;Lin and Ma, 2021;Luan et al., 2021). To alleviate data scarcity, augmentation has been widely explored in both vision and language settings.

text: Ficler and Goldberg (2017) control the stylistic aspects of the generated text with a conditioned RNN (Recurrent Neural Network) LM. Holtzman et al. (2018) compose a committee of discriminators to guide an RNN generator towards the generations with the desired linguistic quality. Hu et al. (2017) aim at controlling the sentiment and tense of the generated text by combining variational autoencoders (VAE) and attribute discriminators. Con-trolling these attributes of text generation has manifold applications, such as knowledge-grounded conversation (Dinan et al., 2019) and poetry generation (Ghazvininejad et al., 2017). More recently, with the advent of Transformers and large pretrained language models, such as GPT2, an extensive body of work has focused on controlling the generation of these Transformerbased models. Keskar et al. (2019) train a 1.63 billion-parameter conditional transformer LM from scratch with 55 attribute control codes to guide generation. However, this method is expensive and lacks flexibility since the control codes are fixed. Dathathri et al. (2020) address these limitations by developing a plug-and-play model which leverages an attribute discriminator to perturb the LM's hidden activations. However, updating gradients at the token level results in slow inference. Instead of updating the hidden activations, Krause et al. (2020); Yang and Klein (2021); Lin and Riedl (2021) introduce generative discriminators to re-weight the next token distributions on the fly during inference, thus improving the inference speed.

text: Recently, studies start to focus on improving the parameter-efficiency of adapters. Diff-pruning (Guo et al., 2020) achieves parameter efficiency by adding a sparse, task-specific difference-vector to the fixed original parameters. The vector is adaptively pruned during training with a differentiable approximation to the L 0 -norm penalty to encourage sparsity. Rücklé et al. (2020) introduced Adap-terDrop, which has been recently integrated into AdapterHub (Pfeiffer et al., 2020b) by removing adapters from lower transformer layers during training and inference, which can dynamically reduce the computational cost. Mahabadi et al. (2021) proposed Compacter, which improved the trade-off between performance and trainable parameters per task with low-rank optimization. Recent explorations further diversify adapter design and related parameter-efficient fine-tuning, including prefix-tuning (Li and Liang, 2021), prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021), LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), IA3 (Liu et al., 2022), parallel and serial adapter variants (Pfeiffer et al., 2020a; He et al., 2021), and task routing across adapter banks (Pfeiffer et al., 2021), with empirical evaluations reported on GLUE (Wang et al., 2018), SuperGLUE (Wang et al., 2019), and XTREME (Hu et al., 2020), alongside multilingual extensions such as MAD-X (Pfeiffer et al., 2020c) and cross-lingual transfer via language adapters (Chronopoulou et al., 2022).

text: Prompt Tuning GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) demonstrates remarkable few-shot performance by prepending textual prompts before the inputs and thus help the PLM to generate desired outputs of NLP tasks directly. Motivated by this, many works have tried to improve various NLP tasks by creating manually-crafted (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b;Mishra et al., 2021) or automaticallysearched (Jiang et al., 2020;Shin et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2021) hard prompts, which are discrete tokens but not necessarily human-readable. Furthermore, soft prompts (Li and Liang, 2021;Hambardzumyan et al., 2021;Zhong et al., 2021; are proposed, which are tuneable embeddings rather than tokens in the vocabularies and can be directly trained with task-specific supervi-sion. Recent advances span manual prompt engineering and automatic prompt induction as well as continuous prompt learning, with representative efforts including PET and Pattern-Exploiting Training (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b), prompt source and example-based prompting (Mishra et al., 2021), LM-BFF and AutoPrompt-style search (Jiang et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021), and soft-prompt or prefix-based tuning variants such as Prompt Tuning, P-Tuning, and Prefix-Tuning (Li and Liang, 2021; Hambardzumyan et al., 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022). demonstrate that prompt tuning (PT) method can match the performance of full-parameter fine-tuning when the PLM has billions of parameters. This suggests that PT is promising to utilize extremely large PLMs. However, the much more training time needed to reach the convergence makes PT inefficient. In this work, we show that prompt transfer can remedy, improve the effectiveness to some extent with knowledge transfer, and empirically analyze the transferability of prompts across tasks and PLMs.

text: Visually Grounded Representation Learning. We revisit the literature that grounds language in vision to inform representation design. A large body of multimodal research explores aligning images and text through joint objectives and cross-modal encoders, including image–sentence embedding models based on contrastive ranking losses (Kiros et al., 2014;Frome et al., 2013;Faghri et al., 2018;Mithun et al., 2018), vision–language pretraining with region-level grounding (Lu et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2020;Li et al., 2020;Zhou et al., 2020), end-to-end masked multimodal transformers (Tan and Bansal, 2019;Li et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2019;Zhu et al., 2020), and datasets that pair captions with images for representation learning (Lin et al., 2014;Young et al., 2014;Krishna et al., 2017;Sharma et al., 2018). Prior work shows that vision can enrich textual semantics for downstream tasks. We extend this line by asking how visual grounding can regularize sentence-level similarity geometry.

text: Knowledge Selection for Dialog. Knowledge selection can be tightly coupled with the response generator (Ghazvininejad et al., 2018) or performed separately prior to response generation. Some approaches adapted question answering models (Moghe et al., 2018;Qin et al., 2019;Wu et al., 2021) or summarization models (Meng et al., 2020a) for knowledge selection. With a pool of knowledge candidates, knowledge selection has been commonly set up as a sentence classification or ranking problem (Dinan et al., 2019;Lian et al., 2019;Kim et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2020;Meng et al., 2020b;Zhao et al., 2020). Some work has modeled the underlying knowledge as a latent variable (Lian et al., 2019;Kim et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2020). Others have explored modeling the knowledge transition over dialog turns to improve selection accuracy (Kim et al., 2020;Meng et al., 2020b;Zhan et al., 2021). In comparison, we model knowledge selection as a node selection task on the document semantic graph. Recent advances also consider leveraging structured and semi-structured resources alongside neural retrievers and encoders in dialogue and related conditional generation tasks, including retrieval-augmented generation frameworks and dense passage retrievers (Lewis et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020), sentence-level and span-level selectors trained with contrastive or margin-based objectives (Dinan et al., 2019;Zhao et al., 2020), hierarchical selectors over multi-turn contexts (Lian et al., 2019;Kim et al., 2020), and graph-enhanced selectors that incorporate entity linking or discourse coherence signals (Liu et al., 2019b;Xu et al., 2020;Zhan et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2021).

text: Benefiting from the strong power of pre-training techniques in natural language processing (NLP), such as GPT (Radford et al., 2018), BART , and T5 (Raffel et al., 2020), some recent works attempt to pre-train language models on the corpus of source code for generation. Svyatkovskiy et al. (2020) proposed CodeGPT follows the architecture of GPT-2 , which is pre-trained with a causal language modeling (CLM) objective on large-scale source codes.  proposed CugLM, which adopts the same architecture as CodeGPT, and is pretrained by Masked bidirectional Language Modeling (MLM), Next Code segment Predicting (NCP), and Unidirectional Language Modeling (ULM) objectives.  proposed PLBART follows the architecture of BART , which is pre-trained on large-scale Java and Python functions paired with natural language comments via denoising autoencoding. Wang et al. (2021b) proposed CodeT5 based on the T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) architecture, which is employs denoising sequence-to-sequence pre-training on multiple programming languages.

text: Beyond standard multi-task learning. Multitask learning is a long-standing goal for AI (Caruana, 1997) and has led to successful models that can support a wider range of tasks (McCann et al., 2018;Khashabi et al., 2020;Aghajanyan et al., 2021;Ye et al., 2021;Raffel et al., 2020). Recent efforts on instruction tuning and task collections span large-scale mixtures and prompt libraries, including T0 and FLAN (Sanh et al., 2021;Wei et al., 2021), BIG-bench (Srivastava et al., 2022), Super-NaturalInstructions (Wang et al., 2022), HELM (Liang et al., 2022), instruction induction methods (Honovich et al., 2022), and prompt repositories such as PromptSource and PromptBench (Bach et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2023), alongside studies on in-context learning and meta-learning with task descriptions (Brown et al., 2020;Min et al., 2022;Xie et al., 2022). Most of the conventional setups in the multi-tasking literature evaluate on instances that belong to the tasks that are seen, i.e., their labeled instances were observed during training (1st column of Table ). We augment this setup by introducing natural language instructions which enable our models to bridge to tasks that were not seen during training.

text: Meanwhile, related research on textual robustness and adversarial detection surveys and methods spans HotFlip (Ebrahimi et al., 2018), TextFooler (Jin et al., 2020), BERT-Attack (Li et al., 2020), DeepWordBug (Gao et al., 2018), checklist-style perturbation testing (Ribeiro et al., 2020), universal adversarial triggers (Wallace et al., 2019), certified robustness approaches (Jia et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019), and robust pretraining objectives (Si et al., 2021), as well as out-of-distribution and confidence calibration baselines like ODIN (Liang et al., 2018), Energy-based OOD detection (Liu et al., 2020), and Mahalanobis distance detectors (Lee et al., 2018). This body of work highlights the diversity of attack and defense paradigms pertinent to text classifiers. However, there remains a practical need for detectors that operate without access to adversarial training data and that generalize across attack families. We therefore focus on detection signals that are intrinsic to token distributions and model-internal activations, rather than attack-specific cues. Concretely, we study whether lexical rarity, subword fragmentation, and activation consistency across layers can expose imperceptible manipulations. We also examine the interaction between frequency-based indicators and confidence calibration under distribution shift. To this end, we assemble a benchmark spanning synonym substitution, character-level noise, paraphrastic rewriting, and trigger-based attacks across sentiment and natural language inference tasks. Our evaluation isolates the contribution of token-level features versus representation-level metrics using ablations. We further analyze threshold stability under varying base model sizes and decoding settings. Finally, we report cross-attack generalization and data-efficiency results to assess deployment viability.

text: Beyond token-level substitution, document- and sentence-level augmentation has also been explored across diverse architectures and tasks, including paraphrase generation with back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016; Edunov et al., 2018), sequence-level perturbations via mixup and manifold mixup in NLP settings (Zhang et al., 2018; Verma et al., 2019), masked-span infilling for style-agnostic rewriting (Lewis et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020), and contrastive learning with dropout or view-based augmentations for representation robustness (Fang et al., 2020; Giorgi et al., 2021; Carlsson et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021). These studies broaden the design space from lexical changes to distributional and structural variations that may reduce overfitting in low-resource regimes. However, most prior approaches face a tension between semantic fidelity and diversity when perturbing inputs or intermediate features. In addition, methods that rely on autoregressive proposals can suffer from exposure bias or cascading errors during multi-token edits. Embedding-space perturbations, while label-preserving in expectation, may drift if not aligned with task-relevant subspaces. These challenges motivate approaches that incorporate stronger contextual constraints while maintaining efficiency.
