text: There has been a great deal of recent interest in providing explanations of blackbox machine learning models, focusing on explaining why the model makes an individual prediction (Ribeiro et al., 2016;Lei et al., 2016;Ribeiro et al., 2018;Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018;Liu et al., 2018), or achieving better understanding of the limitations of models (Wallace et al., 2019;Ribeiro et al., 2020). Recent studies survey textual and multimodal explanation techniques that attribute importance to tokens, spans, or regions and introduce perturbation- and gradient-based methods across tasks such as sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and vision-language reasoning (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2016; Sundararajan et al., 2017; Shrikumar et al., 2017; Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018; Jain and Wallace, 2019; Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019; Serrano and Smith, 2019), while separate lines examine stability, faithfulness, and human factors through perturbation tests, randomization controls, and user studies in both classification and sequence modeling (Adebayo et al., 2018; Wallace et al., 2019; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Pruthi et al., 2020; Slack et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2022). In contrast, our goal is to explain how the input can be changed to achieve a desired outcome, which is called a counterfactual explanation (Wachter et al., 2017;Ustun et al., 2019). Counterfactual explanations in NLP seek minimally edited inputs that flip a model decision while satisfying fluency and plausibility constraints, often formalized through sparse edit sets, semantic similarity bounds, and classifier-consistent constraints. Foundational work in vision and tabular domains has inspired NLP-specific formulations that trade off edit costs and classifier responses using differentiable surrogates or combinatorial search. Current approaches in text differ in whether they operate in the input space of tokens and characters, the latent space of encoders, or the discrete space of structured outputs for tasks like parsing and translation. Methods such as gradient-guided token replacement, masked-language-model proposals, and constrained beam search have been adapted to maintain grammaticality while pursuing decision flips. However, guarantees of faithfulness, robustness to rephrasing, and user comprehensibility remain open challenges. There has been work on leveraging natural language descriptions to help generate counterfactual explanations for image classifiers (Hendricks et al., 2018), but not tailored at counterfactual predictions for natural language tasks. Recent work has also connected counterfactual explanations to causal reasoning, framing edits as interventions and outcomes as potential responses under do-operations, which motivates evaluation protocols that measure counterfactual validity across perturbation neighborhoods. Parallel efforts in data-centric counterfactuals cover causal data augmentation, factual-contrastive training, and evaluation via targeted edits across tasks including question answering, summarization, and dialogue, drawing on benchmarks and toolkits that operationalize minimal changes and contrast sets for systematic stress testing (Gardner et al., 2020; Kaushik et al., 2020; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Kaushik et al., 2021; Ross et al., 2021; Gardner et al., 2021; Uttamchandani et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022). Finally, there has been interest in improving the performance of semantic parsers through interaction (Wang et al., 2016(Wang et al., , 2017; our approach is complementary to this line of work, since it aims to make the system more transparent to the user. To situate our contribution, we formalize counterfactual generation as a constrained optimization that respects linguistic well-formedness and domain validity while minimizing edit distance. We extend recent constrained decoding techniques with task-specific semantic constraints learned from weak supervision. We evaluate on intent classification and semantic parsing benchmarks where small edits can yield large changes in predicted structure. Our experiments test whether counterfactuals transfer across model families and whether human-verified edits retain utility under model retraining. We report both flip rate and plausibility metrics, and we conduct user studies to assess interpretability. We further analyze distributional shifts induced by counterfactual augmentation and their effects on calibration. Our results highlight the interaction between constraint strength and edit minimality. We release code and annotation guidelines to facilitate reproducibility and future comparisons. We conclude by discussing open questions around interactive counterfactual generation and personalized constraints.

We extend recent constrained decoding techniques with task-specific semantic constraints learned from weak supervision. We evaluate on intent classification and semantic parsing benchmarks where small edits can yield large changes in predicted structure. Our experiments test whether counterfactuals transfer across model families and whether human-verified edits retain utility under model retraining. We report both flip rate and plausibility metrics, and we conduct user studies to assess interpretability. We further analyze distributional shifts induced by counterfactual augmentation and their effects on calibration. Our results highlight the interaction between constraint strength and edit minimality. We release code and annotation guidelines to facilitate reproducibility and future comparisons. We conclude by discussing open questions around interactive counterfactual generation and personalized constraints.

text: Prior explorations of multi-task learning, intermediate-task transfer, and curriculum-style pretraining span diverse settings and objectives, including adversarial or uncertainty-based task weighting (Kendall et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018), gradient surgery and conflict mitigation (Yu et al., 2020; Sener and Koltun, 2018; Chen et al., 2020), task grouping and hierarchical transfer (Ruder et al., 2019; Standley et al., 2020), linguistic-probing or syntax-informed auxiliaries (Tenney et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019), and intermediate-task pipelines such as STILTs, multitask-to-single-task adaptation, and adapter-based transfer (Phang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019; Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). In parallel, data-centric perspectives have examined how label space structure, class imbalance, and annotation noise impact transfer behavior across tasks. Complementary lines assess domain shift sensitivity, robustness to spurious correlations, and calibration under distributional drift. Methodologically, scaling laws and compute-aware evaluations have begun to quantify when additional auxiliary tasks yield diminishing returns. Several benchmarks aggregate heterogeneous tasks to probe negative transfer, interference, and sample efficiency under constrained budgets.

text: Prompting. Natural language prompting freezes pretrained models and reformats the natural language input with example prompts. GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) introduces in-context learning, using manually designed and discrete text prompts. Sun et al. (Sun and Lai, 2020) also leverage prompts as keywords to control the sentiment or topic of the generated sentence. AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) searches for a sequence of discrete trigger words and concatenates it with each input to elicit sentiment or factual knowledge from a masked LM. Different from the discrete text prompt, some methods examine continuous prompts (a.k.a. soft prompts) that perform prompting directly in the embedding space of the model. Prefix-Tuning (Li and Liang, 2021) prepends a sequence of continuous task-specific vectors as virtual tokens to the input. Following early progress on prompt-based tuning, numerous studies explore discrete and continuous prompting across diverse architectures and tasks, including GPT-3 style in-context prompting (Brown et al., 2020), AutoPrompt for eliciting factual and sentiment knowledge (Shin et al., 2020), prefix-based continuous conditioning (Li and Liang, 2021), prompt ensembling and calibration (Zhong et al., 2021), gradient-based soft prompt initialization (Qin and Eisner, 2021), reparameterized prompt tuning for stability (Hambardzumyan et al., 2021), P-tuning with deep virtual tokens (Liu et al., 2021c), and compositional template assembly with logic rules (Han et al., 2021). Ptuning (Liu et al., 2021c) uses continuous prompts which are learned by inserting trainable variables into the embedded input. Ptr (Han et al., 2021) adopts manually crafted sub-templates and generates complete templates by logic rules. In ProbES, we prepend continuous task-specific vectors to the embedding of the input instruction and directly tune the embeddings of these vectors. After prompt tuning, the model can be adapted to VLN and REVERIE tasks.

text: Visual Storytelling (VIST) Visual storytelling was introduced by Huang et al. (2016) as the task of generating a coherent story given five images. They provided a dataset, Sequential Images Narrative Dataset (SIND), containing images and references in which references are human-written short stories describing images. For every image prompt (one sequence of photos), there are 2 to 5 references. VIST requires deeper understanding of the photo events to prevent descriptions in isolation (i.e., image captions). Researchers have proposed various methods for this task. Early work on visual narrative generation studies a range of modeling strategies spanning sequence-to-sequence encoders with attention, hierarchical decoders for multi-sentence outputs, and multimodal fusion of CNN and RNN features, with notable systems including AREL (Wang et al., 2018a), GLAC Net (Kim et al., 2018), KG-Story (Hsu et al., 2020), and XE-SS (Huang et al., 2019), alongside pretraining on COCO Captions (Chen et al., 2015), Flickr30k (Young et al., 2014), and visual-semantic alignment objectives (Kiros et al., 2014). Knowledge graphs are often integrated in models to encourage diversity of terms and plots in the stories (Hsu et al., 2020(Hsu et al., , 2021a. Some studies use reinforcement learning to reward models that generate stories that contain fewer errors and are more topically-focused Hu et al., 2020a). However, existing evaluation methods are unable to capture the true quality of the generated stories. Thus we examine automatic metrics to devise a better way for machines to evaluate stories.

text: VIST-Human Evaluation Several VIST generation models use human evaluation to evaluate model performance. Recent studies apply aspectbased rating evaluation. Hu et al. (2020b) and Wang et al. (2020b) ask workers to rate stories based on pre-defined aspects. 1 However, it is difficult to normalize these aspects as the definition of aspect varies from paper to paper. Also, these aspects are not mutually independent, making it difficult to analyze results based on these ratings. Therefore, we consider the ranking method as it is commonly used (Hsu et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020b;Hsu et al., 2021a)  Automatic Metrics Automatic evaluation metrics are widely used in language generation tasks. Most reference-based metrics (e.g., BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and ROUGE (Lin, 2004)) evaluate the ngram similarity between a generated text and the reference. However, referenced metrics correlate poorly with human judgment (Wang et al., 2018b;Hsu et al., 2019;Modi and Parde, 2019) in dialog generation and story generation tasks: the generated text is given unreasonable scores due to incongruity with the reference. To account for this, several reference-free metrics (Sinha et al., 2020;Guan and Huang, 2020) have been designed to measure generated texts without any reference. BERT-Score (Zhang et al., 2019), for instance, uses contextual embedding to calculate the similarity between candidates and references, and BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020) uses referenced automatic metrics as supervision signals for pretraining and is fine-tuned on a human judgment evaluation dataset. UNION (Guan and Huang, 2020) uses pre-defined negative samples to train a model in an attempt to provide a metric that specializes in story generation. Beyond VIST, automatic evaluation in open-ended generation spans machine translation metrics such as BLEU and chrF (Popović, 2015), summarization metrics like ROUGE and BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2019), dialogue metrics including ADEM (Lowe et al., 2017) and USR (Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020), learned quality estimators such as COMET (Rei et al., 2020) and BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020), and reference-free variants including MoverScore (Zhao et al., 2019), BaryScore (Colombo et al., 2021), and QuestEval (Scialom et al., 2021). In our analysis, current metrics remain unable to mimic human judgment to discern quality differences in story pairs.

text: Argument mining aims to detect claims, premises, and their relations to structure reasoning in text. Value-centric argument mining would extend this by linking argumentative units to human values such as fairness, security, or autonomy. While initial taxonomies and psychological theories provide conceptual clarity, operationalizing them for automatic annotation remains difficult. Prior research on value representation and social choice in computational settings spans value-based argumentation frameworks, crowd-sourced moral judgments, moral foundations in text classification, and ethical benchmarks for language models (Bench-Capon, 2003; Mikhail, 2007; Graham et al., 2009; Alkhatib, 2021; Forbes et al., 2020; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lourie et al., 2021), as well as datasets on stance and persuasion such as UKP ConvArg2, IBM Debater, Persuasion for Good, and Moral Stories, and methods involving weak supervision, prompt-based learning, and rationalization extraction.

text: Knowledge Distillation Recently, many attempts have been made to accelerate large neural networks . Knowledge distillation is a prominent method for training compact networks to achieve comparable performance to a deep network. Hinton et al. (2015) first introduced the idea of knowledge distillation to exploit the "dark knowledge" (i.e., soft label distribution) from a large teacher model as additional supervision for training a smaller student model. Since its introduction, several works (Romero et al., 2015;Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017;Tung & Mori, 2019;Park et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2019) have investigated methods that align different latent representations between the student and teacher models for better knowledge transfer. Recently, several strands of research have explored complementary or alternative supervision signals and distillation setups, including logit-based temperature scaling (Hinton et al., 2015), feature-map transfer and hint layers (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017), attention and relational knowledge transfer (Park et al., 2019; Tung & Mori, 2019), contrastive or instance-level objectives (Tian et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020), self- and data-free distillation (Yuan et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2019), and task- or architecture-agnostic protocols spanning vision and language benchmarks (Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2019; Sanh et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019). In the context of knowledge distillation, MetaDistil shares some common ideas with the line of work that utilizes a sequence of intermediate teacher models to make the teacher network better adapt to the capacity of the student model throughout the training process, including teacher assistant knowledge distillation (TAKD) (Mirzadeh et al., 2020) and route constraint optimization (RCO) . However, the intermediate teachers are heuristically selected independently of the training process and the evolution of the teacher network is discrete. In contrast, MetaDistil employs meta learning to make the teacher model adapt to the current state of the student model and provide a continuously evolving meta-teacher that can better teach the student. Concurrently, Park et al. (2021) and Shi et al. (2021) propose to update the teacher model jointly with the student model with task specific objectives (e.g., cross-entropy loss) during the KD process and add constraints to keep student and teacher similar to each other. Their approaches makes the teacher model aware of the student model by constraining the teacher model's capacity. However, the teacher models in their methods are still not optimized for knowledge transfer. In addition, Zhang et al. (2018) introduced deep mutual learning where multiple models learn collaboratively and teach each other throughout the training process. While it is focused on a different setting where different models have approximately the same capacity and are learned from scratch, it also encourages the teacher model to behave similarly to the student model. Different from all aforementioned methods, MetaDistil employs meta learning to explicitly optimize the teacher model for better knowledge transfer ability, and leads to improved performance of the resulting student model.

text: Beyond GLUE-style robustness benchmarks, adversarial stress-testing for sequence labeling has drawn on a wide array of resources and techniques, including perturbation lexicons and counterfactual templates (Kaushik et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021), character-level noise and keyboard-aware edits (Eger et al., 2019; Pruthi et al., 2019), entity replacement using gazetteers and Wikidata-derived aliases (Rahimi et al., 2019; Ghaddar and Langlais, 2018), and cross-domain transfer evaluations spanning OntoNotes, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17, and CrossNER (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Derczynski et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2021; Hovy et al., 2006). In addition to adversarial generation, calibration and uncertainty estimation are closely related to robustness in NER. Temperature scaling and label smoothing have been shown to reduce overconfidence in token classifiers under shift. Data augmentation strategies for NER extend beyond entity swaps to include paraphrasing and back-translation, though these can dilute entity boundary fidelity without careful constraints. Recent work also considers structure-aware perturbations that preserve BIO consistency while varying mention spans.

text: Out-of-Domain Generalization. Generalization in machine learning is often defined as the ability to do well on a test set after learning from a training set, where all examples in both sets are drawn independently from the same distribution (i.i.d. generalization). However, as Gu et al. (2021) argue, in real-world applications such as semantic parsing, the test data may involve new compositional structures (compositional generalization), or new domains (domain generalization) that are not encountered during training. Existing work in compositional generalization for semantic parsing has focused on using synthetic datasets (e.g., Keysers et al., 2020;Lake and Baroni, 2018), or repartitioning existing text-to-SQL datasets into new train and test splits (e.g., Finegan-Dollak et al., 2018). Both approaches have generally shown that compositional generalization remains an important challenge (e.g., Shaw et al., 2021). We focus on the arguably even more challenging domain generalization problem, also known as domain adaptation, where entire domains may never be encountered during training or may only be encountered a small number of times (Motiian et al., 2017). Even though this problem has been studied extensively in the context of classification (Daumé III and Marcu, 2006), machine translation (Daumé III and Jagarlamudi, 2011), and question answering (Talmor and Berant, 2019), it remains underexplored for semantic parsing. However, to be applicable in real scenarios, semantic parsers should be able to generalize to new domains, since collecting domain-specific labeled data is often prohibitively expensive. Recent approaches have focused on data synthesis (Yin et al., 2021), meta-learning (Wang et al., 2021), relation-aware schema encoding (Wang et al., 2020), and encoder pre-training (Yin et al., 2020;Herzig et al., 2020;Yu et al., 2020;Deng et al., 2021), alongside prompt-based finetuning methods for semantic parsing and retrieval-augmented modeling (Liu et al., 2021;Schick and Schütze, 2021;Rajpurkar et al., 2016;Lewis et al., 2020), schema linking strategies such as global graph encoders and relation networks (Guo et al., 2019;Bogin et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020), and data augmentation with paraphrase generation and SQL sketch mining (Iyer et al., 2018;Yu et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2019;Pouran Ben Veyseh et al., 2020). In this paper, we hone in on one aspect of domain generalization that we shall broadly refer to as column operations and which was introduced in §1 and illustrated in Figure .

text: Setting Recent multilingual translation researches suggest that adapting subnetworks for each language or language pair rather than for all of them gives better results. Li et al. (2020) train a shared multilingual model, then select layers for each language pair. Lin et al. (2021) also prune a shared multilingual model for each language pair, but on entries in weight matrices instead. Gong et al. (2021), on the other hand, prune attention heads and feedforward networks for each language. Xie et al. (2021) first identify general and language-specific neurons in a shared multilingual network, then tune those neurons using the data of their corresponding language only. Recent multilingual pruning and adaptation methods vary widely across components and granularity, including layer selection in shared models (Li et al., 2020), entry-wise weight pruning in shared architectures (Lin et al., 2021), attention-head and feedforward pruning tailored per language (Gong et al., 2021), neuron-level identification of general versus language-specific units with language-restricted tuning (Xie et al., 2021), language-specific adapters and routing in multilingual Transformers (Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Bapna and Firat, 2019), cross-lingual transfer with shared subword vocabularies (Conneau and Lample, 2019), mixture-of-experts routing for language specialization (Fedus et al., 2021; Lepikhin et al., 2020), and task-specific sparse fine-tuning for parameter efficiency (Hu et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021). These findings inspire our non-shared pruning setting and to see whether its results on multilingual translation could extend to multilingual pre-training.

text: Data augmentation has been used for resolving artefacts in training datasets before (Gururangan et al., 2018;Srivastava et al., 2020;Kaushik et al., 2021), and related strands include counterfactual augmentation with editing operations (Kaushik et al., 2020), back-translation and noising for robustness (Sennrich et al., 2016;Xie et al., 2020), paraphrase-driven transformation using PPDB and ParaNMT (Ganitkevitch et al., 2013;Wieting and Gimpel, 2018), synonym substitution via WordNet or contextual embeddings (Miller, 1995;Kobayashi, 2018), augmentation for vision-language models using CLIP-derived prompts (Radford et al., 2021;Yuksekgonul et al., 2023), and automated counterfactual generation for sentiment and toxicity (Wang and Culotta, 2021;Madaan et al., 2021;Vidgen et al., 2021;Yang et al., 2021). In particular, previous work (Kaushik et al., 2020) relied on large-scale crowd-sourcing to generate useful augmented data. More recently, , and Wang and Culotta (2021) investigated the efficacy of the automatically generated counterfactuals for sentiment analysis. Similar to our work, these methods also consider the most salient features that a model uses when generating augmented data, which is in line with our rationale definition. However, they use sentiment lexicon matching for identifying rationales, which is task-specific and not necessarily fully relevant. In contrast, we employ human annotators to identify rationales, which can be task-agnostic and robust. Moreover, our method generates semi-factuals instead of counterfactuals used in previous work. Human-the-loop Machine Learning (Wu et al., 2021a) has received increasing research attention. Active learning (Settles, 2009;Margatina et al., 2021), the most common example of human-in-theloop machine learning, asks human annotators only to provide high-level annotations (i.e. labels) for important examples. There is also a growing body of work on human-in-the-loop model steering with feature feedback and explanations across modalities, including local post-hoc methods like LIME and SHAP (Ribeiro et al., 2016;Lundberg and Lee, 2017), concept-based interpretability (Kim et al., 2018;Koh et al., 2020), interactive debugging with explanatory teaching (Kulesza et al., 2015;Cai et al., 2019), rationale supervision in NLP (Lei et al., 2016;Zaidan et al., 2007;DeYoung et al., 2020), and interactive labeling systems that prioritize informative instances (Settles, 2009;Huang et al., 2017;Monarch, 2021;Margatina et al., 2021). Such methods use relatively simple models such as Naïve Bayes (Stumpf et al., 2009;Kulesza et al., 2015) and Linear Regression with bag-of-words features (Jia and Liang, 2017;Teso and Kersting, 2019;Ghai et al., 2021;Shao et al., 2021), because these classifiers are relatively intuitive in generating explanations and amenable to incorporating human feedback. Some other work uses simple neural networks such as multi-layer perceptrons (Shao et al., 2021) and shallow CNNs (Lertvittayakumjorn et al., 2020;Teso et al., 2021) because the predictions of such models can be explained in the form of features. Very recently, Yao et al. (2021) proposed a human-in-the-loop method to inspect more complicated models (e.g. BERT) with the help of some model-agnostic post-hoc explanation algorithms (Ribeiro et al., 2018) that can explain predictions of any linear or non-linear model without exploiting its weights. However, previous work focuses on increasing the explainability of AI systems for high-stake domains such as health and finance, instead of improving the model robustness or generalisation ability. Also, they assume access to a large amount of labelled data. In contrast, we focus on few-shot learning scenarios which are more compelling.

text: The third line, which our work lies in, focus on the redundancy in maintaining a full-length sequence of token-level representation across all encoders (Dai et al., 2020;Wu et al., 2021b;Pietruszka et al., 2020;Ye et al., 2021;Kim and Cho, 2020). This work is particularly inspired by the sequence-level NLP tasks such as text classification and ranking, where the state-of-the-art approach utilizes a single embedding from the top encoder layer of a Transformer, such as the CLS token, for prediction. Under such regime, retaining the full-length sequence till the last encoder creates unnecessary complexity. Dai et al. (2020) applied a simplest strided mean pooling to each sliding window of the sequence to gradually compress tokens. The paper proposed a specialized pre-training procedure for this process that achieves a good balance between speedup and accuracy drop. In comparison we aim to avoid the costly pre-training step and focus on a method that requires only a lightweight fine-tuning. Wu et al. (2021b) define a centroid attention operator that given centroids, computes their embeddings via an attention mechanism. These centroids are chosen either as a random subset of the original tokens, or via strided mean pooling. This results in a similar technique to that of Dai et al. (2020), in terms of having a naive sequence length reduction method. Pietruszka et al. (2020) provide a variant of length 2 strided mean pooling where instead of taking the unweighted average of each pair, they provide learnable weights via a differentiable linear function. In our experiment we did not compare our methods with (Wu et al., 2021b;Pietruszka et al., 2020) since both worked on a limited (non-standard) collection of datasets and at the time of writing this paper, did not provide code allowing us to reproduce their result. Since our paper is focused on techniques to select a subset of tokens and these papers use either random sampling or pooling, we do not believe a thorough comparison is required. Ye et al. (2021) proposed a reinforcement-learning based technique to rank the tokens, thereby allowing it to remove the least important ones. This RL policy must be trained in an expensive process that requires the full network structure. Since we focus on methods to improve both training and inference, we do not include it in our experiments. Vision Transformers (Pan et al., 2021;Heo et al., 2021), which apply various types of pooling techniques to reduce input length, is specially designed for image data and thus non-trivial to compare with our method. Recent works also explore dynamic token pruning, token merging, and adaptive computation in Transformers across diverse tasks and modalities without a unifying methodology or consistent evaluation, including dynamic token sparsification and early exiting for language understanding (Liu et al., 2021;Xin et al., 2020;Schuster et al., 2022), adaptive token selection in ViTs using saliency or learnable gates (Rao et al., 2021;Tang et al., 2022;Bolya et al., 2023), token clustering and token pooling for scalable attention (Goyal et al., 2020;Kitaev et al., 2020;Ainslie et al., 2020), inference-time computation routing and conditional execution (Graves, 2016;Bapna et al., 2018;Elbayad et al., 2020), and hybrid schemes that combine pruning with distillation or quantization (Sanh et al., 2019;Shen et al., 2020;Kurtic et al., 2022). developed an attention based mechanism to progressively eliminate tokens in the intermediate encoders in the fine-tuning, while maintaining the classification accuracy.

text: Few-shot Learning is often tackled by meta learning (Li and Zhang, 2021;Bansal et al., 2020;Sharaf et al., 2020), data augmentation (Arthaud et al., 2021;Wei et al., 2021;Kumar et al., 2019), and prompt-based fine-tuning (Gao et al., 2021;Tam et al., 2021;Schick and Schütze, 2021). Basu et al. (2021) applies contrastive learning in their fewshot semi-supervised intent classification, by using a momentum encoder to stabilize representations under limited labels and consistency regularization across augmented views. Prior work spans multiple paradigms and benchmarks, including prototypical networks (Snell et al., 2017), model-agnostic meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017), relation networks (Sung et al., 2018), MixUp and MetaMix for data augmentation (Zhang et al., 2018; Yoon et al., 2021), PET and iPET for prompt-based classification (Schick and Schütze, 2021), LM-BFF and P-tuning for prompt optimization (Gao et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021), CLIP-style contrastive alignment for vision-language transfer (Radford et al., 2021), and evaluation on MiniImageNet, CIFAR-FS, FewRel, and SuperGLUE few-shot tracks. Despite this diversity, methodological choices often hinge on the target modality, the granularity of labels, and the availability of unlabeled data. Meta-learning methods emphasize episodic training to mimic test-time scarcity and reduce distribution shift between train and test episodes. Data augmentation approaches synthesize task-preserving perturbations to increase coverage of the input space and regularize decision boundaries. Prompt-based methods instead reframe classification as masked token prediction, relying on template design and verbalizers to bridge label spaces to language model vocabularies. In intent classification, label semantics and domain shift exacerbate the brittleness of handcrafted templates and verbalizers. Semi-supervised contrastive objectives help by shaping the representation geometry such that positive pairs cluster while negatives disperse, leveraging unlabeled utterances. However, contrastive learning can underperform when the temperature or queue size induces excessive collapse or when positive sampling does not reflect task-specific invariances. Recent studies incorporate pseudo-label refinement and agreement-based filtering to curtail confirmation bias in low-resource regimes. Others focus on calibration, noting that few-shot predictors are often overconfident, particularly under domain transfer or class imbalance. Evaluation practices vary widely, with differences in episode composition, prompt initialization, and hyperparameter budgets complicating fair comparison. Robust benchmarking has thus emphasized fixed seeds, standardized splits, and reporting across multiple sample draws to capture variance. We follow this perspective by adopting consistent episodes, shared tokenization, and hyperparameter ranges across baselines. Additionally, we analyze sensitivity to prompt templates and verbalizers to clarify whether gains stem from representation learning or label-space engineering. Finally, we discuss compute-accuracy trade-offs, since episodic pretraining and large prompt-tuned backbones can be prohibitive in practical deployments. Our introduction frames the landscape needed to interpret the empirical results reported later and to understand the design constraints implicit in low-label intent classification.

text: Other methods use parallel corpus in multilingual pre-training. XLM (Conneau and Lample, 2019) introduces a Translation Language Model (TLM) based on the parallel corpus which shows significant improvement on downstream tasks. Unicoder (Huang et al., 2019) introduces a multitask learning framework to learn cross-lingual representations with monolingual and parallel corpora, achieving further gains. ALM (Yang et al., 2020) allows the model to learn cross-lingual code-switch sentences, enhancing the transfer ability. Recent studies INFOXLM (Chi et al., 2021), HICTL , VECO  and ERNIE-M (Ouyang et al., 2021) use contrastive learning, back translation and other tricks further enhancing the performance of the multilingual model. Our work focus on studying the model only with multilingual MLM, and leave the study of works with parallel data as future work.

text: Pre-trained Representation in TTS. It is believed that prosody can also be inferred from language information in both current and surrounding utterances (Shen et al., 2018;Fang et al., 2019;. Such information is often entailed in vector representations from a pre-trained LM, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). Some existing work incorporated BERT embeddings at word or subword-level into autoregressive TTS models (Shen et al., 2018;Fang et al., 2019).More recent work  used the chunked and paired sentence patterns from BERT. Besides, a relational gated graph network with pretrained BERT embeddings as node inputs  was used to extract word-level semantic representations, thus enhancing expressiveness. Recent advances in self-supervised learning for speech and text provide complementary contextual cues that have been leveraged in TTS pipelines in various ways without a unified perspective on design choices or limitations, including the use of phoneme-aligned contextualized embeddings for prosody conditioning (Kharitonov et al., 2021;Tsai et al., 2021), hierarchical discourse-aware encoders to capture inter-utterance dependencies (Li et al., 2022;Zhang et al., 2022), cross-modal adapters that fuse ASR pretraining with TTS decoders (Huang et al., 2022;Chen et al., 2023), semantic prosody prediction from large language models (Kreuk et al., 2023;Ronneberger et al., 2023), and multi-scale prompting strategies derived from instruction-tuned LMs (Wang et al., 2023;Sun et al., 2024).

text: However, these methods have not been commonly studied for NLP tasks and do not consider the performance metrics during training. Recent work considers a wide range of stopping heuristics across domains including computer vision and speech, with approaches such as Bayesian early stopping based on marginal likelihood approximations (MacKay, 1992; Graves, 2011; Duvenaud et al., 2016), gradient-noise-based criteria and uncertainty-aware schedules (Smith and Le, 2018; Mandt et al., 2017; Welling and Teh, 2011), geometry- and curvature-informed rules (Sagun et al., 2017; Dinh et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2019), and dimensionality or compression indicators tied to representation dynamics (Amsaleg et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2018; Achille and Soatto, 2018; Pope et al., 2020). Furthermore, comparisons among the non-validation stopmethods have not been reported. In this study, we compare our method with the EB, LID, PE, and validation-based stopping methods on five text classification datasets. text: Many recent studies use external knowledge to improve the ERC performance. KET (Zhong et al., 2019) is used as external knowledge based on ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017) and emotion lexicon NRC_VAD (Mohammad, 2018) as the commonsense knowledge. ConceptNet is a knowledge graph that connects words and phrases in natural language using labeled edges. NRC_VAD Lexicon has human ratings of valence, arousal, and dominance for more than 20,000 English words. COSMIC (Ghosal et al., 2020) and Psychological (Li et al., 2021) improve the performance of emotion recognition by extracting commonsense knowledge of the previous utterances. Commonsense knowledge feature is extracted and leveraged with COMET (Bosselut et al., 2019) trained with ATOMIC (The Atlas of Machine Commonsense) . ATOMIC has 9 sentence relation types with inferential if-then commonsense knowledge expressed in text. ToDKAT (Zhu et al., 2021) improves performance by combining commonsense knowledge using COMET and topic discovery using VHRED (Serban et al., 2017) to the model. Recent efforts span knowledge-augmented encoders and generative inference over commonsense graphs, including KET (Zhong et al., 2019), COSMIC (Ghosal et al., 2020), Psychological (Li et al., 2021), and ToDKAT (Zhu et al., 2021), as well as auxiliary resources such as ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017), NRC_VAD (Mohammad, 2018), COMET (Bosselut et al., 2019), and ATOMIC (Sap et al., 2019), alongside topic-aware models like VHRED (Serban et al., 2017) and dialogue benchmarks MELD (Poria et al., 2019) and IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), with related conversational modeling advances reported in Zhang et al. (2018a), Zhou et al. (2018), Rashkin et al. (2018), and Majumder et al. (2019).

In general, the multi-party conversations have higher speaker dependency than the dyadic-party dialogues, therefore have more conditions to consider and result in poor performance. Zhou et al. EDA (Bothe et al., 2020) expands the multi-modal emotion datasets by extracting dialog acts from MELD and IEMOCAP and finds out that there is a correlation between dialogue acts and emotion labels. Parallel lines of work in multimodal and dialogue modeling include MELD (Poria et al., 2019), IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), ICON (Hazarika et al., 2018a), EmoryNLP (Zahiri and Choi, 2018), dyadic baselines (Hazarika et al., 2018b; Zadeh et al., 2017), multi-party architectures (Jiao et al., 2020; Ghosal et al., 2020), commonsense-driven systems (Zhou et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018a; Bosselut et al., 2019), and augmentation or discourse-oriented methods (Bothe et al., 2020; Rashkin et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), together with resources such as ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017) and NRC_VAD (Mohammad, 2018), and pre-trained encoders including BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019).

text: Injecting Structured Knowledge into LMs. Conceptually, our work is most related to recent work on knowledge injection into PLMs. Know-BERT (Peters et al., 2019) connects entities in text and KGs via an entity linker and then recontextualizes BERT representations conditioned on the KG embeddings, KG-BERT (Yao et al., 2019) trains BERT directly on knowledge triples by linearizing entities and relations into a sequence and predicting plausibility, Wang et al. (2021a) refine scoring with a dual/Siamese architecture over split subject–relation and object encodings, ERNIE (Zhang et al., 2019) integrates entity embeddings during pretraining to inject factual signals, KEPLER (Wang et al., 2021b) jointly learns textual and knowledge embeddings with a knowledge embedding loss, and K-Adapter (Wang et al., 2021c) attaches lightweight adapters trained on factual and linguistic tasks to BERT to encode external knowledge without full retraining, while E-BERT (Poerner et al., 2020) aligns entity and word embeddings to infuse encyclopedic information. KG-BERT (Yao et al., 2019) trains BERT directly on knowledge triples by linearizing their entities and relations into a sequence and predicting plausibility of the sequence. Wang et al. (2021a) improve KG-BERT by splitting a subject-relation-object knowledge triple into a subject-relation pair representation and an object entity representation, then modeling their similarities with a dual/Siamese neural network. While prior studies have focused on incorporating monolingual (English) structured knowledge into PLMs, our work focuses on connecting knowledge in many languages, allowing knowledge in each language to be transferred and collectively enriched. We center our investigation on practical mechanisms that align text and graph signals without sacrificing multilingual coverage. Our approach emphasizes scalable training objectives that respect both entity disambiguation and relation semantics across scripts. We further consider robustness to entity drift and ontology mismatch observed in evolving KGs. The proposed framework targets high-recall retrieval of candidate facts before controlled injection. We also analyze the trade-offs between adapter-based and full finetuning regimes. Finally, we outline evaluation protocols for knowledge-centric multilingual tasks.

text: KB Completion and Construction. Before PLMs, rule-based systems and multi-staged information extraction pipelines were typically used for automatic KB construction (Auer et al., 2007;Fabian et al., 2007;Hoffart et al., 2013;Dong et al., 2014). However, such methods require expensive human effort for rule or feature creation (Carlson et al., 2010;Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014), or they rely on (semi-)structured corpora with easy-to-consume formats (Lehmann et al., 2015). Petroni et al. (2019) showed that modern PLMs such as BERT could also be used as KBs: querying PLMs with fill-in-the-blank-style queries, a substantial amount of factual knowledge can be extracted. This in turn provides an efficient way to address the challenges of traditional KB methods. Jiang et al. (2020) and Kassner et al. (2021) extended the idea to extracting knowledge from multilingual PLMs. DBpedia Spotlight (Mendes et al., 2011) provides entity linking over DBpedia, TAGME (Ferragina and Scaiella, 2010) enables on-the-fly annotation of short texts, REL (van Hulst et al., 2020) offers a modular neural pipeline, BLINK (Wu et al., 2020) introduces bi-encoder and cross-encoder ranking for large-scale linking, mGENRE (De Cao et al., 2021) performs multilingual constrained generation for disambiguation, Wikidata5M (Wang et al., 2021d) supplies large-scale entity–text alignments, T-REx (Elsahar et al., 2018) curates relation-centric extractions, and WikiHop (Welbl et al., 2018) targets multi-hop reasoning across documents. Work in monolingual settings closest to ours is COMET (Bosselut et al., 2019): Prix-LM can be seen as an extension of this idea to multilingual and cross-lingual setups. Prix-LM's crucial property is that it enables knowledge population by transferring complementary structured knowledge across languages. This can substantially enrich (limited) prior knowledge also in monolingual KBs. In another line of work, multilingual KG embeddings (Chen et al., 2017Sun et al., 2020aSun et al., , 2021 were developed to support cross-KG knowledge alignment and link prediction. Such methods produce a unified embedding space that allows link prediction in a target KG based on the aligned prior knowledge in other KGs (Chen et al., 2020). Research on multilingual KG embeddings has made rapid progress recently, e.g., see the survey of Sun et al. (2020b). However, these methods focus on a closed-world scenario and are unable to leverage open-world knowledge from natural language texts. Prix-LM combines the best of both worlds and is able to capture and combine knowledge from (multilingual) KGs and multilingual texts.

text: Prior work on nested named entity recognition has largely centered on English and German benchmarks with a mix of classical sequence labeling and span-based formulations, including ACE-2004 and ACE-2005 (Doddington et al., 2004; Walker et al., 2006), GENIA for biomedical entities (Kim et al., 2003; Ohta et al., 2002), OntoNotes-style conversions for nested spans (Pradhan et al., 2013; Finkel and Manning, 2009), and fine-grained resources such as NNE (Ringland et al., 2019) and NoSta-D (Benikova et al., 2014), alongside multilingual efforts like WikiAnn (Pan et al., 2017) and cross-lingual transfer via mBERT and XLM-R (Devlin et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020).

text: Methodologically, nested structures have been addressed through hypergraph models (Lu and Roth, 2015), layered CRFs (Ju et al., 2018), region-based or span classification (Sohrab and Miwa, 2018; Wang et al., 2020), constituency-inspired parsers (Finkel and Manning, 2009), sequence-to-nugget decoders (Zhang et al., 2020), and transition systems (Wang and Lu, 2018), with pre-trained encoders such as BERT, SpanBERT, and SciBERT (Devlin et al., 2019; Joshi et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2019), as well as datasets spanning legal, news, and biomedical domains (GENIA; ACE-2005; LitBank; NoSta-D).

text: A broad body of work on contrastive representation learning has emerged across modalities and tasks, including instance discrimination and momentum encoders for visual representations (Wu et al., 2018; He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2020b), alignment-based objectives for multilingual sentence embeddings (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019; Feng et al., 2020; Reimers and Gurevych, 2020; Yang et al., 2020), mutual-information estimators and InfoNCE-style bounds (Hjelm et al., 2019; Poole et al., 2019; Oord et al., 2018; Tschannen et al., 2020), and hard-negative mining strategies in dense retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2021; Zhan et al., 2021; Qu et al., 2021).

text: Our contributions add to a large body of work on grounded representation learning. Much of this work augments language modeling objectives with images (Silberer and Lapata, 2012;Lazaridou et al., 2015;Kiela et al., 2017) and videos (Sun et al., 2019). In this work, we focus on representations that encode verb semantics. Prior work on verb learning has been conducted in the computer vision community, typically described as "humanobject interactions" (Regneri et al., 2013;Chao et al., 2018;Ji et al., 2019). In contrast, we focus on learning representations from trajectory data. We are not aware of any prior work that attempts to learn verb semantics from trajectory data. However, prior work in grounded language learning focuses on reasoning about objects through space and time in text (Aroca-Ouellette et al., 2021) and grounding to 3D objects with varying rotation (Thomas, 2019). Outside of NLP, models have been trained on trajectory data for applications like human motion path forecasting (Giuliari et al., 2021) and human activity recognition (Wang et al., 2018). Recent multimodal grounding approaches integrate contrastive objectives, masked modeling, and alignment losses across text, image, audio, and video, with large-scale datasets enabling pretraining at web scale (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Bain et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022; Zellers et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2021), while compositional generalization and structured grounding have been explored via synthetic benchmarks and neuro-symbolic pipelines (Lake and Baroni, 2018; Johnson et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2019; Hudson and Manning, 2019; Bahdanau et al., 2019; Nye et al., 2021; Yi et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2019). Our work lies at the intersection of grounded language learning and spatiotemporal machine learning, using representations of trajectory data to study verb semantics. We situate our method relative to prior grounded language research by emphasizing temporal reasoning and motion-centric cues. Specifically, we concentrate on the mapping between discrete linguistic predicates and continuous kinematic traces. This focus allows us to examine action granularity beyond categorical labels tied to static visual frames. We also explore whether trajectory-derived embeddings capture relational structure among verbs. To that end, we evaluate lexical and event similarity judgments using movement-based features. Finally, we discuss the implications of trajectory alignment for context-sensitive verb interpretation. We conclude by outlining how spatiotemporal priors can complement text-only distributional learning.

text: In the case of implicit relations between EDUs without clear connectives, it is crucial to introduce sequential information from the context to resolve ambiguity. Feng and Hirst (2014) rely on linearchain CRF with traditional feature engineering to make use of the sequential characteristics of the context for discourse constituent parsing. However, they greedily build up the discourse structure and relations from bottom up. At each timestep, they apply the CRF to obtain the locally optimized structure and relation. In this way, the model assigns relation gradually along with the construction of the parsing tree from bottom up, but only limited contextual information from the top level of the partially constructed tree can be used to predict relations. Besides, at each time-step, they sequentially assign relations to top nodes of the partial tree, without being aware that those nodes might represent different levels of discourse units (e.g. EDUs, sentences, or even paragraphs). In contrast, we explicitly train our sequence labeling models on both intra-and inter-sentential levels after a complete discourse tree is constructed so that we can infer from the whole context with a clear intention of capturing different writing patterns occurring at intra-and inter-sentential levels. Recent neural and hybrid discourse parsers explore multi-granular architectures and contextualized encoders across corpora and settings (Li et al., 2014; Ji and Eisenstein, 2015; Braud et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Kobayashi et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Gessler et al., 2021), and complementary lines of work have examined EDU representation learning with BERT-like models and sequence labeling strategies for relation identification (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Nie et al., 2020; Nguyen and Joty, 2020; Kishimoto et al., 2020; Shi and Demberg, 2019; Huber and Carenini, 2020; Xu et al., 2021), along with evaluations on RST-DT, STAC, GUM, and TED-MDB that report incremental gains from hierarchical modeling and context-sensitive features (Carlson et al., 2001; Asher et al., 2016; Zeldes, 2017; Zeyrek et al., 2020).

text: Disentangled Representation Learning Recently, there has been a growing amount of work on learning disentangled latent representations in NLP tasks (Zhang et al., 2019;Hu et al., 2017;Yin et al., 2018). In this aspect, the most related work to our syntax-semantics decoupling method is the vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) model proposed by Chen et al. (2019). It is a generative model using two latent variables to represent semantics and syntax of the sentence, developed for monolingual setting and trained with paraphrases. It uses paraphrase reconstruction loss and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word order information for syntactic representations. Recent cross-lingual MRC efforts explore translation-based augmentation, multilingual pre-training, and alignment supervision across typologically diverse languages without a unified protocol (Artetxe et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Asai et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2021). We adapt this model to multilingual syntax-semantics disentanglement. We use bilingual sentence pairs to train our model with a cross-lingual reconstruction loss and semantic discrimination loss. To better disentangle semantics from complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce two additional syntax-related losses for incorporating POS tags and syntax trees.

text: Multiple efforts have looked into defining, measuring, and mitigating biases in NLP models (Sun et al., 2019;Mehrabi et al., 2019a;Sheng et al., 2021). Dwork et al. (2012) present foundational notions of fairness that motivate later operationalizations in machine learning and NLP. Multiple recent works also focus on developing new dataset and associated metrics to capture various types of biases. Recent advances catalog a wide array of datasets, measurement protocols, and mitigation strategies spanning contextualized embeddings, pre-trained language models, and multimodal systems, including WEAT and related association tests (Caliskan et al., 2017; May et al., 2019), Bias-in-Bios and occupation-level audits (De-Arteaga et al., 2019a), StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs for sentence-level stereotype sensitivity (Nadeem et al., 2021; Nangia et al., 2020), regard and toxicity-based probes (Sheng et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018), intrinsic embedding debiasing and hard de-bias methods (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018), causal and counterfactual data augmentation (Zhao et al., 2018; Maudslay et al., 2019), bias-toxicity correlations in generation (Gehman et al., 2020), metric learning perspectives on fairness (Speicher et al., 2018), and large-scale audits of toxic generation in open-ended dialogue (Dinan et al., 2020). For example, Nangia et al. (2020) propose dataset and metrics to measure social biases and stereotypes in language model generations, Bolukbasi et al. (2016); Caliskan et al. (2017); Manzini et al. (2019) define metrics to access gender and race biases in word vector representations, and recent vision-language studies define metrics to quantify and mitigate biases in visual recognition task. Ethayarajh (2020) propose Bernstein bounds to represent uncertainty about the bias. Majority of these bias metrics are automatically computed, for example, using a regard classifier (Sheng et al., 2019), sentiment classifier, toxicity classifier (Dixon et al., 2018) or true positive rate difference between privileged and underprivileged groups (De-Arteaga et al., 2019b). A few works additionally validate the alignment of these automatically computed bias metrics with human understanding of biases by collecting annotations of biases on a subset of test data from crowdworkers (Sheng et al., 2019). Blodgett et al. (2020) discuss the limitations of several of these bias datasets and measurements, emphasizing construct validity and socio-linguistic context. However, the majority of existing bias metrics are specific to the model type and the application domain used, they may not be tested for correlation with human judgement of biases, and their relationship to existing definitions of fairness has not been explored. Additionally, metrics such as true positive or error difference between groups requires ground truth labels, thereby making their computation in real-time systems difficult. Speicher et al. (2018) have attempted to present unified approach to measuring group and individual fairness via inequality indices, however we note that such metrics are non-trivial to extend to unstructured data such as text. For example, gender information in a text may be subtle (e.g. mention of softball) and it is unclear whether presence of this word should be considered to impact the genderness of the text. Prior work on counterfactual fairness in text further highlights the importance of lexical and syntactic perturbations for isolating sensitive attributes (Garg et al., 2019; Maudslay et al., 2019). Contextualized encoders exhibit bias amplification under domain shift, complicating cross-domain evaluation protocols (Zmigrod et al., 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020). Post-processing calibrations can alter group-level rates without improving semantic fairness, creating evaluation blind spots (Pleiss et al., 2017; Chouldechova, 2017). Accumulated prediction sensitivity metric, presented in this paper, attempts to address all the above limitations of existing bias metrics. We acknowledge that the proposed metric is yet to be associated with other notions of fairness (e.g. preference based notion of fairness (Zafar et al., 2017)).
